This study investigates the multi-layer brine system of southern Laizhou Bay, the world’s only coastal brine district under large-scale commercial extraction, using Cl− concentrations and Br/Cl ratios from 129 leachate-reconstructed porewater samples across eight boreholes, combined with major ion time-series data from three sampling campaigns spanning non-pumping and pumping periods. The results reveal systematic geochemical contrasts between the eastern and western sectors, with all eastern samples yielding Br/Cl below the seawater reference value, whereas 75% of western samples exceed this threshold, with the maximum reaching more than twice this value. Multi-ion ratio analysis excludes evaporite dissolution and freeze-concentration, indicating that western porewaters retain a relict signal from a stage when the original brine had approached halite saturation, despite subsequent dilution. Time-series comparison shows that lateral freshwater infiltration during pumping periods produces spatially variable but ultimately reversible effects on ion ratio patterns; aquitard porewaters consistently yield higher Br/Cl than coeval aquifer samples, indicating more effective preservation of the original signal. This spatial heterogeneity reflects differential sedimentary evolution under the regional tectonic framework of western subsidence and eastern uplift: sufficient initial salt supply and superior aquitard confinement in the west preserved the evaporative signal, whereas the east is disadvantaged in both respects. Combining porewater and aquifer Br/Cl with multi-ion ratios and time-series data provides a reliable framework for brine genesis discrimination in long-term intensively exploited coastal settings.

title: Hydrogeochemical response of Fe-enriched saturated soils to controlled mechanical disturbance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Szymon Świątek, Konrad Proczek, Karolina Lewińska
abstract: Earthquakes and mechanical disturbances can modify groundwater and soil geochemistry by altering redox conditions, fluid redistribution, and mineral–water interactions. However, the coupled physicochemical mechanisms controlling these changes remain insufficiently understood, particularly in Fe-rich saturated systems. This study investigates the hydrogeochemical response of saturated soil–water columns subjected to controlled low-amplitude mechanical disturbance under varying water mineralization and contrasting iron amendments: a reactive Fe(II)-rich system represented by ferrous sulfate (FeSO4) and a comparatively stable Fe(III)-oxyhydroxide system represented by goethite (FeOOH). Over a 12-month incubation experiment, changes in pH, redox potential (Eh), and dissolved Fe, Mn, and Al concentrations were monitored before and after vibration treatment. The strongest physicochemical response occurred in FeSO4-amended systems, where initially acidic conditions (pH < 3.1) evolved toward progressive stabilization during incubation. Mechanical disturbance induced rapid but temporary increases in pH, accompanied by pronounced decreases in Eh and transient peaks in dissolved Fe and Mn concentrations, particularly in low- and medium-mineralized waters. In contrast, FeOOH-amended systems displayed comparatively stable pH–Eh conditions and weaker metal mobilization. The experiment also produced liquefaction-related soft-sediment deformation features, including injection structures, disturbed lamination, Fe-rich bands, and nodular accumulations. The observed pH–Eh evolution is interpreted as the result of coupled physical–geochemical processes involving pore-water redistribution, microscale redox mixing, Fe2+ oxidation, oxygen consumption, Fe(III)-oxyhydroxide precipitation, CO2 degassing, and buffering reactions. Although the experiment represents a controlled laboratory model rather than a direct field-scale earthquake analogue, the observed hydrogeochemical trends are consistent with transient pH–Eh anomalies and Fe–Mn mobilization reported from natural post-seismic groundwater systems. The study provides a process-oriented framework for understanding how mechanically disturbed Fe-rich saturated environments may respond to changing redox conditions and repeated physical perturbation.

title: Hydrogeochemical assessment and vulnerability analysis of mountain springs in a karstic water system in northeastern Italy
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Mauro Masiol, Maria Battistel, Lucio D’Alberto, Marianna D’Amico, Giovanni Mario, Raffaele Marciano, Giuliano Dreossi, Alessandro Pozzobon, Barbara Stenni
abstract: Mountain springs are essential freshwater resources for both communities and ecosystems, but they are increasingly threatened by climate variability and human pressure. This study investigates the vulnerability and recharge dynamics of two springs (LAR and CAN) in the Cansiglio Massif karst system (NE Italy). The novelty of this work lies in applying an integrated hydrogeological, hydrogeochemical, isotopic, and vulnerability-based framework to two springs in the foothills of a main karst system, showing how multiple complementary techniques can support the definition of recharge areas and protection zones even for small sources that remain essential for local water-supply management. Monitoring (September 2018 to September 2021) shows that recharge likely originates from the Mt. Pizzoc area and follows structurally and topographically controlled pathways toward the springs. Results reveal a dual recharge regime: rapid infiltration through fractured and karstified carbonates and coarse slope deposits, and slower, laterally redistributed flow where marly-silty-clayey layers hinder vertical percolation. A simplified water budget constrained the minimum and net recharge areas, while isotope-elevation relationships estimated mean recharge elevations of about 732–879 m a.s.l. for LAR and 617–767 m a.s.l. for CAN. Hydrological patterns and vulnerability indicators show that CAN responds much faster and is far more vulnerable (VESPA V = 14–38.7; MDHT 1–4 days) than LAR (VESPA V = 0.36–0.77; MDHT 9–22 days). By combining multiple approaches, this integrated framework offers practical support for identifying protection priorities, especially in shallow and highly responsive mountain spring catchments.

title: A pore-scale hydraulic conductivity model for frozen saturated soils incorporating wall-first and center-first freezing mechanisms
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Xinye Song, Sai K. Vanapalli, Junping Ren
abstract: Hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils exhibits strong nonlinearity with temperature due to progressive changes in pore-scale liquid connectivity. To capture this behavior, a physically based hydraulic conductivity model for frozen soils is developed within a freezing-modified capillary-bundle framework that represents the potential coexistence of wall-first and center-first freezing mechanisms. An effective pore radius is derived to reflect both the volumetric distribution of unfrozen water and the geometry of hydraulically active pore classes. The model is parameterized directly from the soil freezing characteristic curve (SFCC), providing a physics-consistent link between temperature, unfrozen water content, and pore-scale flow properties. A machine-learning model based on a weighted ensemble of Transformer architecture and XGBoost is developed to estimate SFCCs from basic soil properties to facilitate its use when measured SFCC information is unavailable. The measured or estimated SFCCs serve as inputs to the proposed pore-scale saturated hydraulic conductivity model. The proposed model was validated against independent experimental datasets covering a wide range of soil textures and testing methods. Predictions show strong agreement with measured hydraulic conductivity over several orders of magnitude and successfully reproduce the observed nonlinear dependence on temperature and unfrozen water content. The results indicate that accurate prediction of hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils requires information of both unfrozen water content and pore-scale freezing geometry. Overall, the proposed framework provides a robust and scalable approach for predicting the hydraulic conductivity of saturated frozen soils in cold regions.

title: Attention-based terrestrial heat flow reconstruction across the Tibetan Plateau: Insights into tectono-thermal coupling, hydrothermal activities, and geothermal targets
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yingchun Wang, Yi Wang, Haiwen Chen, Xintian Li, Yuhe Fan, Yinlei Hao, Jiao Tian
abstract: Accurate identification of the spatial distribution pattern of terrestrial heat flow (HF) in the Tibetan Plateau is crucial for geodynamic research and geothermal resource development. In this study, the TabPFN (Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network) model was used for HF prediction in the Tibetan Plateau, a tectonically complex and data-sparse region. By integrating 13 geological and geophysical features, the model has been trained and evaluated on three spatial scales: global, Tibetan Plateau and its surroundings, and the Tibetan Plateau itself. The performance comparison with other three mature machine learning algorithms (GBRT, DNN, SVM) reveal that, at the global scale, TabPFN achieved the highest predictive performance (R2 = 0.963). Additional statistical validation and spatial block cross-validation further confirmed the robustness and spatial generalization capability of the model. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis is further used to interpret model decisions, and the key controls on geothermal distribution are pointed out: plate tectonic boundaries, topography, gravity mean curvature, and Moho depth. These predictions successfully reproduced known thermal anomaly zones, such as the Yarlung Zangbo Suture (YZS), with average heat flow values of ∼ 90 mW/m2 and local anomalies exceeding 120 mW/m2, while also uncovering new patterns, including northeastward extensions and continuous distributions along faults in the southeastern margin. Three geothermal potential areas are delineated, each dominated by normal, strike-slip, or thrust faulting, reflecting the coupling among heat flow anomalies, active tectonics, and hydrothermal springs. A prioritized list of ten counties (e.g., Bangor, Seni, Shenzha, Gonghe, Damxung) defines the potential exploration targets. The results construct a high-resolution prior thermal field and provide direct guidance for geothermal exploration.

title: Hierarchical water partitioning across different scales in sloped field: evidenced by soil pore water isotopic signatures
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Jinzhuo Li, Xianwen Li, Mo Li, Liu Liu, Xiaorong Wei, Yaxian Hu
abstract: Soil pore water is like blood cycling in soil and plant system. However, beyond enrichment or depletion in bulk water content, we know little about how the heterogeneous turnover rates of soil water in differently sized pores affect or are affected by slope-scale water cycling. In this study, a Mollisol was collected from the Upper, Middle and Lower position along a typical rolling slope. At each position, bulk soil cores were sampled from three depths (10, 20, and 45 cm), and respectively centrifuged to step-wisely collect soil water stored in five differently sized pores. After comparing the stable isotopic signatures of H and O (δ2H and δ18O) in each soil pore water, we observed that: (1) On average, > 83.5% of soil water was stored in pores < 6 μm, with stronger predominance at the Lower slope position and 45 cm deep. (2) Pore water δ2H and δ18O decreased with slope positions and depth, jointly resulting in enhanced Deuterium excess (d-excess) by 5.67‰ at the Lower slope position and by 3.56‰ at 45 cm deep. (3) Pore water δ2H and δ18O generally increased as pores became finer, and the d-excess maximized at 5.13‰ in Mesopores but minimized at –0.7‰ in Fine pores. The heterogeneous isotopic signatures and d-excess suggested that soil pore water did not cycle at the same rate but much more slowly in finer pores, resulting in much more advanced evaporative fractionation in smaller pores. Soil pores restructuring along the slope and profile, together with unequal evaporative fractionation and infiltration recharge, may have collectively contributed to the enhanced d-excess at Lower slope position and deeper layer. This is the first pore-scale evidence to decipher how water was partitioned across different spatial scales along hillslopes.

title: Global patterns and declines of precipitation persistence over the past six decades
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yunqiu Zhou, Xiuyu Liang, Tzung-May Fu, Yi Zheng, Lian Feng, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Precipitation persistence influences how long wet or dry conditions last, influencing drought and flood risks, water resource planning, and agricultural stability. Yet its global distribution and long-term evolution remain poorly known. Using six decades of daily ERA5 reanalysis, together with independent comparisons with GHCN, GPCC and HOAPS/GPCC datasets over their available periods, we show that precipitation persistence, quantified by the temporal “memory” exponent (βP ) in spectral analysis, displays strong spatial heterogeneity and a widespread decline under a 5-year moving window. Precipitation persistence is highest over tropical and subtropical continents and lowest over mid-latitude oceans. Meanwhile, βP correlates positively with the duration of wet and dry spells and with potential precipitation predictability (PPP). Cross-dataset comparisons further show decreasing tendencies in domain-mean βP over the common periods and valid domains of GPCC and HOAPS/GPCC, although the strong tropical belt-like decline in ERA5 is not consistently reproduced by independent products. These results suggest that spectral βP provides a useful diagnostic of precipitation temporal organization, and that weakening persistence may imply more fragmented precipitation variability with potential implications for hydrological forecasting and water resource management.

title: Seasonal river-level fluctuations regulate riparian nitrate removal through coupled hydrologic exchange and redox dynamics
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Jiaxin Chen, Huiqiang Wu, Zhenbiao Xie, Chunhui Lu
abstract: Riparian zones function as dynamic biogeochemical reactors that can attenuate river-borne nitrate, yet the role of seasonal river-level fluctuations in regulating this process remains poorly constrained. Here, we develop an idealized two-dimensional, coupled variably saturated flow and reactive transport model to examine how seasonal hydrologic dynamics control nitrate attenuation in riparian zones. The model resolves transient hyporheic exchange and simulates reactive transport of dissolved organic carbon, dissolved oxygen, nitrate, and ammonium under constant river-water chemistry. Results show that seasonal river-level fluctuations substantially modify the spatiotemporal dynamics of nitrate removal by regulating hydrologic exchange, solute delivery, and redox zonation within riparian aquifers. Sensitivity analyses indicate that net nitrate removal increases with fluctuation amplitude and sediment permeability because stronger exchange enhances river-water infiltration and expands denitrification hotspots, and that nitrate removal is greater under losing-river conditions than under gaining-river conditions. By contrast, the fraction of nitrate removed relative to the river-derived nitrate input is controlled primarily by carbon availability, as represented by the DOC concentration of the infiltrating river water. These results suggest that, under the modeled conditions, seasonal hydrologic forcing plays an important role in riparian nitrate attenuation by coupling flow dynamics with redox evolution, and that hydrologic exchange intensity and carbon availability play distinct roles in regulating total nitrate removed and percent nitrate removed.

title: Pore-scale sedimentary architecture controls the emergence and constitutive scaling of asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Kuldeep Singh, Alexander Miller, Lichun Wang
abstract: This study demonstrates that the magnitude and spatial organization of pore-scale heterogeneity jointly govern the emergence of asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion in porous media. Two-dimensional digitally constructed pore networks representing graded, laminated, and random sedimentary architectures were generated with systematically varied heterogeneity index σ g . Flow and solute transport simulations were performed over longitudinal domains exceeding 20 cm across multiple Péclet numbers to quantify the evolution from pre-asymptotic to asymptotic transport behavior. Results show that spatial architectural organization—rather than the magnitude of heterogeneity alone—exerts a first-order control on emergent continuum-transport behavior. Bulk velocity variance remained comparatively insensitive to σ g , yet the asymptotic hydrodynamic dispersion coefficient and accompanying longitudinal dispersivity varied by orders of magnitude following the hierarchy laminated > graded > random, reflecting how spatially coherent velocity segregation imposed by sedimentary architecture governs emergent continuum-transport behavior. In the graded and laminated architectures, both transport metrics increased exponentially with σ g , while the laminated architecture additionally exhibited power-law relationships with the permeability contrast between coarse and fine sediment layers, defining architecture-specific constitutive relationships absent in random architectures. The transition length to asymptotic Fickian transport depended on both sedimentary architecture and σ g , exhibiting only a weak dependence on the Péclet number in the laminated and graded domains. In contrast, the relative increase from early-time to asymptotic dispersion showed no systematic Péclet number dependence, indicating primary structural control. Once asymptotic conditions were reached, longitudinal dispersivity became independent of the Péclet number, consistent with classical hydrodynamic dispersion theory. Asymptotic dispersivity values reproduced both the magnitude and vertical scatter of compiled field dispersivity–length datasets, supporting the interpretation that much of the observed field-scale variability at a given length likely reflects the impact of geological architectural heterogeneity rather than measurement uncertainty.

title: Global plateau regions face rapid groundwater loss
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Dong Wang, Bo-Hui Tang, Menghua Li, Guokun Chen, Dong Fan, Junyi Chen, Liang Huang, Xingming Zhu, Zhiwei He, Lei Wei, Fangliang Cai, Zhao-Liang Li
abstract: Plateaus, which host numerous glaciers, are recognized as critical reservoirs of global groundwater storage (GWS). Although GWS has been widely investigated at regional and global scales, a comprehensive assessment of GWS dynamics across global plateau regions (GPR) remains lacking. Here, GWS anomalies across GPR were reconstructed from 2002 to 2022 using GRACE and GRACE-FO observations combined with GLDAS-derived hydrological components. The reconstructed GWS was further validated against the Mascon solution and an independent GWS product, demonstrating strong consistency among different datasets. The results reveal that GWS in global plateaus has been undergoing an accelerating decline, accompanied by pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in both amplitude and phase. On average, plateau regions have experienced a GWS decline of −0.213 ± 0.027 cm/yr, with the steepest reductions recorded in North America (−0.816 ± 0.061 cm/yr) and Europe (−0.579 ± 0.085 cm/yr). In contrast, major high-altitude lakes exhibit a modest increase in water storage (0.103 ± 0.03 cm/yr), thereby partially compensating for groundwater declines. Our findings provide new insights into GWS dynamics across GPR and offer scientific support for sustainable groundwater management under ongoing climate change.

title: Deep learning-based precipitation nowcasting integrating radar echoes and rain gauge data
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Leijing Li, Jianzhu Li, Yongtao Wang, Chongju Shang, Zhixia Li, Jin Liu
abstract: For flood protection and disaster mitigation, reliable and accurate short-term heavy rainfall forecasts are essential. Yet precipitation nowcasting is a very difficult task due to the great temporal and spatial variability of precipitation at small spatial scales. To improve precipitation nowcasting accuracy, a radar echo extrapolation model (SAAR-UNet) and quantitative precipitation estimation model (RST-RainNet) were developed. By using an ASPP module, residual convolution, and a spatial attention mechanism, the SAAR-UNet greatly improved the extrapolation ability for the variation of strong echoes. Based on the extrapolated echoes, RST-RainNet employs a dual-branch framework that combines radar echo sequences with gauge-constrained QPE priors and performs residual-aware fusion for precipitation nowcasting. Extensive comparative experiments against attention-based and convolutional U-Net variants showed that SAAR-UNet achieved the most robust performance for strong echo extrapolation. For precipitation nowcasting, RST-RainNet was evaluated against optimized Z-R relationships, machine-learning models (MLP, RF, and XGBoost), and radar-only single-branch deep-learning baselines (UNet-ConvLSTM and UNet-Transformer). Across two independent storm events within the Liulin watershed, RST-RainNet consistently achieved the highest correlation coefficients and the lowest overall errors at both the one-hour and two-hour lead times, while more faithfully reproducing the temporal evolution and spatial structure of rainfall. The results indicate that combining radar echoes with gauge-constrained physically guided priors and residual correction can improve precipitation nowcasting accuracy and event-level robustness within the study watershed.

title: Nonlinear flow behaviors through rough fractures in shale: Effects of fracture roughness and stress-induced closed-region evolution
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Hao Yin, Yan-Hua Huang, Sheng-Qi Yang, Huan Sun, Zhen-Ni Ye, Shuang-Mei Wang, Jing-Hua Qi, Shi-Ao Wang
abstract: Nonlinear flow through rough shale fractures is governed by the coupled effects of stress-induced closure, geometric heterogeneity, and fluid inertia. In this study, CO2 seepage experiments, three-dimensional fracture reconstruction, and COMSOL simulations were combined to quantify these effects. The experiments showed that the standard-state outlet flow rate increased with injection pressure, whereas the apparent gas-flow index decreased with injection pressure, indicating progressive deviation from the linear squared-pressure response. The index also decreased with increasing confining pressure, reflecting stress-induced degradation of gas-flow capacity. Calibrated equivalent-aperture single-fracture core models reproduced the measured pressure-flow trends, with mean absolute percentage errors of 7.88%, 8.00%, and 20.87% for the three samples, respectively. The models also showed a rapid initial decline followed by a more gradual decrease in equivalent fracture permeability with increasing confining pressure. Dual-walled rough-fracture models further revealed that stress-induced closure increased the closed-region ratio, partitioned the connected flow domain, and localized flow within constricted channels. In the dual-walled water-flow model of Sample 3#, the fitted nonlinear coefficient increased by more than two orders of magnitude when the closed-region ratio reached 15.1%, relative to the 0 MPa open-fracture baseline. The resulting flow localization intensified pressure-field partitioning, velocity gradients, vorticity concentration, and viscous dissipation, thereby enhancing nonlinear resistance. These results establish a quantitative link between closed-region growth, flow localization, energy dissipation, and Forchheimer-type resistance. Water-flow simulations under the same fracture geometry were used to isolate the effects of fracture closure and fluid inertia on nonlinear resistance.

title: A systematic approach to assess fused drone-satellite data for vertical water quality profile estimation in a deep reservoir
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Sadegh Mishmast Nehi, Mohammad Reza Nikoo, Malik Al-Wardy, Sadegh Vanda, Reza Kerachian
abstract: In-situ sampling for deep-reservoir water quality monitoring is accurate but often impractical for routine, high-resolution vertical monitoring. Remote sensing (RS) provides an alternative for estimating multiple water quality variables (WQVs), including both optically active and non-optically active variables. However, most existing studies have focused on surface-level estimations, which are inadequate for deep reservoirs where WQVs’ profiles vary significantly with depth. While previous studies have compared remote sensing data sources for estimating water quality, this work addresses a critical gap by providing one of the first systematic evaluations of different data sources specifically for assessing WQVs at lower levels in deep water bodies. To achieve this, we introduce a novel multi-platform systematic framework that evaluates multiple RS data sources (including Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9 satellite imagery as well as unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) observations), alongside fused datasets and machine learning models to estimate vertical profiles of WQVs. The framework was applied to the Wadi Dayqah Dam (Oman), where seven WQVs (temperature, chlorophyll-a, turbidity, EC25, pH, oxidation–reduction potential, and dissolved oxygen) were modeled across depth zones using coincident in-situ measurements for training and validation. Results show that RS-based models can reproduce vertical WQV patterns beyond the surface layer, and that multi-source fusion improves estimation for several non-optically active variables compared with single-source models. Key contributions are: (1) a reproducible evaluation process for selecting RS sources and models for vertical profiling, (2) evidence that multi-source RS improves estimation of depth-varying WQVs in a deep reservoir, and (3) a demonstration on a large reservoir that the approach can extend operational RS monitoring below the surface. This framework can guide future vertical water-quality monitoring and multi-source RS integration.

title: Is every flood rough on built environment? Flood fragility and vulnerability modeling for residential buildings
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Suraj Gautam, Vivek Dumre, Pooja Lamichhane, Alok Dahal, Sanjay Kumar Sah, Binod Parajuli, Sneha Bhatta, Nitesh Sharma, Aakash Khanal, Biddhya Bhandari, Shudarshan Hamal, Dinesh Gurung, Shraddha Acharya, Sanjaya Devkota, Basanta Raj Adhikari, Dipendra Gautam
abstract: Flood is one of the most frequent natural hazards, which often causes fatalities, injuries, physical damage to the built environment, and economic consequences. Although widely recognized as a frequent natural hazard/disaster, damage quantification models are sparsely reported in the literature, and most of those models consider well-known structural systems only. To quantify physical damage to buildings, plan flood-resilient housing construction, conduct risk/loss assessments, deploy insurance systems, and formulate evacuation and relocation programs, flood fragility/vulnerability models are instrumental at both local and regional scales. However, challenges persist in obtaining reliable data to construct high-fidelity models. To address this, the present paper develops high-fidelity fragility models for reinforced concrete (RC), wattle and daub, masonry, and hybrid construction systems using one of the largest actual damage survey datasets. Uncertainties are also quantified for each fragility/vulnerability model. We propose a new damage state definition framework that captures contents, nonstructural components (NSCs), structural components, and global damage in residential buildings. Equivalent damage ratios are also proposed for each damage state. The results highlight that the wattle and daub system is the most vulnerable construction system under flooding. In addition, functionality loss cannot be ruled out even in robust construction systems such as RC. Comparison between the proposed and existing models from other basins highlights that scalability and generalizability considerations are instrumental in adopting flood fragility/vulnerability models.

title: From longitudinal dispersal to vertical sequestration: Hydraulic regulation drives divergent antibiotic fates via suspended particulate matter dynamics across natural and engineered waterways
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yang Cui, Hui Xie, Jianwei Dong, Meiqi Shang, Shiya Gu, Wu Wen
abstract: Hydrodynamic conditions fundamentally regulate contaminant transport, yet it remains unclear how anthropogenic hydrodynamic shifts drive divergent antibiotic fates across coexisting natural and artificial waterways, particularly through their impacts on suspended particulate matter (SPM) dynamics. This study compared antibiotic occurrence, transport, and fate between a natural river and a sluice-regulated canal within the same agricultural watershed. Aqueous-phase antibiotic concentrations were significantly higher in the river (p < 0.05), while solid-phase levels were comparable between the two systems. However, the river exhibited greater compositional complexity, whereas the canal showed a simplified solid-phase profile dominated by tetracyclines. In the natural river, high connectivity and active flow maintained antibiotics in dissolved and SPM-bound phases, promoting longitudinal transport and spatial dispersal. Conversely, the regulated canal functioned as a segmented reactor, divided into hydraulically distinct sections with distinct aqueous antibiotic compositions under closed-gate conditions (p < 0.05). Low-energy flow and finer-grained sediment accumulation synergistically enhanced the sediment-partitioning affinity of particle-reactive antibiotics, thereby transforming SPM from a mobile carrier in the river into a settling shuttle in the canal that sequestered contaminants locally. Additionally, gate operation may remobilize retained particles and sediment-associated antibiotics, shifting the canal from a sequestration-dominated state toward a transport/release state. Our findings revealed that hydraulic regulation fundamentally dictated antibiotic transport, sequestration, and remobilization by altering SPM dynamics. Consequently, optimizing infrastructure operations and managing particulate fluxes emerge as critical strategies for mitigating localized ecological risks in agriculturally impacted waterways.

title: Wet-season observations of dissolved carbon and CO 2 –CH 4 emissions in inland waters of the Lower Ogooué floodplain (Gabon)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Vérelle Patience Nsa Assoumou, Oleg S. Pokrovsky, Auguste Paulin Mbonda, Achille Toussendj, Sakaros Bogning, Annick Rebecca Nyengui Mayombo, Jan Karlsson, Mike Castane Makaya M’voubou, Jean-Jacques Braun
abstract: Floodplain wetlands in tropical river basins play a disproportionate role in carbon cycling, yet their contribution to greenhouse-gas emissions in Central Africa remains poorly constrained. We quantified dissolved carbon, CO2 and CH4 concentrations, together with floating-chamber fluxes, across small streams, flooded forests, lakes, and the main channel of the Lower Ogooué River floodplain (Gabon) during two representative wet-season campaigns. Dissolved organic carbon (5–50 mg L−1), pCO2 (1500–16,000 µatm), and dissolved CH4 showed their highest observed values in small tributaries and flooded forests, whereas the main stem generally exhibited lower values. The highest observed chamber-measured CO2 fluxes occurred in tributaries, although differences among water body types were not statistically significant. Despite 5–10-fold spatial variability in concentrations, CO2 fluxes varied by only ∼2-fold among water body types and showed little diel or between-campaign variability. Dissolved oxygen was strongly associated with CO2 distributions, whereas its relationship with CH4 was weaker and season-dependent. First-order area-based upscaling suggests that flooded forests and floodplain lakes were the principal contributors to wet-season CO2 evasion, whereas the main river contributed a smaller share. Limited chamber-based CH4 flux observations (n = 5, one campaign) suggest that flooded forests may be methane-emission hotspots, but do not support quantitative floodplain-scale partitioning. Scenario calculations applying wet-season CO2 emission factors to assumed regional water coverage suggest that aquatic evasion could exceed downstream dissolved-carbon export by several-fold; however, these values represent order-of-magnitude illustrations rather than measured annual budgets. These results highlight the need to explicitly account for floodplain hydrology, wetland extent, and aquatic-landscape heterogeneity when constraining carbon budgets and projecting responses of humid tropical river basins to climate-driven changes in flooding dynamics.

title: InSAR-driven characterization of “ungauged” aquifer systems: Insights from the Gediz River Basin, Türkiye
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yueting Li, Alper Elçi, Claudia Meisina, Elif Aysu Batkan, Ali Hakan Ören, Pietro Teatini, Claudia Zoccarato
abstract: Accurate characterization of key hydro-geomechanical properties, specifically hydraulic conductivity K and specific storage S s , is essential for predicting the responses of aquifer systems to natural and anthropogenic stressors and ensuring sustainable groundwater management. However, such characterization remains particularly challenging in “ungauged” basins, i.e., where piezometric records, pumping test data, and information about production wells are sparse or unavailable. We propose an iterative framework based on coupling a three-dimensional (3D) groundwater flow (GW) model with a 3D geomechanical (GM) model, using a nested inversion scheme. The workflow begins with calibrating the GW model against piezometric records to acquire an initial estimation of heterogeneous K distribution given a homogeneous S s . The resulting hydraulic head changes are then fused with Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) measurements to estimate point-wise S s values that are subsequently interpolated across the basin scale. This S s field is validated using the GM model and fed back into the GW model for a next iteration of K calibration. This iterative cycle continues until the estimated parameters stabilize and further updates provide limited improvements in model performance. We apply this approach to the Gediz River Basin (GRB) in western Türkiye, a region experiencing severe land subsidence from groundwater over-exploitation for irrigation. Our results reveal significant heterogeneity in aquifer properties, and the inferred K and S s distributions allow for the reproduction of both hydraulic head evolution and land subsidence patterns, with a consistent modeling set-up.

title: Depth-dependent lag, persistence, and hydro-thermal coupling of soil moisture in a basin of Northern China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Quanshan Liu, Ningbo Cui, Shunsheng Zheng, Daozhi Gong, Zhihui Wang, Fei Chen
abstract: Understanding how soil moisture (SM) varies with depth is important for characterizing profile-scale water movement and storage behavior. However, the vertical propagation, persistence, and soil moisture–temperature (SM–ST) coupling of profile SM remain insufficiently quantified. Using multi-site observations at five depths (3, 5, 10, 20, and 50 cm) in the Shandian River Basin of northern China during the non-frozen periods from 2019 to 2022, this study quantified the temporal dynamics, vertical propagation, persistence, SM–ST coupling, and environmental controls of SM. Results showed a clear shift from a highly variable shallow layer to a delayed and persistent deep-soil regime. SM persistence increased by 164 % from 14 d at 3 cm to 37 d at 50 cm, accompanied by stronger spatial heterogeneity at depth. Vertical coupling between adjacent layers weakened downward by 18 %, with the median maximum correlation decreasing from 0.93 in the shallow intervals (3–5 and 5–10 cm) to 0.76 in the 20–50 cm interval, while the corresponding median lag increased from 0 to 5 d. For SM–ST coupling, shallow soil showed weak evaporation-related decoupling, whereas deeper soil showed positive hydrothermal co-variation; the median lag remained near zero but became spatially more constrained with depth. Environmental controls were predominantly nonlinear: clay content was more closely associated with deep-layer lag and persistence, whereas elevation showed a stronger influence on deep SM–ST coupling. These findings provide profile-scale observational evidence for representing depth-dependent soil moisture memory, vertical transmission, and SM–ST coupling in hydrological and land-surface studies.

title: Selective transferability mapping for cross-basin prediction of river electrical conductivity
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Tom Lotz, Wenjun Chen, Thomas Hennig, Shoubao Su
abstract: Electrical conductivity (EC) is an important water-quality indicator, but measurements are unavailable for many rivers. Cross-basin prediction is difficult because models often assume that relationships learned in one basin remain valid elsewhere without evaluating hydrological similarity or failure risk. This study introduces Selective Transferability Mapping (STM), a suitability-guided framework that uses catchment similarity to evaluate whether model transfer is supported. Using 578 USGS stations, pairwise Random Forest models quantified transferability for four flow-conditioned EC statistics (mean, median, minimum, and maximum), and a classifier linked transfer success to differences in catchment and runoff characteristics. Twenty repeated holdouts excluded 100 target basins from all training steps. Under observed-flow conditions, STM achieved the highest mean R2 for mean, median, and minimum EC when compared with controls, but not for maximum EC. Under predicted-flow conditions, target-basin streamflow was withheld, and flow-duration curves were estimated from catchment attributes and modeled runoff characteristics. STM outperformed all comparison approaches, including methods based on catchment similarity and pooled donor data, for all four statistics on targets with sufficient donor support. STM also produced fewer negative and severe failures than models trained using all available donors. STM donor support also identified basins less prone to severe errors, providing reliability information that could inform other prediction approaches. Spatial-residual and stability analyses further characterized prediction reliability across locations and flow conditions. Overall, STM balances predictive reliability against spatial coverage by selecting donors in a transparent and hydrologically interpretable manner and withholding predictions for target basins with insufficient donor support.

title: The role of surface water-groundwater mixing in regulating nitrogen hotspot distribution and nitrate fate
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Xue Ping, Zhang Wen, Yang Xian, Stefan Krause, Songhu Yuan, Zhixin Zhang, Menggui Jin
abstract: Hyporheic zones (HZs) modulate water quality by acting as natural buffers for groundwater-borne nitrate contaminants, facilitating biogeochemical reactions in surface water and groundwater (SW-GW) mixing zone (the colocation region of SW and GW) by complementary reactants delivery. However, how SW and GW mixing regulates mixing triggered nitrogen hotspot distribution (regions with higher turnover productions and rates) and GW-borne nitrate reduction remains unclear. Here we combined a flume experiment, characterizing coupled hydrodynamic, biogeochemical processes, microbial functions and communities in a simulated HZ with a numerical model, integrating flow, reactive solute transport, and microbial activities, to address this gap. In lowland HZs, a typical setting where nitrate-polluted GW discharges into streams with high available organic carbon, SW and GW mixing induces denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), with their hotspots segregated spatially: denitrification prevails in the mixing zone interior and downstream, whereas DNRA is localized to the upstream mixing zone. This stems from their distinct C/N demands: denitrification prefers low C/N conditions, while DNRA favors high C/N conditions, both are optimally met at the margins of mixing zone. DNRA-produced ammonium is subsequently nitrified under upstream aerobic conditions, impairing HZ self-purification and exacerbating stream eutrophication. Prior studies exclusively emphasizing mixing-triggered denitrification likely overestimate GW-borne nitrate attenuation by neglecting DNRA. Our findings advance understanding of mixing-driven nitrogen cycling and nitrate fate in hyporheic/riparian ecosystems.

title: Balancing segmentation accuracy and hydrological plausibility in multi-source remote sensing flood inundation mapping with adaptive terrain-constrained learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yuping Tan, Guoqiang Wang, Yinglan A., Baolin Xue, Jin Wu, Yuntao Wang, Qiao Wang
abstract: Remote sensing-based flood inundation mapping is commonly optimized as a semantic segmentation task using pixel-overlap objectives. However, flood extent is also a terrain-controlled spatial process, and accuracy-oriented models may generate locally implausible patterns, including downstream discontinuities, false positives on steep slopes, and incomplete detection of low-lying inundation. This study frames flood inundation mapping as a multi-objective problem that requires balancing image-based segmentation accuracy with terrain-hydrological plausibility. We propose an adaptive terrain-constrained learning framework that dynamically coordinates pixel supervision, regional overlap, boundary refinement, and DEM-derived terrain-consistency within a unified U-Net architecture. The terrain constraints are not intended to reproduce hydrodynamic processes; instead, they serve as lightweight soft constraints for reducing terrain-implausible patterns in discrete flood probability maps. Cross-regional 10-fold validation on the Sen1Floods11 dataset shows that reliable multi-source observability is a prerequisite for terrain-constrained optimization. Under the full SAR-optical-terrain input setting, fixed terrain-constrained losses reduced flow-direction violations but degraded F1-score and IoU, revealing an accuracy-plausibility trade-off. In contrast, the proposed Adaptive-Dynamic strategy achieved the best overall segmentation performance, with an F1-score of 0.864 and an IoU of 0.761, while maintaining low high-slope false positives and good lowland flood recovery. These results indicate that terrain-derived hydrological priors are most effective when introduced as adaptive soft constraints that regularize image-derived flood predictions without dominating image-based flood evidence, thereby reducing local prediction patterns that contradict basic terrain logic rather than simulating hydrological processes.

title: Predominant vegetation control on baseflow index variations across China’s climatic basins
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yanzhong Li, Kaiwen Wang, Xiaomang Liu, Huan Wu, Xiaojun Guo
abstract: Baseflow refers to the subsurface runoff component sustained solely by groundwater, expressed in units of mm or m3 s⁻1. The baseflow index (BFI), by contrast, is a dimensionless metric calculated as the ratio of baseflow to total streamflow, which is vital for evaluating ecosystem health and planning irrigation demands. To date, the long-term spatiotemporal dynamics and driving mechanisms of BFI (baseflow proportion) across China’s climatic basins remain poorly understood. Here, we conduct a novel systematic assessment of 12 baseflow separation methods (zero-, one-, and two-parameter) along a complete climatic gradient (humid-transition-arid) in China, and identify the most robust approaches for multi-climatic applications. We then investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of the BFI in 17 typical watersheds across diverse climatic regions from 1982 to 2020, and provide quantitative evidence of the impacts of vegetation greening on BFI variability. Our results demonstrate that the two-parameter digital filter methods, including Boughton, Furey, Eckhardt, and Willems, perform optimally with the highest Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values. The multi-year mean BFI across all watersheds is 0.55 ± 0.10, with higher values observed in arid watersheds (0.60 ± 0.10) than in humid watersheds (0.52 ± 0.08). A significant increasing trend (p < 0.05) in BFI is detected in 8 of the 17 watersheds, with this upward trend being particularly pronounced in arid and transitional basins. Quantitative attribution analysis reveals that vegetation greening (Leaf Area Index, LAI) acts as the statistically dominant driver, explaining 54.4% of BFI variations-far exceeding the contributions of precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, aridity index, and precipitation seasonality. Our findings provide robust evidence that large-scale vegetation restoration has profoundly altered baseflow generation processes and streamflow partitioning across China’s climatic gradient.

title: Integrating deep-learning detection and hydrological monitoring for driftwood flux estimation in a steep tropical watershed during a typhoon-driven flood
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Qian-Yun Kong, Ci-Jian Yang, Cheng-Hua Tsai, Meng-Yu Lee
abstract: Extreme climatic events, such as typhoons, mobilize massive amounts of deadwood in steep mountain watersheds, serving as a critical link in the global carbon cycle. However, capturing the event-scale dynamics of driftwood flux remains challenging due to the hazardous conditions and limitations of traditional monitoring. Here, we developed a reproducible workflow integrating deep learning (YOLOv8) with fixed-interval surveillance cameras and drone imagery to quantify driftwood flux and storage in the Liwu watershed, Taiwan. We used a comprehensive dataset comprising Swiss, Arctic, and local imagery to train separate domain-specific YOLOv8 models for three driftwood domain types: instream, riverbank, and nearshore. Two detection models were used: object detection for localisation, and instance segmentation to provide the polygon areas used in the quantitative calculations. To translate detection into volume of driftwood, we established an area-to-volume conversion using radio-frequency identification (RFID)-tagged logs. The YOLOv8 model demonstrated exceptional performance for instream detection (mAP50 = 94.36%; F1 = 92.59%), validating its feasibility for automated fixed-interval monitoring. Applying this model to Typhoon Kong-rey (2024), where the water stage rose from 40.5 to 45 m (increasing discharge from 19.94 to 705.73 m3 s−1), yielded an estimated instream driftwood mass of 1.12 ± 0.22 × 104 t and a corresponding carbon stock of 5.26 ± 1.05 × 103 tC. Moreover, post-event drone mapping revealed that driftwood preferentially accumulates along outer river banks and forms banded deposits on nearshore beaches. Our findings highlight pulsed driftwood transportation as a quantifiable component of green carbon and demonstrate the feasibility of integrating deep learning-based detection with hydrological monitoring for carbon budget assessments.

title: Hierarchical multi-objective management of cascade reservoirs: coordinating long-term strategy and daily operation under hydrological variability
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Haotian Wu, Zhaoyang Zhu, Zhaocai Wang, Jiachen Kong, Qikai Liu, Zuowen Tan, Chenye Liu, Tianyu Ren
abstract: A core challenge in large-scale cascade reservoir operation is the ineffective transmission of macro-scale planning to short-term scheduling, leading to conflicts among strategic objectives under increasing hydrological variability. To address this scale dilemma, this study proposes a Multi-scale Socio-Economic-Environmental Reservoir Management (MSEE-RM) framework. The core innovation lies in a novel “annual-periodic” hierarchical paradigm. The upper-layer model (operating on a 10-day time step) formulates annual strategic water level trajectories that serve as dynamic boundary conditions for the lower-layer model. The lower-layer model performs daily-scale optimization, explicitly tailored to the distinct hydrological and functional characteristics of three key periods: the drawdown period (focusing on fish spawning requirements), the flood season (balancing flood risk distribution), and the storage period (coordinating impoundment with navigation). To efficiently solve the resulting high-dimensional non-linear problems, a reinforcement learning-enhanced evolutionary algorithm (SPEA2-RLS) is developed to adaptively balance search exploration and exploitation. Additionally, an RF-AdaBoost-based surrogate model is integrated to provide computationally efficient predictions of water temperature at a key downstream section, thereby supporting repeated ecological-temperature evaluations during optimization. Results demonstrate that the framework significantly restores long-neglected ecological functions: in wet years, Effective Ecological Hydropeaking Days (EEHD) increased from 0 to 17; in dry years, the Ecological Flow Deficit (EFD) was substantially reduced by 42.9%. Crucially, ecological improvements and economic benefits are enhanced synergistically. In normal years, Total Power Generation (TPG) and System Minimum Power Output (SMPO) increased by 4.4% and 14.9%, respectively, while Navigation Interruption Days (NID) were reduced by 30.5%. Overall, this study quantifies the comprehensive benefits of reservoir operation and reveals the dynamic trade-offs among objectives, providing technical support for multi-objective coordination and watershed management in cascade systems.

title: Long-term increases in tree water-use efficiency across China are associated with CO 2 and hydroclimatic variation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Yali Ding, Li Wen, Jingzhi Zhang, Wei Zhang, Hongsong Chen, Shanshan Song, Zongrui Lai, Jinxing Zhou, Guanghui Lin
abstract: Rising atmospheric CO2 and hydroclimatic variability jointly shape forest carbon–water relations, with important implications for carbon sequestration, drought resilience, and water resources. However, their interactive effects on long-term intrinsic tree water-use efficiency (iWUE) remain difficult to quantify because atmospheric CO2 and calendar year are highly collinear over centennial timescales. Using a nationwide tree-ring δ13C dataset spanning the twentieth century across China’s major biogeographic zones, we examined long-term iWUE trajectories and tested whether non-trend CO2 deviations were associated with iWUE after accounting for zone-specific temporal trends and hydroclimatic variation. To address collinearity between CO2 and time, we decomposed atmospheric CO2 into a long-term trend and residual deviations (CO2_resid) and incorporated these into generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) with zone-specific year smooths, tree-level random effects, and AR(1) temporal correlation. Model comparisons based on AIC, concurvity diagnostics, and blocked cross-validation showed that raw CO2 models achieved the lowest AIC but suffered severe concurvity with year, limiting attribution of long-term iWUE trends. In contrast, the CO2_resid parameterization markedly reduced concurvity while maintaining comparable predictive performance, allowing more stable inference about non-trend CO2 associations. Across all biogeographic zones, iWUE increased markedly over the twentieth century. The residualized CO2 model showed that positive non-trend CO2 deviations were associated with higher iWUE under lower annual precipitation contexts, had weak effects under intermediate precipitation, and were attenuated or slightly reversed under the highest annual precipitation contexts. Temperature exerted weaker moderating effects. Because CO2_resid represents departures from the long-term CO2 trajectory, these results should not be interpreted as a direct estimate of the contribution of rising CO2 to the centennial iWUE increase. Rather, they show that CO2-related iWUE responses are strongly hydroclimate-dependent. This study provides a statistical framework for separating long-term temporal trends from short-term CO2 variability and highlights the importance of moisture context when predicting forest carbon–water coupling under environmental change.

title: Interpretable modeling of spatiotemporal variations of groundwater total hardness across China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Chenglong Cao, Qing Zhou, Junliang Jin, Fenghua You, Lei Yao, Hongzhe Pan, Wei Gan, Jiangjiang Zhang, Yijun Yao
abstract: High groundwater total hardness (GTH) poses significant risks to human health, agriculture, and industry, yet field observations suggest severe conditions in China. To investigate the spatiotemporal variations of GTH and its key predictors, we developed an interpretable machine learning model (validation R 2 = 0.76) linking GTH observations compiled from published studies with 34 natural and anthropogenic variables, including geology and soil properties, climate conditions, human activities, and vegetation cover. The results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with higher GTH in northern and coastal regions and lower values in southern China, as well as distinct dominant predictors across land-use types. National mean GTH increased from 381.60 mg/L in 1980 to 399.26 mg/L in 2015, followed by a slight decline to 393.75 mg/L in 2020. Future projections indicate continued increases under constant 2020 human activity levels and under high-emission scenarios, while a low-emission pathway leads to a modest reduction. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identifies geology and soil properties (46.31%) and climate conditions (28.37%) as the most important predictor groups in GTH predictions, followed by human activities and vegetation. These findings provide insights into groundwater hardening and support targeted mitigation strategies combining climate regulation, geological and soil management, reduction of anthropogenic pressures, and vegetation restoration.

title: Human pressures exacerbate the impacts of hydroclimatic extremes on river greenhouse gas emissions
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Diego G. Panique-Casso, Peter Goethals, Long Ho
abstract: The natural release of greenhouse gas (GHG) from rivers is intensified by the deterioration in water quality caused by the combined effects of hydroclimatic extremes (droughts, heatwaves, rainstorms, and floods), and human activities (agriculture, urbanization). Yet, current models largely overlook these interactions, representing a critical gap in GHG inventories. To elucidate the general responses of water quality parameters and GHG fluxes to hydroclimatic events, this work combined global datasets on river water quality and streamflow, with measured GHG fluxes across four continents. By integrating random forest models and SHAP values, we identified the intricate interplay between climatic, land-use, geomorphic, water quality and riverine GHG fluxes during hydroclimatic extreme events. Our models showed that during drought-heatwave events, CH4 emissions from the rivers can increase by 18% on average likely because of intense urban pollution. In particular, reduced slopes from channel modifications were associated with disrupted river connectivity, pollutant accumulation, and emission hotspots. During rainstorm-floods, CO2 and N2O fluxes can rise by 6% in downstream rivers, where enhanced hydrological connectivity to pollution sources, including agricultural fields and wastewater overflows, was associated with higher pollution loads and turbidity, and elevated GHG emissions. These findings are highly relevant under future climate scenarios, where more frequent and prolonged hydroclimatic extremes could further elevate riverine GHG emissions.

title: Hydrologic connectivity from cryospheric waters to groundwater in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China: recharge pathways and seasonal regulation from multiple tracers
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 679, Part A Author(s): Zejun Wang, Zhi Dou, Jinguo Wang, Liang Chen, Zhen Liao, Hao Yu, Zhifang Zhou
abstract: Groundwater is a critical but insufficiently constrained component of water storage and transfer in cryosphere-influenced headwaters of the Tibetan Plateau. During 2024 − 2025, hydrologic connectivity from rainfall, snowmelt, glacial lake water, and river water to shallow and deep groundwater in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau was investigated using hydrologic monitoring, major ions, hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes, radon-222, tritium, and radiocarbon. Estimated recharge elevations exceeded sampling elevations, indicating dominant lateral recharge from higher terrain rather than local infiltration across the catchment. Summer snowmelt yielded the highest recharge elevations and greatest apparent circulation depths, whereas glacial lakes buffered and mixed source waters and rivers transferred integrated cryospheric signals to groundwater. Bayesian apportionment showed that direct snowmelt contributed 4.6 − 16.1% of modeled groundwater, while glacial-lake and river water together accounted for 71.2 − 75.3%. Hydrochemical evolution toward groundwater involved increasing mineralization, stronger water − rock interaction, and enhanced cation exchange. Cave groundwater exhibited pronounced hydrochemical heterogeneity and very high summer radon-222, indicating seasonally activated fracture flow, rapid shallow recharge, and active groundwater − surface water exchange. In contrast, borehole groundwater represented a more buffered system, including river-coupled pathways in H1-H2 boreholes and a distinct lake-buffered pathway in H3 borehole. Measurable tritium in all groundwater samples demonstrated widespread modern recharge, whereas depressed radiocarbon activities and corrected apparent ages revealed simultaneous mixing with older stored water. This work shows that groundwater circulation in Tibetan Plateau is organized as a hierarchical and seasonally shifting multi-source connectivity network, providing critical insights for water and element cycling in the plateau’s critical zone.

title: Photovoltaic panel arrays reshape soil erosion patterns and hydrodynamic processes on hillslopes
description: Publication date: Available online 22 August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Nufang Fang, Rui Fan, Yue Du, Yi Zeng
abstract: Solar photovoltaic (PV) installations on hillslopes alter rainfall redistribution and create spatially heterogeneous erosion patterns, yet the underlying hydraulic mechanisms remain poorly quantified. Using simulated rainfall experiments, this study evaluated the effects of PV panel installation height (0.4, 0.6, 0.8 m), tilt angle (30°, 35°, 40°), and arrangement type (linear, block) on runoff, sediment yield, hydraulic parameters, and rill morphology across 18 configurations. PV coverage reduced cumulative sediment yield by up to 56.6%, yet spatially disaggregated measurements revealed localized erosion intensification beneath panel drip lines. Transverse rills perpendicular to the slope formed exclusively beneath drip lines in all configurations, with spacing largely controlled by panel geometry rather than by hydraulic self-organization. Installation height was the dominant variable, as lower heights (0.4 m) maximized slope-scale sediment reduction (46.3%) through rainfall interception, whereas higher heights (0.8 m) intensified drip-line erosion through greater impact energy. Flow velocity, Reynolds number, shear stress, and stream power all amplified stepwise across successive covered zones, confirming a progressive downslope intensification of erosive force. Targeted drip-line mitigation with turf mats and gravel strips reduced localized sediment yield by 74% and 32% relative to untreated PV slopes. This study identifies a geometrically forced erosion regime beneath PV arrays and provides a hydrodynamic basis for erosion-resilient siting and design of hillslope solar installations.

title: TS-PINN: a dual-branch physics-informed neural network based on two-source theory for evapotranspiration estimation
description: Publication date: Available online 22 August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology Author(s): Xing Rong, Chunlin Huang, Feinan Xu, Jinliang Hou, Peng Dou, Ying Zhang, Qiang Bie, Tianwen Feng, Zhihua Zhang
abstract: Accurate estimation of surface energy fluxes and evapotranspiration (ET) is essential for understanding land–atmosphere interactions. While data-driven methods efficiently fit observations, their “black-box” nature makes it challenging to guarantee physical interpretability and reliable extrapolation from instantaneous to daily ET. To address these limitations, we propose the Two-Source Physics-Informed Neural Network (TS-PINN), driven by both physical structure and physical constraints. The model constructs a vegetation-soil dual-branch architecture structurally aligned with the Two-Source Energy Balance (TSEB) theory, embedding partitioning mechanisms as structural inductive biases. For optimization, we design a multi-constraint physical loss that integrates instantaneous energy balance, component energy balance, the Priestley–Taylor (P–T) upper bound, and daily-scale consistency. We also adopt an adaptive weighting strategy to balance data fitting and physical consistency. Validation against eddy covariance (EC) data in the Heihe River Basin (HRB) (2015–2021 growing seasons) shows that TS-PINN significantly outperforms Random Forest (RF) and Deep Neural Network (DNN) baselines. Its root mean square error (RMSE) values are 31.22 W/m2 for sensible heat flux (H) and 44.03 W/m2 for latent heat flux (LE), with corresponding coefficients of determination (R 2) of 0.79 and 0.85, respectively. Ablation experiments reveal that the structural inductive bias enhances component-level representation, while the physical loss terms effectively constrain prediction boundaries. Specifically, the instantaneous energy balance constraint dominates H prediction accuracy, and the P–T constraint guides LE estimation. Daily ET converted from LE also presents good consistency with observations, with a Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.88 and an R 2 of 0.81. Overall, TS-PINN offers a novel, accurate, and physically interpretable approach for simulating surface energy fluxes and ET.

title: 3D seismic imaging of a fracture damage zone controlling reservoir compartmentalization at the Raft River EGS using multi-azimuth walkaway VSP
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Benxin Chi, Kai Gao, David Li, Joseph Moore, Clay Jones, Lianjie Huang
abstract: Accurate imaging of steeply dipping fracture zones in crystalline enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) is critical for constraining permeability architecture and guiding stimulation design. However, such structures remain poorly resolved by conventional surface seismic methods. We present a fully three-dimensional (3D) elastic-waveform inversion–migration workflow applied to multi-azimuth walkaway vertical seismic profiling (VSP) data acquired in a deviated borehole at the Raft River EGS. The workflow integrates first-arrival traveltime tomography, multi-scale elastic waveform inversion (EWI), and elastic least-squares reverse-time migration (ELSRTM) to recover high-resolution compressional- and shear-wave velocity models and to image structural discontinuities in the crystalline basement. The results reveal a laterally continuous low-velocity anomaly, with shear-wave velocity reductions of 25–30%, consistent with fracture-induced mechanical weakening. Two steeply dipping discontinuities bound a 50–80 m wide fracture damage zone. Independent constraints from microseismic clustering and geochemical compartmentalization corroborate the geometry and structural significance of this feature. Synthetic modeling further confirms that structures of this scale are resolvable (∼30 m). These findings indicate that the Narrows structure is a distributed fracture damage zone rather than a discrete fault plane. By resolving fracture-zone geometry at the tens-of-meters scale using a single borehole, this workflow provides a practical and transferable approach for improving structural characterization, reducing uncertainty in permeability architecture, and supporting reservoir modeling and stimulation design in fractured crystalline EGS reservoirs.

title: Influence of thermal treatment on the petrophysical and microstructural properties of saturated limestone
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Natalino da Silva Souza, Jéssica Nascimento Pereira, Igor Alexandre Rocha Barreto, Marcondes Lima da Costa, Daniel Nobre Nunes da Silva, Pedro Tupã Pandava Aum, Cláudio Regis dos Santos Lucas
abstract: Thermal fracturing in limestone is relevant to geothermal operations, thermal stimulation of low-permeability reservoirs, underground energy storage, and the assessment of structural integrity under elevated temperatures. However, the thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) behavior of fluid-saturated limestones under undrained conditions remains poorly understood, particularly regarding the interaction between saline pore fluids and thermally induced microstructural damage. This study systematically investigated the effects of heating from 100 to 800 °C under undrained conditions, using two NaCl concentrations (10 and 20 wt%) and deionized water, on the petrophysical properties and microstructure of Pink Desert limestone, a monomineralic limestone composed of >99.9% calcite. Saturated samples were subjected to confined heating and subsequently characterized by bulk density, effective porosity, permeability, X-ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric and differential scanning calorimetry analyses (TG/DSC), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The rock exhibited high thermal stability up to approximately 625 °C, with minimal variations in density, porosity, and permeability. More pronounced changes were observed only at 800 °C, where permeability increased by up to approximately 4.2 times relative to its initial value (observed for a single specimen), whereas porosity exhibited only a modest increase (∼1.1 times). These results suggest the existence of a threshold for accelerated thermal damage development somewhere between 625 and 800 °C. The FWHM analyses confirm the preservation of calcite crystallinity throughout the thermal interval, indicating that damage occurs predominantly at the intergranular scale. Within the resolution of the analytical techniques employed and under the experimental conditions investigated, no systematic influence of salinity on the evaluated properties was detected. In summary, Pink Desert limestone exhibits high thermal resistance, with significant degradation of its transport properties occurring only as temperatures approach the initial decomposition interval of calcite. The observed permeability increase is associated with the development of a more interconnected network of thermally induced microfractures. These findings provide relevant parameters for evaluating the performance of fluid-saturated limestones in applications involving intense thermal gradients and highlight temperature as the primary controlling factor governing thermal degradation in monomineralic calcitic limestones under undrained conditions.

title: Frictional response of thermally treated granite joints under oscillatory normal stress: implications for fracture stability in enhanced geothermal systems
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Wengang Dang, Shixiao Li, Yuyong Jiao, Yu Liu, Yunhan Sheng, Kang Tao, Linchong Huang, Hongfei Duan, Xiang Li, Yu Feng
abstract: In enhanced geothermal systems, thermally altered fractures may experience cyclic normal stress perturbations during injection, production, and seismic disturbance. However, the frictional response of thermally treated granite joints under oscillatory normal stress remains insufficiently constrained. To address this issue, this study employed a large DJZ-500 direct shear apparatus to conduct laboratory research on the granite joint that had experienced different temperature heat treatments (23–500 °C) under constant normal load (CNL) and dynamic normal load (DNL). The results revealed that the joint shear strength exhibited a nonlinear evolution process dependent on temperature. Both static and dynamic shear strengths showed initial thermal strengthening (23–200 °C), followed by severe thermal degradation (200–500 °C). Moreover, when the heat treatment exceeded 300 °C, the shear strength dropped below the pre-treatment strength. With increasing dynamic amplitude, dynamic shear strength changes from being higher than to lower than the corresponding static strength. We refer to this phenomenon as frictional strengthening-to-weakening transition. The degree of this frictional strengthening or weakening depends on the temperature. Through three-dimensional surface morphology and results of uniaxial compressive test, we propose a mechanism indicating that the non-linear variation of shear strengths depends on the coupled effects of joint roughness and matrix strength. These findings provide some mechanistic insights into the thermodynamic stability of hot dry rock faults and offer important references for optimizing geothermal energy extraction in deep hot dry rock faults.

title: An investigation of the effects of temperature and clay content on fault gouge material
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Aigerim Sekerbayeva, Ali Mortazavi, Randy D. Hazlett
abstract: To understand fluid flow and permeability characteristics under various clay contents and temperatures, artificially created fault gouge materials were experimentally studied. The aim of the study was to investigate the effects of clay content and temperature on the permeability behaviour of synthetic fault gouge materials under controlled laboratory conditions representative of relatively shallow subsurface storage environments. The mechanical and strength characteristics of the fault gouge material were determined using standard laboratory tests, while water was used as the fluid for permeability measurements under controlled experimental conditions. Temperature changes from 25 °C to 65 °C resulted in only minor changes in permeability under the examined conditions, whereas variations in clay content up to 30% significantly reduced permeability to approximately one order of magnitude, with the largest reduction observed between the 10% and 20% clay compositions, indicating the strong influence of clay-rich compositions on fluid-flow behaviour. Consistent with previous studies, confining pressure remained an important factor controlling permeability reduction. Unlike much of the previous work, which primarily focused on the confining pressure effect, this work examines the combined effects of clay content and temperature, integrating permeability and mechanical characterization. The study combines permeability measurements with uniaxial compression and direct shear testing within a consistent experimental framework. The results provide baseline experimental insights into the relative effects of clay content, stress, and temperature on fault gouge permeability under water-saturated laboratory conditions relevant to the initial assessment of fault behaviour in subsurface storage systems, including geological CO₂ storage.

title: Analytical modeling of tracer pulse tests with significant background concentration at the Utah FORGE geothermal site
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Mahmoud Abdellatif, Smith Leggett, Qingwang Yuan
abstract: Lithium (Li+) and cesium (Cs+) ions show rapid reversible adsorption and desorption on geothermal reservoir rocks, making them potential candidates for sorbing tracer tests to estimate the heat exchange surface area of the geothermal reservoir. However, water geochemistry data from the Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy (Utah FORGE) project show significant background concentrations of Li+ and Cs+, which obscure the tracer recovery response. To address this problem, we extended the semi-analytical Reactive Transport Laplace Transform Inversion model (RELAP) to account for non-zero background concentration and to simulate positive, negative, and multiple tracer pulse tests within a unified background-aware framework. The modified model was first history matched to a previous conservative tracer test at Utah FORGE to estimate the governing flow parameters and provide a data-informed basis for subsequent design calculations. Results indicate that transport between the injection and production well at the Utah FORGE is better represented by a two-component upscaled transport structure than by a single equivalent pathway. Using the history-matched model, the analysis showed that the Li+ or Cs+ tracer mass required to produce detectable positive concentration perturbations is economically prohibitive. In contrast, a negative pulse design based on freshwater injection produces detectable negative perturbations in the tracer recovery response. Expressed in normalized concentration form, the breakthrough curves remain directly comparable to those of a positive tracer pulse and preserve the standard retardation-based interpretation. These results establish a methodological and design-oriented framework for background-aware tracer testing in geothermal reservoirs.

title: Learning with constraints: A physics-guided Bayesian framework for reliable geothermal temperature mapping in northeastern Italy
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Danial Sheini Dashtgoli, Michela Giustiniani, Martina Busetti, Claudia Cherubini, Guillermo A․ Narsilio
abstract: Reliable deep-temperature estimation remains a central challenge in geothermal exploration, particularly in sedimentary–carbonate provinces where borehole data are sparse and vertically imbalanced. These conditions lead to unreliable extrapolation and poor uncertainty characterization in classical interpolation and purely data-driven models. This study develops a physics-guided Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework that integrates heteroscedastic probabilistic learning with conductive heat-transfer constraints to reconstruct the 3D geothermal structure of the Lower Friulian Plain (NE Italy) using 849 irregularly distributed temperature measurements. To explicitly address depth imbalance and evaluate extrapolation performance, a depth-aware training and validation strategy was implemented, including controlled withholding of deep observations (1000–1200 m). The architecture combines Monte Carlo-dropout Bayesian inference with two physics-informed formulations, a monotonicity constraint enforcing non-negative vertical gradients and a gradient-band constraint bounding geothermal slopes within regionally plausible conductive ranges. The resulting models achieve high fidelity in the data-supported domain (<1000 m), with coefficient of determination (R2) ≈ 0.95–0.96 and root mean square error ≈ 2.6–2.8 °C, while classical and data-driven models show reduced reliability under extrapolation conditions. The monotonic BNN attains R2 = 0.877 and RMSE = 1.33 °C, and the gradient-band BNN produces physically consistent geothermal gradients (≈0.014–0.018 °C/m), aligning with regional heat-flow constraints. Both physics-guided models deliver near-ideal uncertainty calibration (≈97–99% prediction-interval coverage) and eliminate nonphysical deep-zone oscillations. Independent validation against the Grado-1 well confirms agreement within ±1 °C across the full 100–1200 m profile. The proposed framework enables extrapolation-robust and uncertainty-aware 3D geothermal mapping, providing a transferable approach for geothermal resource assessment in data-limited subsurface systems.

title: Coaxial direct-expansion CO₂ downhole heat exchanger: thermal resistance and capacity model and heat transfer characteristic analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Xinyue Li, Jing Wang, Jiahui Wu, Taha Rajeh, Yang Li, Jun Zhao
abstract: As the earliest form of ground coupled heat pump, the direct-expansion ground-coupled heat pump is characterized by a simple system structure, high efficiency, and low operating costs. To enhance the heat transfer performance of this technology, this study proposes a novel coaxial downhole heat exchanger utilizing supercritical CO₂ as the working fluid. A transient thermal resistance and capacity model for the coaxial downhole heat exchanger, which has been validated by experimental data, was established. This model was used to compare the performance differences between the proposed system and the conventional U-type structure. Furthermore, the study investigated the effects of insulation layers, flow direction, structural parameters, operating parameters, and soil properties on the heat transfer process.
