In contrast, peak-delay mechanisms evolved with flood magnitude, as floodplain storage increasingly influenced flood-wave propagation during larger floods. Controlled levee breaching also reshaped the spatial distribution of flood hazards, increasing inundation area by 10.89–39.50% and inundation volume by 28.22–150.33% within receiving areas while reducing downstream flood impacts. These findings advance process-based understanding of flood redistribution in highly leveed urban rivers and provide transferable insights into downstream hydraulic responses in highly leveed river–floodplain systems with comparable channel–floodplain hydraulic controls.

title: Multi-layer aquifer hydrogeological responses to deep coal mining and their controlling mechanisms: A hydrochemical and multi-isotope coupling study
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): He Cui, Limin Duan, Hao Pan, Shen Qu, Tingxi Liu
abstract: Study region The Dahaize Coal Mine lies on the southern margin of the Mu Us Sandy Land, a key part of the large coal energy base in northern Shaanxi, China. Study focus Deep coal mining severely disturbs regional groundwater stability, yet the long-term and multi-scale responses of hydrogeological functions of multi-layer aquifers in mining areas remain poorly understood. This study combines hydrochemical approaches with multiple isotopic tracers (δ2H, δ18O, δ34S, δ18Osulfate, and 222Rn) to elucidate spatiotemporal evolution features and dominant driving mechanisms of multi-layer aquifer hydrogeological functions across the whole coal mining cycle. New hydrological insights for the region Phreatic water (PW) and Anding Formation confined water (ADCW) maintained stable hydrogeological functions. PW was mainly affected by sulfate leached from coal gangue under rainfall infiltration, while ADCW was slightly improved owing to weakened vertical leakage recharge. By contrast, Zhiluo Formation confined water (ZLCW) suffered severe functional degradation driven by expanding water-conducting fracture zones (WCFZs). WCFZs lowered hydraulic gradients, slowed groundwater flow and promoted evaporite dissolution. As preferential flow pathways and geochemical reaction interfaces, WCFZs strengthened hydraulic connectivity between ZLCW and mine water (MW), accelerated cation exchange, carbonate dissolution and radon emission, and caused simultaneous enrichment of SO 4 2 - , δ18O, δ34S, and 222Rn in the two aquifers. This study deepens the understanding of the driving mechanisms for the hydrogeological functional evolution of aquifers in mining areas.

title: Beyond prediction accuracy: Causality-driven machine learning models for seasonal flow forecasting in Canada
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Amin Elshorbagy, Duc-Hai Nguyen, Muhammad Naveed Khaliq, Simon Papalexiou, Elena Toth, Cuauhtémoc T. Vidrio-Sahagún, Fisaha Unduche, Mohammad Khaled Akhtar
abstract: Study region Nelson–Churchill River Basin, Canada, spanning mountain, prairie, and non-prairie subbasins from the Rocky Mountains to Hudson Bay. Study focus This study examines the role of causally informed input selection in machine learning (ML)-based seasonal streamflow forecasting. Two approaches were used to identify predictors: partial mutual information (PMI) and convergent cross-mapping (CCM). The selected inputs were used to develop two widely used ML models, Random Forest (RF) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), for forecasting monthly streamflow at lead times of one to three months. Models’ performance was evaluated across multiple natural subbasin groups using Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE). New hydrological insights Although the two approaches produced different predictor sets, ML performance was comparable across subbasin groups based on NSE and KGE, suggesting that multiple equally likely ML model configurations potentially exist for the same forecasting problem. However, the causality-based inputs demonstrated greater physical relevance compared to the information-theoretic set. This conclusion was consistent with the results of ML-based explainability analyses based on RF-based feature‑importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses. The results highlight that the first critical step in ML modeling is to identify sensible, justifiable, and physically meaningful sets of input variables to inform ML modeling. While this study offers insights into causality-based ML, a continued quest for physically meaningful ML models is needed.

title: Synergistic use of bathymetric measurements, ADCP, and SSP for hydromorphological monitoring of the navigable lower Danube River
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Maxim Arseni, Puiu Lucian Georgescu, Adrian Rosu, Mihai Dragomir, Andrei Stanisteanu, Sven Smolders
abstract: Study region The study investigates the Corabia – Turnu Măgurele sector (rKm 601 – rKm626) of the Lower Danube River in Romania. This is a hydromorphologically dynamic area of regional importance for navigation. Spatial and temporal dynamics modify its hydrodynamic behaviour, sediment transport, and channel morphology, changing it into a critical navigation sector. Study focus Modern hydrographic and acoustic survey equipment was used to describe the study area's hydromorphological characteristics. The synergistic use of MBES, ADCP, and SSP delineated five morphological areas grouped into three broad classes: shallow-water zones associated with sandbar formation; moderate-depth sections characterized by relatively stable hydrodynamic conditions and requiring long-term monitoring; and deep-water zones within the main navigable channel, characterized by enhanced erosion and sediment transport. Principal component analysis, K-means clustering, and spatial principal component analysis were used to classify areas with different hydromorphological characteristics. The analysis offers insights into water flow patterns and areas for this regional critical area where the sedimentation rate is excessive. New hydrological insights for the region The integrated analysis identified water-flow patterns and zones of excessive sedimentation. The bathymetric surveys and ADCP measurements were complemented by sediment suspended profiling. The result reveals that the majority of sediment particles fall within the 100–1000 µm range (fine to medium sands). A dominant fraction (100–300 µm) underscores the prevalence of fine sand, indicative of moderate-energy depositional behavior. The low content of fine particles (<10 µm) reflects limited silt and clay retention. The statistical analysis (PCA, K-means, spatial PCA) grouped datasets into three types of areas with different hydro-morphological characteristics. Under extreme low-flow conditions, water depths within the navigable channel often locally drop below 2 m, imposing operational limitations on vessel draught and increasing the risk of navigation disruption. The proposed approach provides a valuable method to understand the importance of the synergistic application of bathymetric, hydrodynamic, and sedimentological analysis, contributes to increasing the level of knowledge on sediment dynamics in regional river systems, such as the Lower Danube, and provides support in decision-making regarding the prioritization of dredging interventions.

title: Modeling climate change impacts on blue and green water in the Ethiopian upper Blue Nile basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Dessalegn Worku Ayalew, Luna Bharati, Navneet Kumar, Bernhard Tischbein, Christian Borgemeister
abstract: Study region Kessie watershed, Ethiopian Upper Blue Nile Basin Study focus This study assesses climate change impacts on blue and green water in Kessie watershed using the enhanced Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT+) model. SWAT+ was configured using observational climate data and calibrated (1994–2001) and validated (2002–2007) using streamflow data at the main outlet and three subwatersheds. Projections considered an ensemble of four Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Global Climate Models (GCMs) for rainfall, and an ensemble of three CMIP6 GCMs for temperatures. Simulations were conducted for the 2030 s (2015–2044), 2060 s (2045–2074), and 2090 s (2075–2100) under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, and SSP4–8.5). Changes were evaluated relative to simulations from observational climate data (1986–2014). New hydrological insights SWAT+ demonstrated sufficient performance across all stations. At the main outlet, calibration (validation) performance statistics were NSE = 0.71 (0.70), KGE = 0.81 (0.80), and PBIAS = −12.7% (−11.9%). Projection relative to the reference period revealed an increase in both blue and green water. By the end of the 21st century, blue water is expected to increase by 17.8%, 36.7%, and 66.5%; green water flow by 8.6%, 13.5%, and 17%; and green water storage by 13.8%, 19.8%, and 65.8% under SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, and SSP4–8.5, respectively. Blue water is more seasonal and sensitive to climate change than green water.

title: Uncertainty assessment of non-stationary stage-discharge relationship with hydrodynamic extensions across flow regimes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Cheng-Wei Yu, Bo-Han Chen
abstract: Study region: Asia Pacific region, Taiwan. Study focus: Accurate discharge estimation in river systems is fundamentally hindered by the scarcity of high-flow measurements and the complexities of channel non-stationarity. This study introduces an integrated framework that reconciles historical in-situ observations with hydrodynamically derived synthetic relationships to bridge critical data gaps. We employ a dual-methodology paradigm, utilizing both a Bayesian inference model (BaRatin) and a fuzzy regression framework to simultaneously address probabilistic variability and inherent measurement uncertainty. This approach ensures a comprehensive evaluation across the full spectrum of flow regimes at two gauging stations in the Wu River Basin. New hydrological insights: This research explicitly incorporates high-flow extensions generated via the Height Above the Nearest Drainage (HAND) method into the uncertainty assessment, offering a physically consistent approach that utilizes hydraulic constraints rarely explored in rating-curve literature. Results demonstrate that while uncertainty is most pronounced under low-flow conditions due to channel irregularities, the bounds converge significantly to within ± 35%–75% in high-flow regimes. The Bayesian method effectively captures structural errors in complex channel–floodplain reaches, whereas fuzzy regression offers a computationally efficient alternative for data-scarce scenarios. Notably, integrating HAND-based hydrodynamic information reduces high-flow bias and enhances the continuity between empirical and synthetic segments. This framework establishes a statistically defensible basis for discharge estimation, significantly improving uncertainty quantification in both gauged and ungauged catchments.

title: Climate forcing and engineering design controls on household rainwater harvesting system reliability in Peri-urban Dar es Salaam, Tanzania
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Rosemary Kiama Gabriel, Patrick Willems, Jacob Kihila
abstract: Study region: Kizito Huonjwa Street in Kimbiji Ward, Kigamboni Municipality, is a peri-urban coastal settlement in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Study focus: This study evaluated how seasonal rainfall structure, moderate extremes, projected climate forcing, and engineering design were associated with simulated household rooftop rainwater harvesting system (RWHS) reliability. Gridded rainfall and gauge observations were combined with six scenario-complete regional climate model chains under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. Seasonal diagnostics, peak-over-threshold (POT) analysis, empirical quantile mapping (EQM), deterministic daily water balance simulation, and Type II analysis of variance were used to distinguish local design responses from formal variance attribution. Different roof catchment areas, RWHS storage capacities, and household demands were evaluated. New hydrological insights for the region: Across the 864 scenario simulations, engineering design terms accounted for 75.7% of simulated reliability variance, compared with 18.9% for the included climate forcing terms. Storage capacity had the largest individual contribution within the fitted design, followed by household demand, climate model identity, and roof area. For the climate model-based stress testing results, the rainfall scenario median differences were smaller than the corresponding inter-modal spread. These results are conditional on the evaluated factor ranges, six-model ensemble, daily rainfall forcing, deterministic RWHS formulation, and the absence of validation against observed household tank operation.

title: Low-flow resilience and anthropogenic influences in mid-sized catchments: Regionalised hydrological modelling in the Creuse basin (France)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Stéphanie Aulong, Gianni Bellocchi, Charly Bequeret, Vincent Cailliez
abstract: Study region Accurate low-flow prediction in small, ungauged catchments is essential for sustainable water resource management, particularly in regions vulnerable to increasing drought severity. This study examines the heterogeneous river basins of the Creuse Department, France. Study focus The GR6J hydrological model was calibrated using a bi-objective function (log-NSE and percent bias) targeting summer low-flows at 12 gauged stations. The calibrated model was then forced by 100 stochastic hydroclimatic trajectories (1995–2024) and regionalised across 170 ungauged basins. New hydrological insights for the region Low-flow regimes show pronounced spatial heterogeneity. Specific discharges (QMNA) range from near-zero in many small headwater basins (< 20 km²), which frequently approach flow cessation, to more sustained flows in larger basins. Some medium‑sized basins also display unexpectedly low specific discharges due to limited storage, high evaporative demand and geological constraints. Basin area influences absolute discharge but fails to fully explain specific flow variability. Anthropogenic regulation further modulates resilience. Reservoir operations distort model parameters (particularly the slow‑storage component X6) and reduce transferability. Small hydraulic structures emerge as critical, yet under‑quantified, contributors to water retention. Empirical (QMNA P20) and probabilistic (QMNA5 GEV and log‑normal) indicators show systematic offsets, with log‑normal estimates proving more conservative, affecting abstraction thresholds. This is the first spatially explicit probabilistic assessment of low‑flow hazards and anthropogenic modifications in the Creuse. It supports adaptive water management under increasing climatic pressure.

title: Benchmarking traditional interpolation and machine learning methods for 3D hydrogeological modeling in complex multi-aquifer systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Abdelrahman Ahmed Ali Abdelrahman, Andrea Cominola, Alberto Guadagnini, Robert Bussert, Irina Engelhardt
abstract: Study region This study focuses on a geologically complex multi-aquifer system in the Berlin-Brandenburg region of the North German Basin. The area is shaped by repeated Quaternary glaciations resulting in a heterogeneous geological architecture characterized by glaciotectonic deformation, overdeepened valleys, erosion windows, and discontinuous aquifers. Study focus We present a scalable and transferable workflow to construct high-resolution three-dimensional hydrogeological models by integrating borehole data and interpreted geological cross-sections within a unified label-based framework. We systematically compare conventional interpolation techniques (inverse distance weighting and nearest neighbor) and machine learning approaches (decision trees, random forests, AdaBoost, XGBoost, k-nearest neighbors, and support vector machines), including deep learning models (artificial neural networks) to evaluate their ability to reconstruct complex heterogeneous subsurface structures. New hydrological insights for the region The Berlin-Brandenburg multi-aquifer system is controlled by highly discontinuous glacial structures, including overdeepened valleys, erosion windows, and fault-related discontinuities that govern aquifer connectivity and potential pathways for vertical groundwater exchange. Our results demonstrate the ability of the proposed artificial neural network to reconstruct key hydrogeological features while preserving their spatial continuity. It also outperforms the benchmark methods evaluated in this study upon achieving a test accuracy of 98% and a weighted F1-score of 0.98. By preserving the spatial continuity of aquifers and aquitards, the reconstructed geological architecture provides the structural foundation required for physically consistent assignment of hydraulic properties in future groundwater models. As such, it supports improved representation of structural heterogeneity controlling groundwater flow and potential salinity migration in the North German Basin.

title: Future runoff responses to dynamic coal mining expansion and climate change in China's Kuye river basin using a modified hydrological model
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Guoxin Sun, Dengfeng Liu, Bo Ming, Guanghui Ming, Jinkai Luan, Qiang Li, Fubo Zhao, Mohd Yawar Ali Khan, Fiaz Hussain, Xiaohui Jiang
abstract: Study Region The Kuye River Basin (KRB), an intensive coal-mining watershed in the middle reaches of the Yellow River, China. Study Focus Despite relatively stable precipitation, the KRB has experienced substantial runoff decline, suggesting strong mining impacts on watershed hydrology. Conventional hydrological models often fail to represent mining-induced surface alteration and groundwater leakage. This study developed a modified SWAT-M model by defining mining areas as an independent land-use category. A multi-basin comparative analysis was conducted to identify the causes of runoff decline, and future runoff (2031–2100) was projected under 16 combined climate–land-use scenarios derived from seven CMIP6 models and the PLUS model. New Hydrological Insights for the Region During the major mining-expansion period (1990–2010), the standardized runoff depth at Wenjiachuan declined at −4.10 mm/a, substantially exceeding the decline in the less-disturbed Jialu River Basin (−1.36 mm/a), indicating that mining-induced hydrological disturbance is a major driver of runoff reduction. Explicit representation of mining areas improved model performance; during 2011–2020, NSE increased from −0.13 to 0.41 at Wangdaohengta and from 0.02 to 0.44 at Wenjiachuan. Future runoff was primarily controlled by climate forcing and generally increased with higher radiative forcing. Relative to the historical period, runoff at Wangdaohengta ranged from −49.75% to + 26.1%, whereas runoff at Shenmu and Wenjiachuan remained below historical levels under all scenarios, with a maximum reduction of 67.0% at the basin outlet.

title: Severe groundwater contamination in an industrialized coastal aquifer of northeastern Algeria: Integrated hydrogeochemical characterization and assessment of environmental and human health risks
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Loubna Nefla, Amira Bergal, Warda Boumaraf, Abderraouf Soukeur, Mostafa R. Abukhadra, May Bin-Jumah, Ahmed A. Allam, Viktoria Mikita, Péter Szűcs, Mohamed Hamdy Eid
abstract: Study region This study investigates the groundwater quality in the Skikda region, northeastern Algeria, an area characterized by intensive industrial activities, agricultural pressures, and seawater intrusion. Study focus Groundwater quality in industrialized coastal regions is under severe threat from anthropogenic contamination. Forty-four groundwater samples were analyzed for 17 physicochemical parameters and heavy metals (Cd, Cr, Pb, Ni, Cu, Zn). An integrated framework combining Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), PHREEQC geochemical modeling, and multi-pathway health risk assessment was employed to identify contamination sources, elucidate hydrogeochemical processes, and quantify environmental and human health risks. New hydrological insight All samples exceeded WHO drinking water standards for Cd, Cr, and Pb. SOM identified three clusters representing extreme industrial contamination, moderate contamination and carbonate dissolution, and seawater intrusion. PCA validated these findings, attributing variance to industrial pollution, seawater intrusion, and geogenic inputs. PHREEQC modeling confirmed carbonate and evaporite dissolution have significant impact on water quality. Environmental indices indicated severe pollution in the aquifer system. Health risk assessment models indicated that potential non-carcinogenic (HI > 1.0) and carcinogenic (CR > 1 ×10⁻⁴) risks substantially exceed standard regulatory thresholds across the sampled area. Based on the exposure models, children represent the most vulnerable demographic, with calculated mean Hazard Index and Total Carcinogenic Risk values indicating a need for urgent groundwater management and alternative water sourcing. The findings provide a replicable methodological framework for assessing similarly impacted industrialized Mediterranean coastal aquifers.

title: Extreme drought evolution and buffering effects of reservoir regulation using a spatially composite drought index in the Poyang Lake Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuge Wang, Xiekang Wang
abstract: Study region Poyang Lake Basin, China Study focus Extreme droughts in large river-lake basins arise from coupled meteorological, hydrological, and ecological anomalies, yet their spatial heterogeneity and regulation by human infrastructure remain difficult to quantify. A spatially adaptive Local Composite Drought Index (LCDI) was developed by integrating precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, NDVI, and soil moisture during 2000–2024 using deseasonalized anomalies and PCA-derived weights. Hydro-climatic zoning and downstream water-body changes were further analyzed to assess spatial drought heterogeneity and reservoir-associated buffering effects. New hydrological insights for the region The LCDI showed strong agreement with SPEI-1, with 99.39% of the basin meeting the correlation criterion, and showed variable skill in identifying hydrological drought at tributary stations. Event tracking identified 2003, 2011, 2019, and 2022 as major drought years with distinct expansion and migration patterns. The 2003 and 2011 droughts affected more than 97% of the basin at peak extent, while the 2022 drought expanded from 11.73% to 98.68% within one month. Severe-extreme drought risk was highest in lowland alluvial and lake-wetland zones. After Xiajiang and Liaofang reservoirs construction, dry-season water body area increased by 26.4–61.6% and 37.4–103.4%, respectively, with positive equivalent water-level residuals of 1.58–7.29 m during recent droughts. These results demonstrate the value of LCDI for monitoring spatially heterogeneous droughts and evaluating reservoir-associated drought buffering in regulated river-lake basins.

title: Multi-mode SAR observations of interannual frozen regimes of glacial lakes in central Himalaya
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Meimei Zhang, Fang Chen, Lei Wang, Hang Zhao, Tonni Agustiono Kurniawan, Lu Yi
abstract: Study region The Koshi River Basin in central Himalaya. Study focus Many glacial lakes (GLs) in the Himalayas may freeze or become buried beneath seasonal snow cover during winter. These frozen or snow-covered lakes can persist through the cold season, altering lake thermal conditions, influencing ice thickness evolution, and affecting the timing and intensity of potential glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the following melt season. However, the spatial distribution characteristics and interannual dynamics of such lakes remain poorly understood, and quantitative assessments of the overall frozen percentage are still lacking. Here, we conduct a multi-mode synthetic aperture radar (SAR) investigation to automatically identify frozen/snow-covered GLs across the Koshi River Basin in central Himalaya from 2014 to 2024. To minimize misclassification from other low-backscatter or snow-covered areas, summer GLs were initially mapped from optical imagery to define their potential lake boundaries. Then an adaptive thresholding approach was developed to identify frozen/snow-covered GLs within the dilated extents of summer lakes, based on histogram edge detection on winter Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR-2 imagery. This method enables the integration of SAR extraction results obtained from various radar configurations. The extracted results demonstrated high consistency with manual interpretation, yielding a precision of 0.84 and a Kappa coefficient of 0.78 for Sentinel-1 VH data, and a precision of 0.78 and a Kappa coefficient of 0.76 for ALOS PALSAR-2 HH data. New hydrological insights for the region From 2014–2024, frozen and snow-covered GLs covered an average total area of 69.28 km², primarily concentrated in central basin and southern high-relief regions. A notable expansion was detected in 2023–2024, particularly in the main mountain range and northern flat areas, where anomalously high temperatures and enhanced surface runoff were observed. In 2015 and 2021, a widespread occurrence of frozen lakes was identified in the western mountains, likely associated with above-average snowfall. Overall, approximately 81% of summer GLs in the Koshi River Basin remained frozen or snow-covered through winter, indicating a significant potential impact on spring melt dynamics and downstream flood hazards.

title: Upper Danube low flow in the Anthropocene: Simulating impacts and changes from 1870 to 2100
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Philipp Stanzel, Harald Kling, Fabio Lerche, Valentin L. Weis, Albert Ossó
abstract: Study region The study region is the Upper Danube Basin upstream of Vienna (∼100,000 km²) in Central Europe. Study focus The study investigates long‑term hydrological changes in the basin with a focus on low flow discharge and seasonal occurrence. An exceptionally long, daily hydrological time series covering 1870–2100 is generated using a hydrological model, which also simulates reservoir operation at major dams and glacier mass balance. The model is driven by observed meteorological data from 1870 to 2023 and bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 for the future. New hydrological insights for the region The hydrological simulations reproduce observed discharge and low flow dynamics well and reveal substantial past and future changes. Historically, Danube low flow discharge at Vienna increased by around 15% during the 20th century. Approximately one third of this past increase can be attributed to the construction and operation of reservoirs and two thirds to regional warming. Future projections show a trend of declining low flow discharge, with stronger decreases under the high emission scenario (SSP5–8.5 multi-model median of −18% until the end of the 21st century). The contrasting past and future responses in low flow discharge are explained by a shift in low flow occurrence from winter to autumn. The demonstrated gradual alteration of the seasonal flow regime of the Upper Danube, and its impact on low flow, have relevant implications for regional water management.

title: Exploratory analysis of short-duration rainfall extremes from sub-hourly observations in Northern Europe
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Sigrid Schødt Hansen, Sara Maria Lerer, Roland Löwe, Hjalte Jomo Danielsen Sørup, Peter Steen Mikkelsen
abstract: Study Region Sub-hourly rainfall records from 2438 rain gauges in Denmark, Germany, Norway, Poland, and Sweden. Study Focus Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves are commonly used for deriving design rainfall events, but estimation methods and accessibility vary across countries. This study explores whether harmonised sub-hourly rainfall observations from multiple countries can be analysed using one uniform baseline framework, and what this analysis reveals about the consistency and spatial structure of transnational IDF estimates. Using Annual Maximum Series (AMS) for durations of 15 min to 12 h, the Generalised Extreme Value (GEV) distribution, and L-moment estimation, we estimated GEV parameters and 10-year return levels and assessed internal and external consistency. New Hydrological Insights for the Region L-moment ratio diagrams and goodness-of-fit tests support the GEV distribution across the study area. While location and scale parameters exhibit large-scale spatial patterns with a latitudinal gradient, shape parameters are spatially heterogeneous. Return levels estimated using our uniform method show moderate to strong agreement with national reference datasets, with mean relative errors from −32 to 15.1% across countries, and most national estimates falling within the bootstrap 95% confidence intervals of our estimates. Discrepancies are largest in Poland and Germany, reflecting differences in record length, temporal resolution, and methodology. The results show that harmonised sub-hourly rainfall records can support consistent transnational IDF estimation and provide a basis for an open-access transnational IDF dataset.

title: Regionalization of a rainfall-runoff model for flood prediction over the Island of Tahiti, French Polynesia
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Garance Tanguy, Lydie Sichoix, Christophe Bouvier
abstract: Study region The Island of Tahiti, prone to heavy rainfall and flash floods that regularly cause severe damage. Study focus The aim of this paper is to build a rainfall-runoff model to estimate floods in any catchment of the island. A distributed conceptual and parsimonious event-based model was designed to fit the observed hydrological spatial variability. It combines the SCS-SMA (Soil Conservation Service - Soil Moisture Accounting) as a runoff production function with a Lag-and-Route routing function, both operating over a mesh of cells. The complete model was calibrated in 11 catchments across the island, and their parameters were related to catchment descriptors related to soil moisture, geology and level of urbanization. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Two parameters were chosen to handle the hydrological variability between catchments: the initial level in the reservoir of the runoff model, H0, and an index linked to the flow velocity in the routing model, µ. For natural catchments, an effective relationship was established between the median values of H0 and the index of regionalized antecedent precipitation. The proportion of urbanization was a secondary factor in explaining H0. µ was related to the geological characteristics of the catchment. This rainfall-runoff model can be used to calculate design floods for the whole island of Tahiti, but needs to be improved for use in flood forecasting for real events.

title: A comprehensive assessment of temporal limit and efficacy of Budyko framework in capturing various climate change and human intervention scenarios using a controlled synthetic environment over ten Indian basins
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Balaram Shaw, Pushkar Sharma, Bramha Dutt Vishwakarma
abstract: Study Region 10 Indian basins Study Focus The traditional Budyko framework (TBF) is a simple model developed for studying the long-term mean behaviour of natural catchments, assuming negligible storage change. However, efficacy of the framework under climate change is still debated, with limited clarity on timescales at which the model can be applied. Moreover, how does storage change driven by climate and humans affect the traditional and modified Budyko framework, remains an open question. Since answering these questions require analysis of alternate scenarios, we developed a controlled synthetic environment that simulates catchment hydrology for various scenarios characterised by plausible climate change and anthropogenic activities, further validated by observation data. New Hydrological Insights for the Region We found that TBF is appropriate for capturing climate change signals but not anthropogenic storage changes, with precipitation change dominating over temperature change in modulating water-balance. The conventional approach of substituting precipitation with effective precipitation (Precipitation – Storage change) is limited in its efficacy and fails when storage changes are anthropogenic. The optimal temporal length over which TBF can be applied is 2 years for arid regions and 1 year for semi-arid regions. These findings advance our insights into TBF’s applicability in regional conditions and the extent to which it can be used in changing environments and prompts a re-evaluation of how the storage change term is incorporated within the framework.

title: Machine learning-based identification of shallow groundwater potential zones for sustainable groundwater management in the Guna-Tana landscape, Ethiopia
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Walelign K. Endalew, Seifu A. Tilahun, Ayenew D. Ayalew, Ashebir Sewale Belay, Nicola Fohrer, Fasikaw A. Zimale
abstract: Study region Guna-Tana landscape of the upper Blue Nile basin, Ethiopia. Study focus Shallow wells are often drilled without proper hydrogeological investigation, resulting in frequent failures. Smallholder farmers and development agents need guiding maps, as trial-and-error well siting consumes significant resources and time. Successful well siting requires delineating shallow groundwater potential zones (SGWPZs) with favorable hydrogeological conditions. This research aimed to identify SGWPZs within the Guna-Tana landscape of Ethiopia. To achieve this, advanced machine learning algorithms (MLAs), Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Classification and Regression Tree (CART), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) were employed. Groundwater yield data from 1903 hand-dug wells (HDWs) were used as the target variable, and a diverse set of environmental and geospatial features were used as predictors. Each model was trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation (5-fold CV) within the R-programming environment. New hydrological insights for the region Groundwater potential classified as very high accounted for 7%, 16%, 20%, 7%, and 7% in RF, XGB, CART, SVM, and KNN respectively. Area under the curve (AUC-ROC) scores for RF, XGB, CART, SVM, and KNN were 0.80, 0.78, 0.74, 0.75, and 0.70, respectively. These data imply that RF and XGB are the most reliable models for mapping SGWPZs. The study supports sustainable groundwater management and improves water security in the area by providing policymakers with insightful information.

title: Has hydrological alteration driven ecosystem service risks in large floodplain lakes? A novel framework for spatiotemporal assessment and hydrological thresholds identification
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haoran Wang, Rongrong Wan, Bing Li, Jing Yao, Guishan Yang
abstract: Study region Poyang Lake, China’s largest freshwater lake, is a critical ecological hub. Study focus Hydrological alteration strongly affects floodplain ecosystem services (ES), yet their spatiotemporal risks and hydrological controls remain poorly understood. We developed an integrated framework based on ecological deviation to assess ES risks and identify hydrological drivers and thresholds for four leading ES: water supply (WS), nutrient retention (NR), habitat support (HS), and flood regulation (FR). New hydrological insights for the region The framework revealed spatiotemporal differences in ES risks following the Three Gorges Dam operation. WS experienced the most severe degradation, with high-capacity areas declining from 22.76% to 8.62%, and risk increased across 97.37% of the lake area. HS remained relatively stable, although low-suitability areas expanded from 34.38% to 47.15%, mainly in sub-lakes and marginal zones. In contrast, NR and FR risks reduced across 81.07% and 97.39% of the lake, respectively. Temporally, WS risk increased (P < 0.01), FR risk decreased (P < 0.05), while HS and NR showed no significant trends. XG-Boost analysis revealed ES-specific and risk-level-dependent hydrological controls. Drivers for WS and HS risks shifted from drought timing (low-risk) to drought duration and water-level extremes (high-risk). NR risk exhibited the largest shift, increasingly controlled by rising and flood-season water levels. The framework provides a tool for quantifying ES risks under hydrological alteration and supporting adaptive management in floodplain lakes.

title: Analytical framework for sensitivity evaluation of multi-objective water resources operations in California's Central Valley
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Khandaker Iftekharul Islam, James Matthew Gilbert
abstract: Study region California's Central Valley, a critical hub of the state's water management system, serves around 40 million people, sustains productive agriculture, and supports biodiversity. Study focus Effective management of California's water resources requires understanding how operational decisions interact across competing objectives, yet isolating individual and combined policy influences remains challenging given the complexity of integrated water system models. The operational structure encompasses both categorical levers, such as regulatory protection and priority allocation, and numeric drivers, including carryover storage, demand management, and flow requirements, which complicate impact evaluation across water resource measures. To address this, we developed a scenario-driven framework that integrates full-factorial design, rank-biserial correlation, and variance ratio into a Combined Sensitivity Score (CSS) using CalLite model outputs. New hydrological insights for the region The CSS framework quantified sensitivities across reservoir storage, water deliveries, river flows, and Delta salinity under contrasting hydroclimatic conditions. Demand reductions yielded the most significant single-lever response (CSS up to 1.09), while regulatory relaxation under D-1641 produced severe salinity deterioration (CSS = 1.27 in dry years). Three-way interactions among demand, minimum flow, and carryover generated compounded responses (CSS up to 1.3) beyond their individual effects. Dry years showed heightened sensitivity, underscoring system vulnerability to drought. The analysis provides insight into specific operational actions that enhance system outcomes and supports decision-making for adaptive, equitable management of multi-objective water systems.

title: Spatial variability of rainfall in the Colorado Rocky Mountains: A comparison of radar-derived and rain gauge data
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): M. Sears, S. Kampf, D. Barnard, R. Schumacher, Q. Miller, M. Richardson, S. Weder Loya, S. Struthers, K.L. Rasmussen
abstract: Study Region Flash floods in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, USA are triggered by intense rainfall during convective storms, and the likelihood and severity of flash flooding increases following wildfires. Middle elevations (∼1500–2500 m) have experienced the largest flash floods in the past, causing researchers to speculate that rainfall intensity may vary with elevation. Study Focus This study combines Multi-Radar/Multi-Sensor System (MRMS), Parameter-elevation Regressions on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM), and Gridded Surface Meteorological (gridMET), and tipping bucket precipitation datasets to evaluate how warm season rainfall intensities vary with elevation and side of the mountain range in northern Colorado. The MRMS data are compared with tipping bucket gauges to evaluate which data source best predicts streamflow occurrence. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The east side of the mountain range experienced both higher warm season total precipitation and rainfall intensities than the west side during 2021–2023. The relationship between elevation and rainfall intensity was inconsistent between years, indicating no strong elevation effect on rainfall intensity. MRMS rainfall intensities predicted binary streamflow occurrence as accurately as tipping buckets east of the mountains in wildfire-affected areas, whereas tipping buckets performed significantly better to the west due to poor radar coverage. The MRMS dataset may outperform tipping buckets for detecting storms that trigger stream occurrences in areas with high radar coverage, due to its broader spatial coverage than most gauge networks.

title: Detailed characteristics and applications of raindrop size distribution under different rainfall types based on multiple disdrometers in the trumpet-shaped terrain of the Western Tianshan Mountains
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yong Zeng, Lianmei Yang, Zepeng Tong, Abuduwaili Abulikemu
abstract: Study region The trumpet-shaped topography of the Western Tianshan Mountains (TSTTM). Study focus Based on observations from multiple Parsivel2 at different locations and elevations within TSTTM during the summers of 2020–2023, this study reveals the fine spatial structure of raindrop size distribution (DSD) and microphysical parameters under various rainfall types (RTs) at TSTTM. Region-specific algorithms for radar-based quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and rainfall kinetic energy estimation (RKEE) were developed for different RTs, and the applicability of regionally consistent algorithms across stations was investigated. New hydrological insights for the region Stratiform rainfall (SR) within TSTTM dominated the rainfall process, occurring nearly 39 times more frequently than convective rainfall (CR). The ratio exhibited its lowest value at Nileke, approximately 16, and its highest value at Xinyuan, approximately 116. Quantitative analysis reveals the fine-scale spatial heterogeneity of DSD within a small-scale complex terrain. In both SR and CR, Tekesi (Nileke) exhibits the highest (lowest) concentration of small drops, while Nileke (Xinyuan) has the highest (lowest) concentration of large drops. For SR (CR), the range of the logarithmic generalized intercept parameter (log10 N w ) was from 3.029 (2.688) m⁻³ mm⁻¹ in Nileke to 3.500 (2.970) m⁻³ mm⁻¹ in Xinyuan. Concurrently, the median volume diameter (D 0 ) ranged from 1.002 (2.375) mm in Xinyuan to 1.315 (2.653) mm in Nileke. The Z − R, KE time −R, KE mm −D m and KE time −Z Ku (Z Ka ) relations for SR and CR at individual stations and for overall data were established, varying across different RTs and stations. The evaluation results confirm that the regional-average radar QPE algorithm and RKEE scheme can lead to significant errors at specific stations. This study is of considerable value in elucidating the fine structure of DSD under different RTs within TSTTM, thereby enhancing the accuracy of radar-based QPE and RKEE at various stations.

title: A machine learning-based framework for basin-specific flood damage warning-support in rapid-response basins
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Soon Ho Kwon, Donghyun Kim, Gunhui Chung, Seungyub Lee
abstract: Study Region The Wangsuk Stream Basin is a rapid-response basin in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, where short travel times and downstream urban exposure constrain flood-warning lead time. Study Focus We developed a machine learning (ML)-based, basin-specific warning-support framework that translates observed hydrometeorological conditions into damage-oriented support levels. Forty flood events from 2008 to 2020 were reconstructed from rainfall, water level, damage, and alert records. Observed damage classes were derived from national disaster records and predicted using peak downstream water level and cumulative 3-h antecedent rainfall. Four ML classifiers were trained on 27 events and evaluated using 10-min prediction records from temporally held-out events. Ensemble agreement and a risk matrix converted modal predicted damage class into four warning-support levels. A 10-min rolling reconstruction evaluated near-peak support using only observations available up to each time step. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The existing alert system kept 13 of 21 damaging events at the baseline Attention level, indicating mismatch between national alert criteria and local damage occurrence. The classifiers produced F1-scores of 0.87–0.90 on held-out 10-min prediction records, and retrospective reconstruction assigned all damaging events above Very Low while keeping non-damaging events at the lowest level. Rolling reconstruction triggered Medium or High support 40–90 min before observed peaks.

title: Characterising recharge, storage and flow pathways in karst aquifers in central Slovenia using stable water isotopes, tritium and chlorine-36
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Vanessa E. Johnston, Filip Šarc, Stanisław Chmiel, Anna Mulczyk, Beata Gebus-Czupyt, Bojan Otoničar
abstract: Study regions Approximately half of Slovenia is underlain by karstified carbonate rocks that host important groundwater resources. The Rovte region in central Slovenia is characterised by fluviokarst, complicating the understanding of aquifer flow pathways and storage. Study focus Determining recharge, storage and flow pathways in karst aquifers remains a major challenge due to the heterogeneity of permeability; ranging from large conduits to micro-fractures. In this study, stable water isotopes (δ²H and δ¹⁸O), together with tritium and chlorine-36, were measured in precipitation, river water, karst springs and deep artesian borehole waters at a biweekly resolution over one year. The aim was to characterise links between infiltration and subsurface flow, and provide information on aquifer properties. New hydrological insights for the region The karst springs emerging from shallow aquifers exhibited rapid and synchronised isotopic trends related with precipitation, indicating rapid groundwater transport through wide conduits and fractures. However, some water storage in soil or near-surface micro-fractures that mobilised only during the heaviest rainfall events was revealed. In contrast, the artesian borehole waters showed little isotopic variability, consistent with well-mixed groundwater deriving from deeper aquifers that likely recharged under cooler conditions and subsequently mixed with small contributions from local shallow aquifers.

title: A wavelet–LSTM framework for mapping large inland water bodies using CYGNSS observations
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuxuan Yang, Yufeng Hu, Zhenhong Li
abstract: Study region This study investigates six representative large lakes distributed across different climatic and hydrological environments: Lake Victoria, Lake Titicaca, Lake Malawi, Lake Tanganyika, Lake Nicaragua, and Lake Maracaibo. These lakes provide diverse conditions for evaluating large-scale inland water mapping using spaceborne Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R). Study focus A wavelet–Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework is developed using Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) observations. Wavelet transform is applied to Delay-Doppler Map (DDM) data to extract multi-scale scattering features, while the LSTM network captures temporal dependencies within the feature sequences. The model is trained using 2021 CYGNSS observations over Lake Victoria and Lake Titicaca, with Global Surface Water data as reference labels. New hydrological insights for the region The proposed framework achieved overall accuracies of 98.53% and 99.10% for Lake Victoria and Lake Titicaca, respectively. Validation over Lake Malawi, Lake Tanganyika, Lake Nicaragua, and Lake Maracaibo yielded overall accuracies of 95.48%, 96.34%, 89.76%, and 93.74%, respectively. The results show that multi-scale DDM features and temporal modeling enable robust large-lake mapping under diverse and complex scattering conditions. Application to Lake Poyang further captured quarterly water variations in 2021 with an average accuracy of 85.24%, demonstrating the potential of GNSS-R for monitoring seasonal lake dynamics.

title: Can we better constrain evapotranspiration estimates in data scarce cold regions? Application of a discharge-constrained modelling framework in Norwegian catchments
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Shaochun Huang, Olga Silantyeva, Emiliano Gelati, Yeliz A. Yilmaz, Kolbjørn Engeland, Lena M. Tallaksen
abstract: Study region 66 Norwegian catchments representing five hydrological regimes in Norway. Study focus This study focuses on estimation of evapotranspiration (ET) in Norwegian catchments where ET estimates are highly uncertain due to sparse ET measurements and high uncertainty in measured precipitation in complex terrain. We propose a large-sample multi-modelling framework to benchmark the ET estimate, using three hydrological models calibrated against daily discharge using three objective functions. The ET simulations were indirectly evaluated using discharge-based criteria in the snow free period, due to lack of direct ET measurements. The ET simulations from model runs fulfilling a set of performance criteria were considered as benchmarks to evaluate and constrain five fine-resolution global ET products. New hydrological insights for the region The results show that the three hydrological models differ in the sensitivity to objective functions and in performance for each hydrological regime. Most global products tend to overestimate ET for the Mountain regime and vary in performance for the other hydrological regimes. By excluding the poorly performing hydrological models and global ET products, the mean uncertainty in annual ET estimates of all catchments reduces from 265 mm to 73 mm. The constrained annual ET is around 332 ± 47 mm in the Atlantic regime, 320 ± 71 mm in the Baltic and Transition regimes, 287 ± 62 mm in the Inland regime and 223 ± 54 mm in the Mountain regime.

title: Hydropower potential derived from streamflow extremes for Alaska, USA
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Abigail Birnbaum, Jeremy Giovando
abstract: Study region: Alaska, USA. Study focus: Alaska is an expansive region known for its abundant natural resources, including thousands of miles of streams and rivers. These reaches represent potential opportunities for future hydropower development that could provide reliable energy supply for local communities. There is limited long-term high temporal resolution streamflow data available for the region, making data-driven estimates of potential hydropower and its variability across the state challenging. This study provides a novel data-driven approach for hydropower capacity estimation across Alaska. We develop supervised machine learning models using basin hydrography and peak annual streamflow to predict average daily flow conditions and estimates of hydropower capacity. New hydrological insights for the region: We perform both deterministic and stochastic hydropower estimation across 67 sites with annual peak streamflow available and identify approximately 800 MW of total potential hydropower capacity distributed across these sites, with a range of 750–860 MW across 10,000 stochastic simulations. Our study provides the first step towards more comprehensive hydropower estimation for this critical region, highlighting the need for future work integrating high-resolution spatial data, community needs, and economic constraints in estimates of potential hydropower development in Alaska.

title: An explainable deep learning framework for torrential rainfall forecasting in Guangdong: Accuracy gains and physical insights
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ruqing Zhang, Wei Shangguan, Wenzong Dong, Yang Shi, Feini Huang, Lina Huang
abstract: Study region The three torrential rainfall centers in Guangdong province, southern China: Haifeng, Fogang, and Enping Study focus This work develops an explainable deep learning framework (named Explainable Two-Stage Spatial-Temporal Multiple Window, ETS-STMW) to (1) improve the accuracy of clear-rain forecasts and the Threat Score of torrential rainfall prediction; and (2) apply Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to identify key meteorological factors and their nonlinear interactions that drive rainfall and torrential rainfall formation in each center. New hydrological insights for the region Outperforming traditional numerical weather prediction model, ETS-STMW better captures precipitation distributions, elevating clear-rain accuracy from 0.66∼0.76 to >0.85 and increasing the torrential rainfall Threat Score from <0.1 to 0.36∼0.44. Notably, the optimal configurations of the spatial and temporal windows vary significantly across the three torrential rainfall centers, reflecting their distinct underlying precipitation formation mechanisms. While atmospheric water vapor is identified as the dominant controlling factor, the specific processes that trigger torrential rainfall differ markedly among the centers. Specifically, torrential rainfall in Haifeng is strongly modulated by low-level jets and orographic lifting; in Fogang, it is closely linked to mid-level trough-ridge systems; and in Enping, it is primarily governed by low-level circulation configuration. Furthermore, distinct diurnal cycles are revealed: Haifeng and Fogang experience peak rainfall from nighttime to morning, whereas Enping shows a pronounced early-morning maximum. These findings provide critical physically grounded, region-specific guidance for enhancing fine-scale torrential rainfall forecasting.

title: Hydrological amplification and landscape-resetting sediment pulses: A 45-year baseline evaluation of the 2025 Mataian River landslide-dam event, Taiwan
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jui-Yi Ho, Che-Hsin Liu, Pei-Chi Chen, Shih‑Chiang Lee, Chih-Hsin Chang, Naoki Sakai, Yi-Chin Chen, Chen-Yu Chen, Hung-Po Huang, Hongey Chen
abstract: Study region The Mataian River catchment, a highly fractured and tectonically active alpine watershed located adjacent to the Longitudinal Valley Fault in eastern Taiwan. Study focus This study investigates the 2025 catastrophic landslide-dam event, the largest sub-aerial landslide in Taiwan's history. The research leverages unprecedented datasets: 1) a 45-year baseline (1980–2024) of daily discharge and sediment flux; 2) high-resolution topographic data captured pre- and post-breach; and 3) high-frequency monitoring capturing the real-time propagation and downstream evolution of the outburst flood wave. New hydrological insights for the region 1) Peak breach discharge reached 8800–8860 m³ /s, nearly four times the 100-year flood design capacity; 2) DoD analysis revealed localized bed aggradation up to 13.9 m, with single-event deposition being 1.68 times the cumulative aggradation of the preceding 45 years; and 3) By October 13, 2025, 305.4 million m³ of residual sediment remained stored, with over 80% retained within the source area and dam remnant. Representing over 23 times the comprehensive annual sediment baseline (including suspended and bed load), the gradual remobilization of this colossal source poses an enduring risk of chronic aggradation under Taiwan's hyper-dynamic climate, necessitating a transition to long-term, catchment-scale sediment routing.

title: Spatiotemporal variation of soil water and response patterns to key influencing factors in plantations on the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yujia Chen, Dongmei Wang, Yanhui Wang, Kun Xu, Yaxiao Dong
abstract: Study region The Loess Plateau, China. Study focus Large-scale afforestation on the Loess Plateau has substantially improved the regional environment but has also intensified soil water depletion, highlighting the conflict between forest water consumption and water scarcity. However, systematic analyses of the spatiotemporal dynamics of post-afforestation volumetric soil water content (SWC) remain limited, particularly regarding response transitions of key influencing factors. A comprehensive understanding of the multi-factor regulation of SWC following afforestation, including the response patterns of key influencing factors, is therefore urgently needed. We compiled and screened data from published literature on Loess Plateau plantations to construct a database of SWC (0–100 cm) and its drivers. Changes in SWC in response to mean annual precipitation (MAP), stand age, mean annual temperature (MAT), land-use conversion type, and soil properties were analyzed, emphasizing breakpoint characteristics of key influencing factors. New hydrological insights for the region The results showed that SWC in the 0–100 cm soil layer declined markedly after afforestation, with an average relative reduction of 13.49%. The relative decline generally increased with stand age but decreased with increasing MAP. MAP and stand age were the primary explanatory factors of the spatiotemporal variation in relative SWC change, with relative contributions of 20.98% and 19.71%, respectively. Moreover, the pattern of relative SWC decline with increasing stand age differed significantly among MAP zones: when MAP ≤ 600 mm, the relative change in SWC exhibited an initial sharp decrease followed by a more gradual decrease, with the stand-age breakpoint delayed from 15 years (MAP ≤ 400 mm) to 22 years (500 mm ≤ MAP ≤ 600 mm); in contrast, when MAP > 600 mm, the relative SWC decline exhibited a continuous but slight reduction without an evident statistical breakpoint. The findings of this study provide a scientific basis for the regional zoning of afforestation and integrated forest and water resources management on the Loess Plateau under the principle of afforestation based on water availability.

title: Divergent drivers of runoff changes in the Indus eastern tributaries: Insights from attribution analysis based on the Budyko framework
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ehab Aletoum, Taihua Wang, Muhammad Umer, Muhammad Ibrar Ihteshaam, Ahmed Samir Abowarda, Zihan Yan, Dawen Yang
abstract: Study region The eastern tributaries of the Indus River Basin: Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi, and Sutlej. Study focus Using discharge records from the Water and Power Development Authority, Pakistan and climatic data from reanalysis datasets, this study constructs long-term, up-to-date hydro-climatic time series spanning 1951–2024 for the eastern Indus tributaries. After identifying the abrupt change years, the observed runoff changes between the pre-change and post-change periods are then attributed to climatic and residual non-climatic drivers based on a Fu-type Budyko framework. New hydrological insights for the region The observed runoff declines are evident at all tributaries during 1951–2024, which could be explained by contrasting drivers. Climatic factors are found to dominate the runoff declines at the western sub-basins. In Chenab, the decline is almost entirely driven by climatic factors. Jhelum shows a positive residual effect that partly offsets the climate-induced runoff decline. Precipitation dominates the climatic signal, explaining ∼43–97% of the absolute runoff change, while reference evapotranspiration only contributes a small share. In contrast, non-climatic drivers play a more important role at the eastern sub-basins. The relatively large non-climatic contributions in Ravi and Sutlej (∼47% and 55%) are consistent with intensive regulation, diversions, and consumptive use in these tributaries. These findings highlight that effective water management policy must differentiate between climate-sensitive and human regulation-intensive sub-basins for sustainable water governance in transboundary river basin systems.

title: A framework to compare the performance of spatial disaggregation methods of statistical climate downscaling in South America
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Cristóbal Aboitiz, Cristián Chadwick, Jonathan Barichivich, Jorge Perez-Quezada
abstract: Study region Chile and South America. Study focus Climate change is simulated at a coarse scale with General Circulation Models. Impact and regional studies require downscaling to increase spatial resolution. Several downscaling methods exist, but most studies do not analyze or compare spatial disaggregation process. To overcome this a framework is proposed, which is tested comparing eight methods (Bilinear (BIL), Bicubic (BIC), Inverse Distance Interpolation (DIS), Largest Area Fraction (LAF), Nearest Neighbor (NN), First-Order Conservative (CON1), Second-Order Conservative (CON2), and Ordinary Kriging (KRIG)) using daily temperature and precipitation data at different spatial scales in Chile (using CR2MET V2.5 dataset) and South America (using ERA5-LAND dataset). The concept of maximum scaling factor is introduced: ratio between the coarse grid resolution and the high grid resolution after disaggregation. The maximum scaling factor allows recommending the resolution of disaggregation to avoid variability inflation. The framework consists in aggregating the data to different resolutions and then disaggregating them back to their original grids. Finally, performance is measured with indices to determine which spatial disaggregation method most accurately recovers the original climatic gridded information. New hydrological insights for the region When spatial disaggregating gridded data one should avoid increasing the spatial resolution more than ∼22 times for daily precipitation and ∼11 for temperature in Chile, and ∼14 for precipitation and ∼8 for temperature in South America to avoid variability inflation.

title: An integrated framework for water allocation and pollution control in inter-basin transfer projects under climate change
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zhipeng Fan, Xiang Fu, Jianan Qin, Yu Li
abstract: Study region The Yellow River Basin (YRB) with water transfer from the South-to-North Water Diversion Project (SNWDP). Study focus This study proposes a multi-model framework for water allocation and pollution control in inter-basin transfer project under climate change. The framework integrates the InVEST-PLUS model to project water yield under diverse shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs). It is further coupled with an Interval Fuzzy-Credibility Constrained Bi-Level Flexible Programming (IFBFP) model to address climatic uncertainty and hierarchical decision conflicts. New hydrological insights for the region Results indicate that climate variability is the dominant driver of water yield changes, with statistically significant differences observed across climate scenarios (p < 0.01). Water yield under SSP1–1.9 averages 705.4 × 10⁸ m³ /yr, compared to 412.4 × 10⁸ m³ /yr under SSP2–4.5 and 560.2 × 10⁸ m³ /yr under SSP5–8.5. The SNWDP western route alleviates water deficits under water-stressed scenarios yet amplifies pollutant loads by 42.0%–79.9%, compared to a moderate increase of 1.0%–18.4% under water-sufficient conditions. The proposed framework accommodates diverse decision-maker risk preferences, providing a transferable methodology for scenario-based evaluation of climate-adaptive water governance in the YRB and similar inter-basin transfer systems.

title: Coupled coordination evaluation of irrigation districts in arid regions from the perspective of the water-energy-food-carbon nexus
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yinbo Li, Yuanyuan Zha
abstract: Study Region The Yerqianghe (YEQH) Irrigation District in Xinjiang, China, is an arid region requiring precision management of agricultural and water resources. Study Focus The water-energy-food-carbon (WEFC) nexus system is widely used to analyze the interdependencies of agricultural resources. Existing studies focus on static macro-evaluations or incomplete dimensions, lacking dynamic synthesis that integrates carbon emission constraints into a micro-scale (irrigation district) framework over long-term historical series. This study adopts the CCD model and footprint-based quantitative indicators to evaluate the spatiotemporal evolution trends and driving mechanisms of the WEFC system in the YEQH District from 1989 to 2020. New Hydrological Insights Regional grain output increased from 1 million to 5.5 million tons. The water footprint (-0.35 m3/(kg·a)), energy footprint (-0.74 MJ/(kg·a)), and carbon footprint (−0.06 kg CO2_eq/(kg·a)) demonstrated a decreasing trend. The CCD level transitioned from an uncoordinated stage (pre-2004) to a coordinated development stage (2005–2014), and stepped into a well-coordinated stage after 2015. Water economic productivity (89%), cash crop production (83%), and water productivity (81%) were identified as the core factors driving the CCD development. Furthermore, significant differences in planting patterns, technology application, and input structures have led to an increased balance in development across sub-irrigation districts. These findings substantiate the indispensability of micro-scale irrigation districts in precision management, providing a theoretical basis for formulating differentiated water allocation quotas and agricultural low-carbon policies in Xinjiang.

title: Contrasting environmental drivers of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) O157 and O26 serogroups in surface water and private groundwater supplies of a karst agricultural catchment in western Ireland
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Robert J. Hynes, Zina Alfahl, Louise O'Connor, Florence de Bock, Paul D. Hynds, Jean O'Dwyer, Liam P. Burke
abstract: Study Region This study was conducted in the karstic Black River sub-catchment in western Ireland, where well-draining soils and rapid groundwater recharge promote strong surface-groundwater connectivity and increase the vulnerability of groundwater supplies to microbial contamination. Study Focus This year-long study assessed the prevalence and environmental drivers of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) O157 and O26 in surface waters and groundwater wells from May 2023 to May 2024. Nineteen sites (5 river sites, 14 groundwater wells) were sampled fortnightly. Detection of O157- and O26-associated genes was performed using enrichment-free low-volume filtration with quantitative PCR. Logistic regression identified climatic and anthropogenic predictors of STEC presence. New Hydrological Insights for the Region O157 was detected in 58% of samples (44% surface water, 63% groundwater), while O26 occurred in 27% (29% surface water, 26% groundwater). O157 presence in groundwater was positively associated with cattle density and rainfall, and negatively associated with well depth, suggesting mobilisation and rapid transport following precipitation. In contrast, O26 presence was positively associated with domestic wastewater treatment system density and negatively associated with rainfall, indicating different contamination pathways. In surface waters, O157 was associated with increased cattle density and low discharge, while O26 was associated with low rainfall. These findings reveal distinct drivers and transport pathways for the two dominant STEC serogroups and provide new insight into the dynamics of clinically significant STEC contamination in Irish surface and groundwater systems.

title: A water–food–energy nexus approach to land subsidence management in Isfahan, Iran
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Amir Molajou, Abbas Afshar, Seyed Mostafa Siadatmousavi
abstract: Study Region The Isfahan–Borkhar Plain in central Iran is an arid, groundwater-dependent basin. Intensive agricultural abstraction, recurrent drought, and reduced surface-water inflows have depleted the aquifer and caused severe land subsidence. Study Focus This study develops an integrated water–food–energy nexus simulation–optimisation framework to quantify trade-offs among subsidence mitigation, agricultural income, and groundwater-pumping energy demand. A system dynamics model distinguishes intra-subsystem interrelations (within-subsystem processes) from cross-sector interactions (resource exchanges across subsystems) and is coupled with a multi-objective optimisation approach based on the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II to derive Pareto-efficient management portfolios. The energy dimension is represented through groundwater-pumping demand and tariff assumptions rather than endogenous electricity-supply dynamics. Basin-scale subsidence is modelled as an irreversible response to groundwater-level decline and used as a screening indicator. New hydrological insights for the region Under business-as-usual (BAU) conditions, groundwater depletion is projected to exceed 40 billion cubic metres, while cumulative subsidence is projected to reach approximately 3.5 m by 2060. Results show irrigation-efficiency improvements alone are insufficient, as reduced return flows diminish aquifer recharge. The simulations indicate that substantial mitigation would require combined demand management and managed aquifer recharge. A balanced portfolio, including a 40% reduction in agricultural groundwater use and 150 million cubic metres per year of managed aquifer recharge, limits subsidence to less than 0.5 m and reduces pumping-energy demand by more than 50%. The framework reveals nexus trade-offs and supports basin-scale screening.

title: Water balance assessment based on a three-dimensional transient groundwater modelling of a phosphogypsum stack in Huelva (SW Spain)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Franco Coscia, Estanislao Pujades-Garnes, Rafael Pérez-López, Manuel Olías, Enric Vázquez-Suñé
abstract: Study Region Approximately 120 million tonnes of uncovered phosphogypsum (PG) were deposited over tidal-marsh sediments in the Tinto River estuary, Huelva, southwestern Spain, forming a complex anthropogenic hydrogeological system connected to surrounding estuarine waters and underlying aquifer units. Study Focus This study characterizes the post-operational hydrodynamic behaviour of the PG stack and quantifies its groundwater balance. A hydrogeological conceptual model was evaluated using a three-dimensional transient groundwater-flow model calibrated over 450 days against groundwater-head and discharge observations. The model represents the principal recharge, drainage, surface-water exchange, and groundwater-storage processes. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Results indicate that rainfall infiltrates mainly vertically through the PG stack, whereas groundwater reaching its base discharges laterally toward the marsh through diffuse flow and preferential pathways associated with buried tidal channels. Tidal oscillations propagate into deeper units with attenuation and phase lag. The simulated water balance indicates near-dynamic equilibrium, with negligible net storage change and a near-zero numerical residual, showing that most inflows are redistributed and discharged rather than retained. Overall, the PG stack behaves as a low- to moderate-permeability anthropogenic unconfined aquifer overlying a leaky estuarine aquitard and a more permeable confined aquifer.

title: Stormwater quality dynamics during urban construction: Insights from a counterfactual paired-catchment analysis in southern Finland
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Mohammad Reza Hassani, Teemu Kokkonen, Nora Sillanpää, Harri Koivusalo
abstract: Study region Saunalahdenranta (SR) catchment, Espoo, southern Finland Study focus Urban construction phases introduce abrupt and nonstationary disturbances to stormwater systems, yet their hydrological and water quality impacts remain poorly quantified. This study investigates construction-phase changes in event-scale runoff–pollution dynamics using a paired-catchment counterfactual modeling framework. A nearby stable urban catchment, Vallikallio (VK), was used to define reference-informed buildup–washoff behavior without active construction disturbance, while the SR model was used to simulate a stable benchmark under observed meteorological forcing. Observed–counterfactual differences were evaluated using non-parametric effect sizes and load decomposition. Understanding this dynamic change improves stormwater modeling and adaptive management under nonstationary conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Results showed a sharp, time-bound degradation in stormwater quality, with the annual median of event-mean TSS concentrations increasing 6.6-fold from 2001 to the 2004 construction peak. Rank-biserial effect-size analysis indicated that the probability of observing higher TSS concentrations in SR than in the reference catchment increased to approximately 70–75% during peak construction. Counterfactual comparison further showed that the 2004 observed EMC median was 3.3 times the corresponding reference-informed counterfactual median, which distinguishes the broader observed temporal change from the peak-year divergence relative to stable urban conditions. Load decomposition showed that early-stage deviations were partly hydrology-related, whereas peak-construction divergence was dominated by concentration-related underestimation, consistent with elevated sediment availability. These findings suggest that construction phases can be associated with short-lived but high-impact stormwater-quality regimes not captured by static buildup–washoff parameterizations.

title: Hyperspectral-based inversion of water conservation distribution in wild fruit forests of Emin County, Xinjiang, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Tingwei Song, Liang Guo, Qian Sun, Guizhen Gao, Jing Chen, Qikun Zhang
abstract: Study region In Emin County, Xinjiang, China, the wild fruit forest is one of the native habitats of the rare germplasm resource wild apple, whose geography and ecological functions are vital for regulating the regional water cycle. Study focus The correlation and sensitivity between hyperspectral data, multiple vegetation indices, and water conservation capacity of wild fruit forests were improved using fractional derivative (FOD) and logarithmic transformation methods. The combination of hyperspectral technology and machine-learning can capture the complex nonlinear relationship between the water conservation capacity and ecological environment of wild fruit forests, which is conducive to the construction of mathematical models. The spatial distribution of the water conservation capacity of the wild fruit forest was inverted using Sentinel-2 images combined with hyperspectral technology. New hydrological insights for the region The water holding capacity of soil layer in wild fruit forests is the main component of water conservation (>80%). In low-lying valleys, normalized difference water index (NDWI) and simple ratio (SR) were higher under the dual effects of higher vegetation cover and valley confluence, ensuring the sustainability of water conservation capacity. Soil erosion was more likely to occur in areas with higher slopes, resulting in reduced water conservation capacity. The water conservation capacity of wild fruit forests in the study area showed clear spatial heterogeneity. Overall, the water conservation capacity was poor. The canopy, soil, and litter play a greater role in water storage only in areas with high vegetation coverage.

title: A statistically integrated approach for assessing typhoon-induced rainfall in Taiwan under climate change scenarios
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Chi-Ying Lin, I-Ting Kung, Tsun-Hua Yang
abstract: Study region Taiwan and the adjacent Northwest Pacific typhoon corridor (20.5°–26.5°N, 118.5°–124.5°E), analyzed at 17 rainfall gauges spanning the northern coast, the windward eastern slopes, the Central Mountain Range, and the western plains. Study focus A Northwest Pacific statistical typhoon model, calibrated on 1977–2022 best-track records, is coupled with a two-stage Bayesian rainfall model separating rainfall occurrence from conditional rainfall amount (cross-validated F1 score 0.845; root mean square error below 40 mm). One thousand Monte Carlo realizations were generated for a baseline (1995–2014) and for mid-century (2041–2060) and end-century (2081–2100) periods under Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5 (SSP5–8.5) forcing, followed by site-specific frequency analysis of simulated annual maxima. New hydrological insights Six-hour typhoon rainfall increases at all 17 gauges and all four return periods examined (10–200 years), by approximately 49% on average, rising from about 45% at mid-century to about 53% at end-century.
