The response is topographically organized, from 10.6% at Dawu to 115.5% at Keelung, strongest along the northern coast and over the mountainous interior, and more moderate in basins sheltered by the Central Mountain Range, while the frequency of moderate (>50 mm) and heavy (>200 mm) 6-hour events rises at nearly all stations. Relative change, not absolute return level, is the appropriate basis for revising Taiwan’s design rainfall.

title: A multi-method bias correction framework for ensemble-based reference evapotranspiration forecasting
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Mengting Chen, Yingying Shen, Haili Wang, Yufeng Luo, Xiaojun Wang, Shufeng Liu, Xueyin Zhao
abstract: Study region This study focuses on Guangdong Province in southern China, a typical humid subtropical monsoon region. Study focus Accurate forecasting of reference evapotranspiration (ETo) is essential for irrigation management, yet raw ensemble forecasts suffer from systematic biases that propagate nonlinearly through ETo models. This study systematically evaluates three statistical post-processing methods—Kalman filter (KF), Bayesian model averaging (BMA), and LightGBM (LGBM). The corrected meteorological variables were used to drive three ETo models with distinct physical mechanisms: FAO56 Penman-Monteith (PM), Hargreaves-Samani (HS), and Priestley-Taylor (PT). A multi-level evaluation framework combining deterministic, probabilistic, and sensitivity analyses was employed to decompose the effects of bias correction versus model structure. New hydrological insights for the region Raw ensemble forecasts exhibit systematic biases across meteorological variables, and the effectiveness of correction methods varies. The PM-based forecasts show the closest agreement with the PM-based reference ETo, and the LGBM–PM combination yields the highest accuracy at 50% of stations (mostly coastal); while the KF–HS combination remains a competitive alternative at many inland stations. Sensitivity analysis reveals that bias correction reshapes the error sensitivity of ETo models: radiation becomes the dominant error source in the PM model after temperature and humidity errors are suppressed. A spatially differentiated strategy is proposed. This framework provides improved deterministic and probabilistic ETo forecasts for subtropical monsoon climates.

title: Long-term daily salinity prediction in a tidal estuary using coupled machine learning and physically-based models
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Boli Zhu, Danitza Salazar, Patrick Willems
abstract: Study region: The Scheldt Estuary, Belgium. Study focus: Saltwater intrusion poses substantial risks to estuarine ecosystems under climate change. This study presents an integrated framework coupling a conceptual hydrological model (MIKE 11 NAM) with advanced machine learning — Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and SVR — to simulate long-term daily salinity. The NAM model estimates spatially resolved river discharge, which drives machine learning layers to forecast salinity dynamics under climate downscaled ensembles. New hydrological insights for the regions: Results demonstrate that the coupled NAM-RF model delivers superior predictive performance. Future scenarios indicate that summer salinity changes vary from -30% to 120%. A key insight is the spatial vulnerability: mid-estuary zones exhibit significantly greater sensitivity to climate-driven alterations in runoff and sea level than downstream areas. Furthermore, by incorporating a newly developed spatial error propagation framework, the future saltwater intrusion distance under extreme dry scenarios is rigorously quantified as a risk-explicit corridor. Specifically, the 0.5 psu freshwater front is projected to migrate landward by +0.65 km [95% confidence interval (CI): -0.07, +1.37 km] for Horizon 2050 and further shift to +1.46 km [95% CI: +0.74, +2.18 km] by Horizon 2100. These bounded spatial projections demonstrate a localized, highly non-linear response to compounding multi-stage hydrological droughts and sea-level rise, offering a robust paradigm for risk-informed estuary management.

title: Assessment of 1000 -year and catastrophic flood waves for the Liptovská Mara reservoir (Slovakia) using historical data and rainfall-runoff modeling
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Pavla Pekárová, Ján Pekár, Igor Leščešen, Veronika Bačová Mitková, Zbyněk Bajtek
abstract: Study region The Liptovská Mara reservoir, a critical water structure built on the Váh River in Slovakia, is located immediately downstream of the Liptovský Mikuláš gauging station. Ensuring its safety requires precise estimation of extreme flood inflows. This study focuses on the upper Váh River basin above this reservoir (area 1107 km2), situated between the High and Low Tatras, where over a century of continuous hydrological data (1921–2024) are available. Study focus Motivated by the need to determine 1000-year and catastrophic flood waves for the Liptovská Mara reservoir, this paper develops and compares two independent methods: (1) frequency analysis using the Log-Pearson type III distribution with the integration of historical floods dating back to 1501, and (2) the BILAN rainfall-runoff model applied with a catastrophic precipitation scenario (300 mm/6 days), based on the September 2024 extreme event in the Morava River basin, Czech Republic. New hydrological insights for the region Results indicate that the Váh River 1000-year flood wave entering the Liptovská Mara reservoir would peak at 922 m³s⁻¹ (95% confidence interval 751–1187 m³s⁻¹), with a 7-day average discharge of 168–214 m³s⁻¹. The model scenario with 300 mm precipitation confirmed similar peak values, validating the consistency of both approaches. These findings provide critical inputs for optimizing the reservoir's retention capacity and flood risk management in compliance with EU Directive 2007/60/EC.

title: Permafrost thaw flattens hydrographs in alpine watersheds of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Li Liu, Yonghong Yi, Huiru Jiang, Taihua Wang, Fan Lu
abstract: Study region Selected permafrost watersheds in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) Study focus With sparse in-situ measurements and discontinuous streamflow records, a full understanding of permafrost-hydrological responses remains limited in the QTP. Land surface models (LSMs) offer a powerful tool for replicating and projecting hydrological changes, yet require multivariable validation prior to practical application. New hydrological insights for the region Through a systematic evaluation of six state-of-the-art LSMs from the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project, our results show that most models reasonably capture hydrological responses to permafrost variations across four basins, with the exception of the H08 model, which lacks dynamic permafrost representation. Permafrost coverage shows a spatially negative correlation with cold-season runoff but a positive correlation with warm-season runoff ratio; meanwhile, basins with relatively lower permafrost cover exhibit longer streamflow recession, and delayed peak flow responses to precipitation with large model divergence ranging from −27.9 ± 13.6 to 53.2 ± 6.5 days. Under ongoing future warming, the ensemble mean of three top-performing models projects an increasingly flattened hydrograph, with the strongest permafrost reduction, seasonal runoff attenuation, and recession delays occurring under RCP8.5. However, runoff-precipitation response time exhibits strong spatial variability, likely due to competing influences of topography and other cryosphere components (e.g., ground ice melting). This study highlights the value of multivariate assessment in understanding complex hydrological processes in alpine permafrost regions, facilitating better water resource management.

title: Attribution of stage-specific runoff alterations and their responses to land-use management in the Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Hongxiang Wang, Siping Yin, Xuyang Jiao, Hai Shi, Keyan Chen, Xinglu Yue, Junjie Huang, Wenxian Guo
abstract: Study region The main stem of the Yellow River Basin (YRB), China, spans contrasting climatic, topographic, and land-use zones from upper to lower reaches. Four hydrological stations—Lanzhou, Toudaoguai, Longmen, and Lijin—represent its longitudinal heterogeneity. Study focus Runoff in the YRB has undergone stage-specific alterations, but shifts in dominant drivers and responses to land-use management remain unclear. We integrated hydrological alteration assessment, a Soil and Water Assessment Tool–Long Short-Term Memory (SWAT–LSTM) model, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), attribution analysis, and land-use scenarios to identify runoff transitions, quantify reach-specific drivers, and assess responses under natural development and ecological protection scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region Runoff transition points occurred around 1986 and 2001, dividing the record into a baseline period (1962–1986), Change Period I (1987–2001), and Change Period II (2002–2022). Hydrological alteration increased from 45%–63–51%–72% between the two change periods. The SWAT–LSTM model improved simulation performance, increasing Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency at Lanzhou from 0.809 to 0.952. Climate change dominated runoff variation during Change Period I, contributing 40.2%–60.1%. During Change Period II, land use/cover change contributed 30.1% at Longmen, while other human activities dominated at Lijin, reaching 70.0%. Ecological protection mainly redistributed runoff within the year rather than changing annual runoff volume, supporting reach-specific water management and land-use regulation.

title: Attribution of sediment load variations to climate and human activities across multiple timescales in the source region of the Yangtze River, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haoyuan Zheng, Yinghui Guan
abstract: Study region The source region of the Yangtze River (SRYZ) Study focus Differing from traditional research that typically conducts attribution analyses on an annual scale, this study quantified the relative contributions of climatic and anthropogenic influences at both seasonal and interannual scales in the SRYZ, using the Mann–Kendall (MK) test and the Slope Change Ratio of Cumulative Quantity (SCRAQ) method. New hydrological insights for the region Our results indicated increasing trends in annual sediment load (3.77 ×10⁴ t/a), precipitation (1.06 mm/a, p < 0.01), and evapotranspiration (0.65 mm/a, p < 0.001) in the SRYZ. These upward trends were also evident at the seasonal scale, with the most significant change occurring in spring. Attribution analysis indicated that sediment load variation in spring was co-driven by precipitation, evapotranspiration, and human activities, with contribution rates of 67.29%, −80.28%, and 112.94%, respectively—greater than their influences at the annual scale (37.77%, −29.03%, 91.26%). These findings further highlight the intensified hydrological processes in alpine regions in spring. However, human activities were the predominant driver in summer and autumn, with contribution rates of exceeding 85%. Overall, human activities and precipitation promoted sediment load increase, whereas evapotranspiration counteracted this effect. The combined influence of these three factors ultimately determined the overall trend in sediment load dynamics.

title: Study on the coupling processes of glaciers, snow and runoff in the Pamir Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Xiaolong Yan, Gonghuan Fang, Yaning Chen, Zhi Li, Bo Cao, Aminjon Gulakhmadov, Farhod Nasrulloev, Xueqi Zhang, Wenting Liang, Haodong Lyu, Ruoyan Li
abstract: Study region The Vakhsh River Basin, the largest tributary of the Amu River, is located in the Pamir Mountains in Central Asia. Research focus The Vakhsh River Basin, contributing ∼24% of the Amu Darya’s discharge and over 90% of Tajikistan’s hydropower, provides a key case for studying climate-driven streamflow changes. However, due to observational constraints, the coupling among glaciers, snow, and runoff in this region remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study employs the SWAT-Glacier-SRD model under a multi-objective calibration framework to investigate hydrological responses to climate change. New hydrological insights Results indicate that the model could well simulate hydrological processes in this catchment with daily NSE being 0.81 and 0.78 during the calibration and validation periods. During 1971–2019, streamflow increased significantly (1.57 mm yr⁻¹), while its composition remained stable, dominated by snowmelt (58.2%), followed by rainfall (30.5%) and glacier melt (11.3%). At the seasonal scale, the contribution of rainfall increased in early spring. Further analysis showed that streamflow timing is highly sensitive to climate conditions, with warmer, drier conditions leading to earlier and more dispersed flow, and colder, wetter conditions producing later and more concentrated flow. Despite significant warming in this region, streamflow timing shows only a slight, insignificant advance (−0.129 d yr⁻¹), likely due to compensatory precipitation effects, but this stability may not persist under intensified warming. This study provides a reliable framework for simulating cryosphere–hydrology processes in Central Asian basins.

title: Quantifying the impact of urbanization and climate change on event-based extreme precipitation in Guangdong Province, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haoting Xu, Chao Gao, Xiongpeng Tang, Silong Zhang, Zhanliang Zhu, Tianyu Wan, Chenchen Zhao
abstract: Study region Guangdong is located on the southern coast of mainland China and is the province with the highest level and fastest pace of urbanization in the country. Study focus This study investigates how five characteristics of hourly event-based extreme precipitation (HEEP) vary over space and time in Guangdong Province from 1973 to 2021. These characteristics are frequency, total amount, duration, intensity, and temporal unevenness, which is measured by the Gini coefficient. HEEP events, defined by hourly precipitation exceeding the 95th percentile with inter-event times under 6 h, were analyzed using nonstationary Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS). The approach uses covariates to assess impacts, including urbanization metrics derived from land use data on impervious surfaces (such as percentage of landscape (PLAND), patch density (PD), largest patch index (LPI), and aggregation index (AI)) and climate metrics (such as Niño3.4, PDO, IOD, and EASM). New hydrological insights for the region Results reveal distinct spatial patterns: higher frequency in the north, greater total amounts and intensity in the Pearl River Delta (PRD) and western coast, longer durations in the east, and more temporally concentrated precipitation in the PRD. Nonstationary models significantly outperform stationary ones, confirming temporal changes in HEEP characteristics. Urbanization exerts a stronger overall influence, with mean relative contributions of 47.0% (total amount), 43.7% (duration), and 40.7% (Gini coefficient) across stations, whereas the mean urbanization contributions are lower for frequency (26.8%) and intensity (32.7%), indicating a more balanced influence between urbanization and climate drivers for these two characteristics. Notably, AI and PDO enhance frequency, PLAND suppresses it, LPI and AI amplify total precipitation, and Niño3.4 increases temporal unevenness. These effects vary with local urbanization rates, highlighting the need to integrate nonstationarity and multifactor drivers in assessing extreme precipitation under urban expansion and climate change.

title: Modelling river ecosystem services in relation to discharge: The lower Jingjiang reach of the middle Yangtze River
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Xinghua Xue, David Gilvear
abstract: Study region Lower Jingjiang, Middle Yangtze River, China. Study focus This study addresses the lack of dynamic process-based quantification of river ecosystem services (ES) assessment responses to flow variability. A dischargedriven framework links three-dimensional flow processes to ES delivery via proxybased models, simulating 19 ES potentials using 60-year flow data. We analyze ES dynamics, synergies, trade-offs, and bundles. New hydrological insights for the region Three ES response types emerge: decreasing (water conveyance), single-peaked (aesthetics, recreation), and increasing, with the latter further divided into threshold-triggered or saturating (e.g., flood mitigation, navigation) and continuous growth (e.g., water supply, nutrient cycling) subtypes. Heterogeneous responses form four synergistic bundles and two key trade-offs (sociohydrological vs. eco-hydrological bundles; downstream vs. local services). The models capture four distinct seasonal patterns of ES, reflecting differential flow dependency. Long-term simulations (1950–2013) show that while regulated flows stabilize overall service potentials, they also increase vulnerabilities in flow pulse-dependent supporting services, such as floodplain habitats and carbon storage, which rely on natural flow variability. Annual average ES potential correlates strongly with runoff via power-law, quadratic, or logarithmic functions, enabling predictions of service shifts under hydroclimatic change. This transferable framework supports adaptive water resource management by enabling scenario-based assessment of trade-offs between ecological integrity and human well-being.

title: Wetlands' e-hydroperiod method: Frequency-of-occurrence-based approach
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Sofía Álvarez-Castrejón, Sergio A. Salinas-Rodríguez, Roberto Rodríguez Bastarmérito, Delma Nataly Castelblanco-Martínez, Alejandro Ortega-Argueta, Rodimiro Ramos Reyes
abstract: Study region the Great Lagoon of Catazajá is a Ramsar site and habitat for the Greater Caribbean manatee (Trichechus manatus manatus). It is located in the floodplain of the Usumacinta River, the mightiest river in Mesoamerica, and a transboundary basin with most of its course running through western Guatemala and southern Mexico. Study focus This study aims to present a methodological approach for the evaluation of the environmental water allocation specific for the wetlands (e-hydroperiod) with the theoretical principles of eflows. The low-volumes are parametrised separately from the peak-events, and the frequency of occurrence at which the hydrological conditions and types of peak events are integrated based on the environmental objective selected from a four-to-five-tier class system. The research in Mexico serves as a proof-of-concept and as a fitness evaluation for the model. The results reveal an overall good level of the method’s performance against the natural regime (R2 ≥ 0.93). New hydrological insight This study addresses the limited availability of wetlands-dedicated frameworks to allocate water for environmental processes that contemplate wetlands’ hydrological dynamics. Frequency-based e-hydroperiod components support the Freshwater Challenge goal of restoring 350 million ha of wetlands by 2030, and its implementation secures water for both sustainable use and ecological functions.

title: Integrating ecosystem service assessment and zoning management for transboundary environmental protection: A case study of the China–Vietnam Beilun river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Kai Jiang, Bin Wu, Wenzhu Zhang, Xuan Zhong, Shengquan Lu, Rucheng Lu
abstract: Study region The China–Vietnam Beilun River Cross-Border Basin (BRCB). Study focus Transboundary basins are ecologically sensitive areas with major management challenges between countries, yet assessments of asymmetric ecological conditions and transboundary zoning remain limited. Taking the BRCB as the study area, this study developed an integrated ecosystem service assessment framework by combining InVEST,GWR, OPGD, hotspot analysis, and SOM. It systematically evaluated the dynamics of five ecosystem services (ESs), their trade-offs and synergies, and explored optimization schemes for transboundary zoning. New hydrological insights Over the past two decades, only water yield (WY) and soil conservation (SC) improved in the BRCB, with better performance on the Chinese side. ES hotspots were concentrated in northwestern forestlands on the Chinese side, while coldspots mainly occurred in southeastern transboundary built-up areas; multifunctional hotspots declined over time. OPGD results showed that ESs were mainly controlled by natural geographical factors, while socioeconomic influences strengthened, highlighting human impacts. Ecosystem service bundles (ESBs) differed markedly across the border: SC bundles and core ES bundles expanded on the Chinese side, whereas the Vietnamese side remained relatively stable. The study reveals country-level ecological imbalance in the BRCB and stresses the need for transnational monitoring and zoning management to support ecological sustainability in transboundary basins.

title: Topographic water redistribution, rather thanclimate, dictates eco-hydrological recovery: Flux- and runoff-based validation in the Upper Minjiang River, eastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yong Liu, Ran Li, Liangshuai Wei, Anbang Huang, Qinfeng Shu, Xin Zhang
abstract: Study region The upper Minjiang River, a 22,954 km² alpine-gorge headwater basin on the eastern margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and a critical water conservation area for the Yangtze River. Study focus Large-scale greening is widely reported across mountain headwaters, yet optical indices demonstrate only that a basin has become greener—not that its water cycle has been physically restructured. This study integrates a 39-year (1986–2024) Landsat-derived Remote Sensing Ecological Index (RSEI) series, GeoDetector-based spatial attribution, MODIS evapotranspiration (ET) fluxes, and 33 years of in-situ discharge records to determine what dictates the spatial pattern of ecological recovery and whether that recovery has genuinely enhanced watershed hydrological regulation. New hydrological insights for the region Eco-hydrological quality declined to a historical nadir in 1997 and then recovered rapidly through 2024 (Sen's slope = 0.0027 yr⁻¹, p 0.05)—indicating that macro-climatic amelioration alone cannot explain the reversal. Elevation dominated the spatial attribution (q = 0.14), roughly sevenfold that of precipitation (q = 0.02), and their pronounced non-linear interaction (DEM∩P, q = 0.194) revealed a “topographic amplifier” whereby rugged terrain intercepts, stratifies, and laterally redistributes an otherwise uniform climatic input, thereby dictating where recovery materializes. Recovery proved hydrologically heterogeneous: arid valleys (< 2000 m) greened most strongly but at the steepest water cost (ET trend = 2.40 mm yr⁻¹); the subalpine belt regenerated most water-efficiently (1.33 mm yr⁻¹); and the nival zone showed rising ET al.ongside declining RSEI, signaling warming-driven rather than restorative wetting. Basin-wide ET rose significantly (trend = 1.458 mm yr⁻¹) and the inter-annual runoff coefficient fell from 0.79 to 0.74, yet the dry-season baseflow contribution increased from 20.16% to 25.02%—two expressions of a single “ecological sponge” effect. Restoration in such basins should therefore be hydrologically constrained rather than area-maximizing.

title: Effects of groundwater level decline on shallow soil water in grassland open-pit mining areas: Water vapor migration and water sources estimation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haibo Feng, Ying Duan, Zhongxia Li, Jianwei Zhou, Yongfeng Gong, Ran Li
abstract: Study region The Chenqi Coalfield in the Hulunbuir grassland, a typical semi-arid grassland open-pit mining area in Inner Mongolia, China, where mining has caused severe groundwater level decline. Study focus This study adopted in situ monitoring and hydrogen-oxygen stable isotope (δD and δ¹⁸O) analysis to clarify the response of shallow (0–100 cm) soil water–vapor–heat dynamics to increasing groundwater level depth (GLD) and to quantify liquid and vapor water sources in the unsaturated zone. New hydrologic insights from the region (1) An integrated isotope-thermodynamic equilibrium method was developed to quantify groundwater contributions to both liquid and vapor water in shallow soils. (2) With rising GLD, the minimum relative humidity (RH) in the surface layer decreased from 67.8% to 20.5%, weakening groundwater's temperature regulation capacity and expanding the active temperature layer from 40 cm to 100 cm depth. (3) Deeper GLDs reduced the frequency and depth range of condensation-favorable conditions, with potential implications for root-zone water availability. (4) When GLD < 4 m, groundwater-derived liquid water averaged 227.13 ± 14.95 kg/m³ and vapor water averaged 0.76 ± 0.06 g/m³ , approximately twice the values under deeper GLD conditions. The results provide a site-specific hydrological threshold and a transferable methodological framework for groundwater management and ecological restoration in grassland mining areas.

title: MODFLOW-informed machine learning for interpretable groundwater level prediction under sparse monitoring conditions in the Eastern Mitidja Aquifer, Northern Algeria
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Fatima Kastali, Mohamed Meddi, Abdelmadjid Boufekane, Ousmane Seidou
abstract: Predicting groundwater levels in semi-arid regions is challenging because groundwater systems are controlled by complex processes and monitoring data are often scarce. This study compares six machine learning models—Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, LightGBM, RBF-SVR, LSTM, and CNN—for groundwater level prediction in the El Hamiz sub-watershed, northern Algeria. A dataset of 3944 records from 136 monitoring wells (2005–2022) was combined with hydroclimatic variables, satellite-derived indicators, and groundwater abstraction data. Two modelling strategies were evaluated: one trained with observed groundwater levels and another using groundwater heads simulated by a calibrated MODFLOW 6 model during a period with limited observations. The latter was intended to examine whether physically based simulations could support machine learning when groundwater observations were unavailable. RF achieved the best performance (R² = 0.883, NSE = 0.873, RMSE = 2.096 m, KGE = 0.850), followed by XGBoost and LightGBM. The MODFLOW-informed RF also performed well (R² = 0.830; RMSE = 2.320 m), although it did not surpass the observation-based model. A Leave-One-Well-Out analysis using MODFLOW heads as an additional predictor produced a pooled R² of 0.869 and an RMSE of 1.744 m. SHAP analysis identified spatial location, evapotranspiration, groundwater abstraction, and precipitation as the most influential predictors. Prediction intervals showed slight undercoverage, indicating that further uncertainty calibration is needed for groundwater management.

title: Assessing future irrigation demand under climate change and bilateral water sharing in the Mahakali command area
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yogendra Mishra, Erica Shrestha, Tulsi Ram Pokhrel, Aditya Nath Jha, Sudan Ghimire, Shrijana Dhakal
abstract: Study region The Mahakali Irrigation Project (MIP) command area, located in the far-western Terai region of Nepal, relies on transboundary water from the Mahakali River governed by bilateral treaties with India. Study focus This study evaluates the impact of climate change on future crop and irrigation water requirements and assesses whether treaty-based water allocations are sufficient to meet projected demand. Bias-corrected outputs from selected CMIP6 models under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios were used to estimate future climate variables. The FAO CROPWAT model was applied to compute crop water requirement (CWR) and irrigation water requirement (IWR) for near (2026–2050), mid (2051–2075), and far (2076–2100) future periods. New hydrological insights Results reveal a strong seasonal redistribution of water demand driven by warming and shifting precipitation patterns. Irrigation water requirement increases sharply during dry and post-monsoon months, with September showing increases up to 564% and February exceeding 6-fold increases under future scenarios. In contrast, monsoon months (July–August) continue to exhibit negligible irrigation demand due to sufficient rainfall. Despite projected increases in annual precipitation, reductions in early monsoon (June) and post-monsoon (October) rainfall, combined with rising evapotranspiration, lead to significant water deficits during critical crop growth periods. Comparison with treaty-based supply (4.25 m³/s in dry season and 28.35 m³/s in wet season) indicates that future irrigation demand may exceed available supply by up to 30–40 m³ /s during dry months, highlighting a substantial seasonal mismatch. These findings demonstrate that timing of water availability, rather than total annual volume, is the dominant control on future irrigation stress, emphasizing the need for adaptive water allocation, storage expansion, and climate-resilient irrigation planning in transboundary river systems.

title: Response of water resources in Jialing River Basin to environmental changes using a remote sensing enhanced hydrological model
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Shanhu Jiang, Mingyan Wu, Fuquan Ni, Liliang Ren, Menghao Wang, Hao Cui, Xinyu Gao, Moran Xu
abstract: Study region Jialing River Basin of southwest China. Study focus Climate change exacerbates the imbalance in water-resource allocation, while land-surface conditions strongly regulate water resources across different spatial and temporal scales. In this study, the spatiotemporal characteristics of blue and green water resources (BW and GW) were evaluated based on the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), and the impacts of climate change (CC) and land-surface change (LSC) on blue-green water resources in the basin were investigated. New hydrological insights for the region First, from 2000 to 2020, both BW and GW showed an increasing trend with 3.61 mm/year and 4.63 mm/year, respectively. The spatial distribution of BW and GW changes is uneven. Second, CC drives the variations in blue-green water within the basin. LSC can locally reverse the dominant influence of climate change. Third, CC not only directly influences the spatiotemporal characteristics of blue-green water, but also alters their dynamic partitioning by modifying the land-surface conditions, notably through vegetation greening. Our results highlight that CC impacts water resources not only directly, but also indirectly by altering vegetation. This implies that water management policies account for these complex climate-vegetation-water feedbacks to ensure sustainability and resilience in the upper Yangtze River.

title: Diverging futures: The overriding influence of climate model generation (CMIP6 vs. CMIP5) on projected river-reservoir water quality and quantity under land-use change
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Vahid Pourbakhshali, Simin Heidari, Mohsen Nasseri, Seyed Taghi Omid Naeeni
abstract: Study region The Tajan watershed and Shahid Rajaei Dam reservoir, Northern Iran. Study focus Climate change, along with land-use and land-cover (LULC) variations, significantly impacts hydrological processes and water quality. Advancing climate science necessitates exploring how the latest CMIP6 scenarios improve impact projections compared to previous generations. This study evaluates the combined effects of climate and LULC changes on water quantity and quality within a river-reservoir system across various SSP and RCP scenarios. To establish a comprehensive framework, the methodology integrates the SWAT and CE-QUAL-W2 models, using downscaled CanESM2/CanESM5 outputs and annual LULC maps to combine CMIP phase comparison with river–reservoir modelling, thereby addressing the underexplored interplay of external factors in the receiving water body. However, downscaling constraints precluded uncertainty assessment of projections through multi-GCM ensembles. New hydrological insights for the region Results indicate a consistent temperature increase across all scenarios, despite variable precipitation trends during 2023–2043 compared with 2003–2022. Among non-aquatic land covers, shrublands are predicted to expand by 24.7%, while croplands shrink by 20.7%, marking the greatest changes between 2023 and 2043. Annual average streamflow is projected to increase by 4.3–19.2% across RCPs, whereas SSPs show mixed changes ranging from –5.9% to +4.3%. Similarly, nitrate loads increase by 3.9–15.1% across RCPs but change heterogeneously within the range of –6.5% to +1.6% across SSPs. Reservoir simulations show greater water-temperature increases under RCP pathways (8.4–9.4%) compared to SSPs (5.6–6.9%). Nitrate concentrations also rise by 1.9–8.2% under RCPs, while SSPs show variations ranging from –3.7% to +0.5%. Overall, RCPs exhibit more pronounced positive effects on water quantity but exert more severe impacts on water quality than SSPs, highlighting the need for mitigation strategies in dynamic, climate-LULC-driven systems.

title: Revealing multiple drought propagation characteristics on the basis of GNSS hydrometeorological data and precipitation
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yongzhao Fan, Fengyu Xia, Xiufeng He, Xiaowei Zou, Pengfei Xia, Rong Zou, Jiaqi Shi, Ze Wang
abstract: Study region Yunnan Province. Study focus This study extends GNSS-based drought propagation analysis beyond time-lag estimation by introducing a risk-oriented framework. High-spatial-resolution ZTD-PE and GNSS-TWSC are first used to construct meteorological and hydrological drought indices, respectively. Subsequently, run theory, copula functions, and Bayesian conditional probability are integrated to quantify propagation time, triggering probability, and meteorological drought thresholds from 2012 to 2022, with GRACE and GLDAS used as complementary references to examine the added value of GNSS-derived water storage information. New hydrological insights Drought propagation across Yunnan is generally rapid, typically occurring within 1–6 months. Influenced by regional runoff patterns and human activities, propagation time exhibits a clear spatial pattern, with longer durations in the south and shorter durations in the north. Under meteorological drought stress, the probability of hydrological drought being triggered is significantly higher in southwestern Yunnan than in northeastern Yunnan. This pattern is closely associated with anthropogenic influences in eastern Yunnan and precipitation variability related to the southwestern monsoon. Integrated analysis using GNSS, GRACE, and GLDAS further indicates that terrestrial water storage changes in Yunnan are particularly sensitive to severe and extreme meteorological drought, especially in the southwest, whereas near-surface water responds more strongly to moderate meteorological drought, with potential implications for vegetation growth and agricultural management.

title: Three-dimensional spatio-temporal propagation dynamics from soil moisture to vegetation droughts across different eco-geographical regions of China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuxuan Du, Tao Peng, Vijay P. Singh, Ji Liu, Xiaohua Dong, Qingxia Lin, Jiali Guo, Chao Song, Dan Yu, Gaoxu Wang
abstract: Study region China. Study focus This study investigated the propagation from soil moisture drought (SD) to vegetation drought (VD) across China during 1981–2020 using a three-dimensional (3-D) spatio-temporal clustering framework. SD and VD events were identified based on the Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI) and Standardized Vegetation Health Index (SVHI), respectively. A spatio-temporal matching algorithm was developed to pair SD and VD events, enabling a quantitative analysis of propagation characteristics (i.e., propagation time, rate, direction, distance, probability, and thresholds). The key contributors were identified using an integrated XGBoost-SHAP approach. New hydrological insights for the region This study identified 144 SD and 59 VD events, among which 24 were successfully matched as propagation events. The average propagation time from SD to VD was 3.76 months, exhibiting a distinct west-to-east gradient. The thresholds for triggering VD increased with drought severity, with SD duration thresholds ranging from 1 to 6 months across most regions. Regional contributors to drought propagation time varied across China: energy-related factors were primary in humid regions, precipitation (PRE) in arid zones, and temperature (TMP) and root-zone soil moisture (SMrz) in semi-arid areas. This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding multi-dimensional drought propagation and offers scientific support for drought early warning and ecological risk management in China.

title: Contrasting effects of flash and slow droughts on maize yield loss and crop failure across Europe
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Xinxin Chen, Yean-UK Kim, Thomas Heckelei, Chenzhi Wang, Josef Baumert, Heidi Webber
abstract: Study region Europe, spanning diverse climatic zones from the semi-arid Mediterranean to the humid continental north, characterized by strong hydroclimatic variability and significant dependence on rainfed maize production. Study focus Agricultural drought risk in Europe is becoming increasingly complex, regional evidence remains limited on how drought onset speed translates to maize yield loss and crop failure across Europe's hydroclimatic zones. This study defines and distinguishes flash and slow droughts using the rate of decline in the Standardized Water Deficit Index and characterizes their spatiotemporal patterns across Europe from 1989 to 2018 and quantifies their effects on maize yield losses and crop failure using fixed effects and mixed effects logistic models. New hydrological insights for the region Firstly, both drought types showed significantly increasing trends across Europe, with slow droughts occurring more frequently than flash droughts. Secondly, flash drought was significantly associated with yield loss across four metrics (count: −208.05 kg ha−1; severity: −138.25 kg ha−1; cumulative severity: −4.13 kg ha−1; duration: −12.78 kg ha−1 day−1; all p < 0.001). Slow drought affected yield only through duration (−9.36 kg ha⁻¹ day⁻¹, p = 0.005). Thirdly, flash and slow drought significantly elevated crop failure odds across all drought metrics, with drought duration producing the strongest effects (flash: OR = 2.10; slow: OR = 2.30, p < 0.001) and slow drought consistently posing greater risk than flash drought across all metrics. This suggests that persistent moisture deficits remain critical for systemic production failure. These findings provide new regional hydrological insight by linking drought onset dynamics, root zone soil moisture deficits, and agricultural failure risk across Europe, underscoring the need for regionally tailored strategies to mitigate drought induced agricultural losses across Europe.

title: Assessment of spatiotemporal compound drought propagation in the Nakdong River basin, South Korea, using a multi-layer complex network
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ho-Jun Son, Jeongwoo Han, Hyun-Han Kwon, Tae-Woong Kim
abstract: Study region The Nakdong River basin (NRB), one of South Korea’s major river basins, exhibits significant spatial and temporal variability in drought propagation. Study focus Drought is a continuous disaster that evolves both temporally and spatially. This complex evolution process is defined as drought propagation. Previous studies have typically addressed the propagation mechanisms between different drought categories and the spatial dispersion of individual drought types as independent processes. To overcome these limitations, a multi-layer complex network approach was adopted to evaluate the spatiotemporal compound propagation of meteorological and hydrological droughts in the NRB. Furthermore, clustering of sub-watersheds by topological indicators was used to highlight distinct physical dynamics across different clusters. New hydrological insights into the region under study A total of 272 sub-watersheds in the NRB were classified into sources (28%) and sinks (72%) based on the propagation strength. Source watersheds were clustered as C1(high-intensity and multi-direction), C2(uni-direction), and C3(multi-direction), while the sink watersheds were grouped into C4(multi-direction), C5(uni-direction), and C6(high-intensity and uni-direction). Spatial analysis showed that watersheds in C1 were concentrated in the southeast, whereas those in C6 predominated in the northwest. This distribution underscored the need for proactive monitoring in the southeast and enhanced resilience in the vulnerable northwest. The propagation features were differentially associated with distinct topological indicators. Attenuation was significantly correlated with source out-strength, and sink entropy, lag with sink in-strength, and lengthening with source out-strength, sink in-strength and sink entropy. These associations demonstrated that the propagation features are linked to the structural role of each sub-watershed within the network, which conventional complex network or probabilistic approaches cannot detect. By quantifying spatiotemporal compound propagation from a network perspective, this study supports tailored drought management strategies including source control, impact mitigation, and proactive implementation of early warning systems.

title: Integrating remote sensing, machine learning, and stable isotopes to diagnose hydrological drivers and water sources of a semi-arid wetland under coal mining disturbance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zheng Yin, Caixia Liu, Ran Sun, Mingfang Tang, Shiqi Zhang, Meng Yuan, Ran Lv, Gang Wu
abstract: Study region The Tangsige Marsh Wetland is situated in the Yanjiga River Basin, Inner Mongolia, China, a semi-arid area under climatic pressure and coal mining disturbance. Study focus We designed an integrated framework that synergistically combines multi-decadal Landsat time-series analysis (Random Forest), XGBoost-SHAP driver attribution, and stable isotope tracers (δD, δ18O, d‐excess) with a Bayesian mixing model (MixSIAR) to diagnose hydrological drivers and water sources of the wetland. New hydrological insights Wetland area declined by 35.5% from 2000 to 2022, exhibiting four distinct stages of decline and recovery. DEM and NDVI dominate wetland distribution. Key drivers—NDVI, population density, and precipitation—exhibit nonlinear thresholds, and synchronous changes in their SHAP values correspond to the different evolutionary stages. Precipitation (47.9%) and groundwater (35.3%) are the dominant water sources, with coal mine drainage contributing 7.6% on average but reaching nearly 10% locally. A south-to-north gradient from groundwater-dominated to strongly evaporated precipitation-dominated explains the northern wetland's greater drought sensitivity. This macro-micro framework bridges long-term dynamics and process-scale hydrology, revealing that wetland evolution arises from the temporal alignment or misalignment of multiple drivers.

title: A TimeGAN-enhanced cross-attention time-frequency transformer for multi-step monthly runoff forecasting in the Huaihe river basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Linhao Fang, Huimin Zuo, Mengtao Zhang, Zhao Zhang, Yifan Chen, Jianyou Zhu
abstract: Study region The upper Huaihe River Basin (HRB), China, with runoff observations from the Xincai (XC) and Zhoukou (ZK) hydrological stations. Study focus Data-driven models have shown considerable potential for runoff forecasting, yet their performance in monthly runoff prediction remains constrained by hydrological non-stationarity and limited data availability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Cross-Attention Time-Frequency Transformer (CA-TFAformer, CTF) framework that jointly exploits the trend, seasonal, and residual components obtained from Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (STL). A time-frequency attention (TFA) mechanism is developed to extract dominant temporal and frequency-domain characteristics, while a cross-attention (CA) mechanism is introduced to capture interactions among runoff components. Furthermore, a TimeGAN-based data augmentation strategy is employed to enrich training samples and improve model generalization. New hydrological insights for the region Monthly runoff dynamics in the upper HRB are jointly characterized by long-term trends, seasonal variability, and irregular fluctuations, indicating the importance of explicitly modeling the interactions among these runoff components. Results indicate that incorporating both time-frequency information and inter-component dependencies substantially improves forecasting performance. In addition, TimeGAN-generated samples provide additional representation of high-flow conditions in the augmented training set, resulting in more robust forecasting and improved flood peak prediction. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating runoff component interactions and data augmentation for reliable medium- and long-term runoff forecasting in non-stationary hydrological environments.

title: Enhanced total phosphorus prediction and explanation for the Minjiang upper reaches using bidirectional long short-term memory, attention mechanism, and particle swarm optimization
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Rongwen Yao, Rongsen Kong, Yungang Wu, Xiaojun Xu, Chengkang Jin, Shiwen Dai, Fuquan Yin, Zhan Xie, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yunhui Zhang
abstract: Study region Minjiang River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, China. Study focus Total phosphorus (TP) is a key contributor to water eutrophication, necessitating accurate forecasting for effective control and management. This study addresses the challenge by developing and evaluating the PSO-BiLSTM-Attn (Particle Swarm Optimization - Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory - Attention) framework for high-frequency TP prediction in the Minjiang River basin. The proposed framework is benchmarked against BP, LSTM, Transformer, and BiLSTM-Attn models using 8-hourly data from three monitoring stations across multiple forecast horizons. This study then further investigates how prediction performance varies across stations with different TP fluctuation regimes and applies explainability analysis to identify dominant drivers of TP prediction. New hydrological insights for the region Performance analysis displayed that PSO-BiLSTM-Attn achieved superior TP-level prediction compared with the baseline model, with R2 values of 0.8963 (station S1), 0.9412 (station S2), and 0.9138 (station S3). Stations with larger TP variability exhibited lower predictive performance, indicating that disturbances or stronger anthropogenic perturbations reduce model predictability. In the prediction step, single-step predictions achieved optimal accuracy for TP concentration, suggesting that TP dynamics were dominated by short-term memory and rapidly changing external inputs. The explainability analysis further indicates that TP predictions correlated positively with TN and EC, reflecting synergistic nutrient co-accumulation and pollutant-driven TP elevation, respectively. These findings provide insight into how TP dynamics respond to spatial heterogeneity and short-term disturbances in human-impacted river systems.

title: Ablation-season dynamics of a temperate glacier in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau revealed by monthly UAV surveys
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Kunpeng Wu, Yunpeng Duan, Daoxun Gao, Danyu Ma, Zhaoqi Ji, Francesca Baldacchino, Tobias Bolch, Shiyin Liu, Cheng Huang
abstract: Study region Yanong Glacier is a large lake-terminating temperate glacier in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, a hydrologically important region influenced by the Indian monsoon. Study focus This study investigates ablation-season glacier dynamics using six UAV surveys conducted over the glacier tongue from June to November 2023. High-resolution DSMs and DOMs were used to quantify elevation change and surface velocity, and to evaluate the links among ice-flow resupply, surface lowering, and velocity variability. New hydrological insights for the region The glacier tongue thinned by 3.43 ± 0.03 m and showed an average horizontal displacement of 0.412 ± 0.001 m d−1 during the ablation season. In the moraine-bounded section, ice-flow resupply partly compensated surface melt, with sensitivity bounds of approximately 14–26% under ±30% ice-thickness perturbations. Short-term velocity variability could not be explained by thickness- and slope-driven internal deformation alone; instead, a substantial residual basal-motion component remained. The covariation among air temperature, surface lowering, and residual basal motion suggests a plausible melt-velocity linkage, but does not provide direct proof of basal-sliding control. These monthly UAV observations help constrain the timing of meltwater production, lake-terminus dynamics, and seasonal glacier-related hazards in this data-scarce region.

title: Differences in water retention performance among multiple water storage media in the karst epikarst under drying-wetting alternation events
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Haijun Ma, Yuan Li, Qiuwen Zhou, Xukun Zheng
abstract: Study region A typical subtropical karst epikarst in southwestern China. Study focus Global climate change has intensified drying-wetting alternation, posing a severe challenge to the water storage capacity of karst regions. This study aims to establish an integrated observation system for different water storage media in a typical karst epikarst, using eight drying-wetting alternation events (DWAE) to quantitatively compare their water retention performance and elucidate hydrological response mechanisms. New hydrological insight The four water storage media in the karst epikarst show a clear gradient in water retention performance: deep fissure soil (120–240 cm) has the highest water content (32.2 ± 3.1%) and the lowest CV (9.5%), demonstrating the best retention; shallow fissure soil (0–120 cm) ranks second (27.1 ± 2.9%, CV 11.1%); topsoil, limited by evapotranspiration and storage capacity, shows greater fluctuations (15.9%-30.4%, CV 16.5%) and relatively weak retention; rock fissures, with limited storage space but high connectivity, exhibit the most dramatic water content variations (rainy season CV 43.8%, dry season CV 28.2%) and the weakest retention (5.1%-24.3%), serving mainly as rapid transport and temporary storage pathways. The study also reveals that, during drying-wetting alternation events, these media exhibit delayed vertical recharge and preferential shallow release. These findings deepen understanding of water regulation in the karst epikarst, providing a scientific basis for water resource management and ecological restoration under karst habitats.

title: Modeling flow persistence in headwater basins using climatic and morphometric data and machine learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Tony Vinicius Moreira Sampaio, Jorge Rocha, Cláudia Morais Viana, Fábio Marcelo Breunig, Elias Fernando Berra, Elaine de Cacia de Lima Frick, Edenilson Roberto do Nascimento
abstract: Study Region Southern Brazil, specifically the state of Paraná, characterized by distinct geomorphological units and subtropical to temperate climatic conditions. Study Focus This study investigates the controls of flow persistence (perennial vs. intermittent conditions) in first-order headwater basins using climatic and morphometric variables within a machine-learning framework. Rather than focusing on the hydrogeological origin of springs, the analysis targets the surface expression of flow regimes in headwater channels. A Random Forest (RF) classifier was applied to 164 basins with field-verified flow conditions using 152 predictors derived from ERA5-Land reanalysis and terrain metrics, including the Roughness Concentration Index (RCI). Model performance was evaluated through 1000 iterations and 10-fold cross-validation and optimized through systematic variable reduction to identify a parsimonious and physically interpretable set of predictors. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Results show that local morphometric properties, particularly terrain roughness (RCI), combined with hydroclimatic variables (runoff, precipitation, and vegetation indices), exert stronger control on flow persistence than basin area alone. The RF model achieved 78.2% accuracy (AUC = 0.84), outperforming traditional mapping approaches, while maintaining stable performance with only eight variables. These findings indicate that flow persistence in subtropical headwaters emerges from nonlinear interactions between terrain structure and climatic forcing, providing a scalable framework for hydrological assessment and water-resource management in data-scarce regions.

title: Thermodynamic intensification and atmosphere-soil coupling of drought in North-West Africa
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Milica Stojanovic, Rogert Sorí, Albenis Pérez-Alarcón, Zeinab Salah, Marwa S. Mohamed, Raquel Nieto, Luis Gimeno
abstract: Drought in North-West Africa (NWA) results from the combined influence of precipitation deficits and increasing atmospheric evaporative demand. This study analyses drought variability across Morocco, northern Algeria and Tunisia during 1981–2024 using the Standardised Precipitation Index (SPI3) and the Standardised Precipitation–Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI3). This study integrates drought indices, copula-based atmosphere–soil coupling, seasonal drought ranking, and event-synchronisation networks into a unified regional drought framework. The SPEI3 identifies a higher number of drought-affected months than SPI3 over most of the region, indicating that atmospheric evaporative demand enhances drought occurrence beyond precipitation deficits alone. The ranking analysis shows that several of the most severe and spatially extensive events were concentrated in the most recent years of the record following a reduced precipitation and increasing atmospheric evaporative demand. In addition, there is a strong coupling and dependence between SPI/SPEI drought and soil water content depletion, particularly over the semi-arid inland belt. The event-synchronisation analysis further show that drought occurrence is organised around a connected inland drought corridor, while Mediterranean, Atlantic-facing, and interior domains are more clearly differentiated in SPEI3 than in SPI3. Finally, seasonal trends indicate widespread drying from winter to summer, whereas autumn shows a more heterogeneous signal. Overall, the results demonstrate that drought intensification in NWA is increasingly controlled by the interaction between atmospheric warming, soil moisture depletion, and spatial drought connectivity.

title: Drought propagation and recovery dynamics across hydroclimatic pathways: Predictors and timescale dependence in Chile
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ignacio Fuentes, Víctor Osorio, Cristian Jordan, R. Willem Vervoort
abstract: Study region Continental Chile, spanning a strong hydroclimatic gradient from hyper-arid northern regions to humid temperate southern catchments. Study focus Drought impacts depend not only on meteorological deficits, but also on how water deficits propagate through soil moisture, streamflow, and vegetation systems. This study investigates drought propagation and recovery across atmospheric, hydrological, and ecological systems along Chile’s hydroclimatic gradient. Standardised drought indices, event-based metrics, cross-correlation analysis, and machine-learning models were used to quantify propagation timing, probability, severity transformation, and recovery across multiple drought pathways and temporal windows. New hydrological insight for the region Drought propagation is pathway-dependent and spatially heterogeneous. Soil moisture was identified as a key intermediary associated with vegetation drought response, while hydrological pathways exhibited greater variability. Drought severity tended to be attenuated within hydrological systems but was often amplified in vegetation, and recovery commonly persisted beyond the duration of the initial water deficit. Propagation probability and recovery are reasonably explained by climatic and catchment attributes (R 2 up to 0.65 and 0.71, respectively), particularly aridity, latitude, and storage-related properties, whereas onset timing remains weakly predictable (R 2 < 0.30). Arid catchments tended to exhibit faster and more frequent propagation, while greater storage capacity was associated with reduced propagation and faster recovery. These findings highlight the importance of integrated, multi-system approaches for understanding drought dynamics in coupled hydro-ecological systems.

title: Effects of reservoir group topological structures on the sediment reduction in large river networks – A case study of the Upper Yangtze River Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zhongwu Jin, Yihui Xiao, Guoshuai Zhang, Guangqiu Jin, Yakun Guo, Zhijing Li, Le Feng, Hao Lin
abstract: Study region Upper Yangtze River Basin (UYRB), China. Study focus Reservoir construction has profoundly altered sediment transport in large river systems, yet the influence of reservoir-group topological structures on basin-scale sediment redistribution remains poorly understood. This study quantified how reservoir-group topology regulates runoff–sediment relationships and sediment reduction across the UYRB using hydrological observations from 1950 to 2024. A topology-based framework incorporating the effective basin area ratio (λ) was developed to improve sediment trapping efficiency estimation for interconnected reservoir systems. New hydrological insights Sediment load at Yichang Station decreased by 98.09% during 1950–2024, primarily due to the rapid expansion of large reservoirs, which account for 88.5% of the basin's total storage capacity. Reservoir-group topology produced pronounced spatial heterogeneity in sediment reduction. The Xiluodu-Xiangjiaba cascade in the Jinsha River Basin contributed 53.7% of the basin-wide sediment reduction, whereas the Wujiang River Basin exhibited substantially lower sediment trapping efficiency despite its large storage capacity. After the Three Gorges Reservoir began operation, the dominant contribution to sediment reduction shifted from the mainstream to upstream tributaries, with the Jinsha River Basin increasing from 30.5% to 54.7%. A revised sediment trapping efficiency equation incorporating λ reduced RMSE by 48.3–75.0% compared with conventional models. These results demonstrate that reservoir connectivity, rather than storage capacity alone, controls basin-scale sediment redistribution, providing a transferable framework for sediment management in regulated river networks.

title: Elucidating groundwater responses of shallow basaltic aquifers in the Ethiopian volcanic highlands
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Getnet Taye Bawoke, Atsushi Tsunekawa, Nigussie Haregeweyn, Mitsuru Tsubo, Ayele Almaw Fenta, Zena Tessema Terefe, Ashebir Sewale Belay
abstract: Globally, basaltic aquifers are crucial for sustaining large populations. In Ethiopia, where volcanic formations predominate, shallow aquifers in basaltic regolith are the most accessible water sources for communities and urban populations, thereby supporting livelihoods. However, these aquifers demonstrate complex hydrogeological characteristics, including significant heterogeneities and compartmentalized flow systems. The lack of comprehensive studies of recharge–storage–discharge processes in basaltic shallow aquifers poses challenges, often leading to overextraction and water scarcity. Here, we examined spatiotemporal groundwater dynamics in basaltic shallow aquifers of the volcanic highlands of Ethiopia by combining recharge–storage–discharge linkages using observations from eight monitoring wells distributed across contrasting litho-structural settings. Lag-time analysis reveals the existence of multiple shallow groundwater recharge mechanisms: rapid recharge within 1–3 days through fractures and lithologic contacts, and delayed recharge persisting up to 44 days driven by slow infiltration into thick basaltic regolith aquifers. Aquifer memory ranged from one day to three months, with longer memory effects observed in weathered/fractured basaltic units constrained by massive volcanic domes. Consistent with these findings, aquifer drainage properties highlight variable recession characteristics: steep recessions characterize fractured aquifers underlain by impermeable basalts, indicating limited storage capacity, whereas gradual recessions occur in weathered/fractured aquifers with extensive regolith and alluvio-lacustrine deposits, reflecting sluggish drainage. These findings highlight the need for integrated, site-specific hydrogeological analyses to elucidate recharge–storage–discharge relationships in basaltic shallow aquifers. Such analyses are essential for addressing aquifer heterogeneity and safeguarding this resource from seasonal climatic variations and anthropogenic influences.

title: Enhancing the WAS physical hydrological model and integrating machine learning and residual decomposition to improve runoff simulation performance in the cold region of the Taoerhe River Basin, Northeast China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yongzhe Wang, Yang Zheng, Lin Wang, Zefan Yang, Xuefeng Sang, Haitao Wu, Changqing Zhang, Debang Huang
abstract: Study region: The Taoerhe River Basin, located in Northeast China. Study focus: Physical hydrological models still have limitations in representing runoff processes in seasonally frozen semi-arid basins. This study improved runoff simulation through physical model modification and hybrid residual correction. First, a temperature-responsive regulation factor was introduced into the water allocation and simulation model (WAS). Subsequently, a multi-level hybrid framework combining a physical model and machine learning (ML) algorithms was developed: Hybrid 1 and Hybrid 2 employed RF to correct WAS residuals; Hybrid 3 and Hybrid 4 integrated Variational Mode Decomposition with multiple ML algorithms (RF, XGBoost and CatBoost) to capture nonlinear signals, and used a stacking strategy to integrate residual predictions. New hydrological insights for the region: The improved WAS model performed well, with NSE above 0.80 and RMSE and MAE reduced by approximately 40%. Hybrid 4 achieved the best overall performance. During testing, R2 and NSE exceeded 0.90, while RMSE and MAE were 47.99 m3/s and 26.50 m3/s, respectively. Compared with the improved WAS model, R2 and NSE increased by more than 0.05, whereas RMSE and MAE decreased by more than 20%. Climate perturbation experiments showed that precipitation mainly determined total runoff, while temperature perturbations mainly altered the partitioning of basin runoff. Thus, small changes in annual runoff may mask seasonal redistribution, offering insight for similar seasonally frozen semi-arid basins.

title: Hydrological modelling in snow- and glacier-fed catchments of the Upper Indus Basin by conceptual and machine learning approaches
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jamal Hassan Ougahi, John S. Rowan
abstract: Study region Upper Indus Basin (UIB), Himalaya and Hindu Kush. Focus of study This study evaluates the performance of a conceptually based glacio-hydrological model (GSM-HBV) and four data-driven models (DDMs), namely LSTM, RF, XGB and SVM, to simulate annualised, seasonal and flood flows for gauged catchments in the globally significant data-scarce catchments of the UIB. New hydrological insights or the region Five modelling schemes were evaluated across 23 snow- and glacier-fed catchments with the best-performing model identified based on achieving the highest ranking in at least two of the three evaluation metrics. In glacier melt catchments, XGB performed best for annualised flow (e.g., achieved the highest ranking in 4 out of 10 catchments) and GSM-HBV for flood events (e.g., 5 out of 10 catchments), whereas SVM, LSTM and RF were superior for predicting spring, summer and winter flows in 5, 4 and 6 out of 10 catchments respectively. In snowmelt dominated catchments, LSTM (e.g., 5 out of 13 catchments) was best for annualised flows, whilst SVM edged ahead of others for flood event prediction. Seasonally LSTM worked best for spring flows, whilst XGB, RF and GSM-HBV tied equally for summer and winter flows. The results show that no single model offers universally superior performance; thus, an ensemble approach is advanced whereby multiple solutions together provide robust ‘envelop’ predictions capturing over 90% of the observed flows.

title: Reference data for actual evapotranspiration in a Mediterranean green roof: Evidence from a monitored green roof system in Genoa, Italy
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Komal Jabeen, Ilaria Gnecco, John J. Sansalone, Anna Palla
abstract: Study region This study investigates the evapotranspiration of a monitored green roof installed in Genoa (Italy) characterized by Mediterranean coastal climate. Study focus Accurate estimation of actual evapotranspiration (AET) and moisture dynamics remains a challenge to fully assess the hydrological performance of green roof systems (GR). This study investigates the AET rates of a GR using high-resolution observation of microclimatic and soil moisture data with a daily water balance model. AET rates are determined for 21 dry weather periods spanning 18 months of a continuous monitoring program. Observed daily AET rates are compared with reference evapotranspiration (ET0) rates determined through a modified FAO-56 Penman-Monteith model by introducing a linear soil moisture extraction function and considering the role of GR system and vegetation with a crop coefficient (Kc). New hydrological insights for the region Examination of AET data indicates that for GR with an abundant soil moisture level, AET is initially driven by energy (temperature and net radiation) but as the moisture decreases during a dry weather period, the soil water availability is mainly driven AET. Kc of 0.89, is estimated through minimization of percent bias for prediction of AET during dry weather periods and provides good AET predictions even if the seasonal trend produces overprediction in warm periods and underprediction in cold periods. Future studies will elucidate seasonal Kc values accounting for the vegetation growth dynamics.

title: From sharing to partitioning: Stable isotopic evidence for flexible water use strategies mediating plant coexistence on the Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zhixue Chen, Xianlong Yang, Lei Hou, Jie Lu, Congze Jiang, Li Liang, Xiaomei Liu, Wenbin Ding, Guohui Wang
abstract: Study region The southeastern Tibetan Plateau, specifically subalpine riparian zones and closed forests dominated by Abies georgei var. smithii. Study focus Alpine plant coexistence shifts from resource sharing to vertical niche partitioning across moisture gradients, yet how these strategies operate in riparian zones versus closed forests remains unclear. We employed δ¹ ⁸O analysis and the MixSIAR model to quantify water source contributions, and assessed niche breadth (WNB) and overlap (Proportional Similarity, PS) to elucidate coexistence mechanisms. New hydrological insights for the region In riparian zones, shrubs showed a distance-dependent decrease in river water use (23.4–18.1%), and coexisting species exhibited high niche overlap (PS > 0.91) and broad niches (WNB: 3.8–3.9), indicating a coexistence strategy based on resource sharing. In fir forests, water use was strongly age-dependent: juvenile and young trees primarily utilized deep soil water (40–100 cm, WNB: ∼3.0), while fir seedlings and understory herbs competed for shallow water (0–20 cm, WNB: ∼2.5, PS up to 0.94), likely constraining fir regeneration. As trees matured, niche overlap decreased (PS to 0.73), demonstrating a shift toward vertical niche partitioning under moisture limitation. Our findings represent a mid‑summer snapshot and require seasonal validation. Nonetheless, they reveal a moisture‑mediated continuum of coexistence mechanisms—from resource sharing to vertical niche partitioning—that is vital for predicting community dynamics and guiding conservation of this vulnerable fir under climate change-induced hydrological shifts.

title: Storm size regulates pollutant flux from aging infrastructure: A case of the San Diego River and its urbanized tributary
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): K. Shipley, A.M. Kinoshita, F. Pinongcos, M. Mueller, M.E. Verbyla, N. Mladenov
abstract: Study region This study examines the San Diego River watershed in southern California, USA, and its highly urbanized tributary, Alvarado Creek. The San Diego River drains a mixed land-use basin with ∼55% urban land cover, while Alvarado Creek is heavily urbanized with 94.4% urbanization. Both systems experience continuous anthropogenic pollution sources, including sanitary sewer exfiltration, and function as hydrologic conveyance corridors transporting urban-derived contaminants during storm events. Study focus The study aimed to evaluate storm-driven transport dynamics of sewage-derived pollutants and assess whether maximum storm discharge reliably predicts cumulative pollutant loading. High-resolution discharge and water-quality data from storm events sampled 2016–2024 were analyzed to characterize pollutant temporal profiles, hysteresis behavior, and event-integrated loadings of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total dissolved nitrogen (TDN), nitrate-N, phosphate, and fecal indicator bacteria. New hydrological insights for the region Statistically significant (p < 0.05) relationships were identified between maximum storm discharge and cumulative pollutant loadings, demonstrating that peak discharge is a robust proxy for storm-scale pollutant export in the San Diego River (∼1030 kg DOC and ∼134 kg TDN per 1 m³·s−1 increase in peak discharge). Larger storms produced disproportionately higher magnitude areal fluxes, and the Alvarado Creek Tributary exhibited DOC and TDN fluxes five times greater than the River. Findings indicate increased storm intensity will amplify pollutant mobilization rather than produce dilution, highlighting the need for targeted urban watershed and sewer infrastructure management under uncertain climatic conditions.

title: Assessing groundwater-river interactions for sustainable water management in the mine-contaminated Mediterranean Bravona catchment (Corsica, France)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): T. Leydier, E. Garel, J. Bassil, S. Santoni, F. Huneau
abstract: Study region The Bravona River watershed (Corsica, France), a Mediterranean coastal catchment affected by legacy arsenic mining pollution. Study focus Mediterranean coastal catchments affected by legacy mining pollution face increasing pressure from climate change and water demand, requiring improved understanding of groundwater–river interactions controlling contaminant dynamics. This study investigates the role of the downstream alluvial aquifer in arsenic dynamics within the Bravona watershed, using a seasonal multi-tracer approach combining hydrochemistry, stable water isotopes (δ¹⁸O, δ²H), radiogenic tracers (³H, ²²²Rn), and arsenic concentrations over a complete hydrological cycle (2022–2023). New hydrological insights for the region Results reveal strong seasonal variability in groundwater–river interactions, with alluvial groundwater contributing between 16% and 43% of downstream river flow. Tritium and radon data indicate longer residence times in the alluvial aquifer and enhanced groundwater support during low-flow periods. Arsenic concentrations in the downstream river are decoupled from upstream mine inputs and primarily controlled by seasonal hydrological connectivity. During low-flow conditions, increased groundwater contribution attenuates arsenic concentrations in the downstream Bravona River, whereas high-flow periods favor upstream-dominated signals. The alluvial aquifer remains weakly contaminated (As < 10 µg/L) and acts as a hydrological buffer rather than a secondary contamination source. These findings demonstrate that seasonal groundwater–river connectivity governs arsenic dynamics and highlight the value of integrated multi-tracer approaches for water management in mining-impacted Mediterranean catchments.

title: Integrated isotope hydrology and hydrogeochemical approach for delineating groundwater flow systems in Denpasar-Tabanan Groundwater Basin, Bali, Indonesia
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ni Putu Sri Wahyuningsih, Takashi Nakamura, Koichi Sakakibara, Putu Doddy Heka Ardana
abstract: Study region Denpasar-Tabanan Groundwater Basin, Indonesia. Study focus Bali Island faces intensifying groundwater exploitation due to rapid urbanization and tourism growth. This generates raising concerns regarding groundwater sustainability of the basin. Previous study in the basin has focused on groundwater head changes, however comprehensive flow system characterization using hydrogeochemical and isotope tracers remains limited. This study aims (1) to elucidate a major hydrogeochemical process controlling groundwater evolution, (2) to determine recharge elevation zones and mechanisms, and (3) to delineate flow systems within the aquifers. In this study, major ion elements (F, Cl, NO3, PO4, SO4, Na, K, Ca, Mg, HCO3, Si) of water samples were determined using ion chromatography, titration, and spectrophotometry methods, in conjunction with environmental isotopes (δ2H, δ18O) were analyzed utilizing isotope ratio mass spectrometer. The major ions and groundwater origins were combined to delineate flow systems within the basin. New hydrological insights for the region Water isotope signatures reveal groundwater recharge originating from effective elevations between 100 and 700 m above sea level. Combination of groundwater origins and hydrogeochemical signatures reveal common recharge signature and progressive groundwater evolution along hierarchical groundwater flow systems. Shallow and deep groundwater indicates the development of intermediate flow systems with human pressure contributes to groundwater evolution. The conceptual model demonstrates that groundwater in the lowland discharge area is sustained by recharge originating from the middle basin.

title: Andean wetlands: Seasonal variability and their interactions with the cryosphere
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Joshua Castro, Catriona L. Fyffe, Thomas E. Shaw, Evan S. Miles, Emily Potter, Martin Hoelzle, Vinisha Varghese, Francesca Pellicciotti
abstract: Study region The Vilcanota Urubamba Basin in southern Peru includes fragile wetland ecosystems that play a key role in mountain hydrology and support grazing for Andean communities. Study focus Mapping of wetlands variability is missing, limiting our understanding of their characteristics, seasonality and link with the cryosphere. We characterise wetland distribution, seasonality and persistence and evaluate their spatial association with glaciers and seasonal snow. Using Landsat 7 and 8 imagery, we build three-month seasonal land cover maps from 2013 to 2022 using a Random Forest classification and an Albedo Retrieval approach. New hydrological insights for the region Wetland area decreases by 38% from the end of the wet season (October to December) to the end of the dry season (July to September). Pixel transitions indicate that wetlands primarily transform to and from agricultural and pasture lands. Highly persistent wetlands are located above 4600 m a.s.l. and closer to glaciers than less persistent wetlands. We identified three wetland seasonal drying patterns. Basins with delayed and slow dry-out wetlands were more common at higher elevations but were not always in glacierised catchments, suggesting meltwater may maintain wetlands in the early dry season. We provide the first large-scale picture of wetland seasonality, and the basis for modelling the processes that sustain wetlands in tropical high mountains.

title: Probabilistic assessment of warning-stage exceedance during ice-jam flooding using physics-guided river-ice simulations and interpretable stacking ensembles
