description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Mingwen Liu, Lu Lu, Jianfeng Gou, Karl-Erich Lindenschmidt, Haishen Lü, Yuantong Li, Jianbin Su, Yonghe Chen, Zelin Tang
abstract: Study region The Sanhuhekou Bend Reach of the Yellow River, northern China. Study focus Ice-jam flooding produces abrupt stage rises, yet probabilistic flood-risk assessment remains challenging because of nonlinear ice–hydraulic interactions and sparse observations. We develop a physics-guided framework that couples Monte Carlo river-ice simulations with interpretable stacking-ensemble surrogates for rapid assessment of breakup ice-jam stage and warning-stage exceedance risk. The process-based model RIVICE is embedded within a Monte Carlo framework to generate 10,000 physics-consistent scenarios spanning uncertainty in boundary conditions and key ice–hydraulic parameters. An interpretable stacking surrogate efficiently emulates the calibrated physics-based simulations, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) quantify predictor contributions and guide reduced-input model distillation. New hydrological insights for the region. Jam-toe location, upstream discharge, and downstream ice thickness were identified as the dominant controls on ice-jam stage because they govern backwater propagation, hydraulic forcing, and ice-induced flow resistance. SHAP further identified model-informed threshold ranges associated with elevated flood risk. The stacking surrogate reproduced simulated stages with high fidelity (NSE = 0.95, RMSE = 0.14 m, R = 0.97), while the distilled surrogate retained strong performance (NSE = 0.92, RMSE = 0.18 m, R = 0.96) using fewer predictors. Surrogate-based ensembles reproduced the observed annual-maximum stage distribution and return-period behaviour, enabling rapid probabilistic assessment of warning-stage exceedance risk and supporting flood-risk management under data-scarce conditions.

title: Drought propagation mechanisms and spatial heterogeneity in the Yellow River Basin based on convergent cross mapping and the geographical detector method
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jiaqi Zhang, Zhao Liu, Jinxia Zhang, Qiang Li, Binfeng Tuo, Yu Bai, Jiaojiao Lyu
abstract: Study region The Yellow River Basin. Study focus Drought propagation, as a key process in the hydrological cycle, exhibits significant nonlinearity and spatial heterogeneity. Based on meteorological and runoff data from 1980 to 2018, the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) were constructed. The Convergent Cross Mapping (CCM) method was employed to identify the causal relationships and dominant propagation timescales between meteorological and hydrological droughts. Moran’s I was further applied to reveal the spatial clustering patterns of drought propagation characteristics. Finally, the optimal parameter-based geographical detector (OPGD) model was used to quantitatively analyze the driving factors and their interaction effects. New hydrological insights for the region Meteorological drought exerts a significant causal influence on hydrological drought. Propagation intensity increases from upstream to downstream, with an average dominant propagation timescale of about 7.7 months, mainly at the 10–12 month timescale. Both propagation intensity and timescale show significant positive spatial autocorrelation with clustered high-value areas. Precipitation and potential evapotranspiration are the dominate explanatory factors, while NDVI and slope play important regulatory roles, and the explanatory power of HFI (Human Footprint Index) becomes more pronounced in downstream regions. Factor interactions are stronger than individual-factor effects, indicating joint control by climate and land-surface conditions. This study reveals drought propagation mechanisms from a “causality-space-drivers” perspective, providing a basis for drought risk assessment and water resources management.

title: Integrated hydrogeological and chemical characterisation of thermal springs in Northern Oman
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Robert Hird, Mohammed Al Kindi, Mei Yin
abstract: Study region Batinah Plain, northern Oman. Study focus Thermal springs constitute an important but understudied component of the hydrogeological system of northern Oman. The springs occur along the flanks of the Al Hajar Mountains in association with major fault and thrust structures. Field measurements, water chemistry, isotope compositions, and discharge estimates are combined with a simplified coupled groundwater flow and heat transport model to postulate circulation depths, flow mechanisms, and thermal regimes. New hydrological insights for the region The thermal waters are of meteoric origin and have undergone deep circulation before discharge. Hydrogeochemical facies are dominated by Na–K cations with variable anion compositions, reflecting contrasting lithological controls along flow paths through ophiolitic, carbonate and mixed sedimentary formations. Quartz geothermometry yields conservative reservoir temperature estimates of approximately 66–103 °C, implying circulation depths of roughly 0.4–1.9 km under the regional geothermal gradient of ∼19 °C/km. Numerical simulations demonstrate that such temperatures can be achieved through deep, fault-controlled groundwater circulation under normal geothermal conditions, without requiring magmatic heat sources or anomalous basal heat flux. Three end-member thermal spring system types are identified: ophiolite-hosted ultramafic systems, carbonate-dominated piedmont systems, and saline sedimentary systems, with a vauclusian spring representing a hybrid carbonate-hosted variant. The results indicate that northern Oman’s thermal springs are structurally and lithologically distinct system operating with a common regional thermal framework.

title: Ecohydrological impacts of photovoltaic construction across aridity gradients in China: Divergent responses of vegetation and evapotranspiration
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Shan Zhu, Xueer Qin, Chenglong Zhang, Qiong Yue, Zailin Huo
abstract: Study Region China, with 14,849 natural-surface photovoltaic (PV) stations distributed across a complete aridity gradient. Study Focus Through using the Kernel Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (kNDVI) and actual evapotranspiration (ET) retrieved via a modified Surface Energy Balance System (SEBS), a spatiotemporal comparative framework was constructed to quantitatively assessed the climate-dependent ecohydrological impacts of large-scale PV construction. Machine learning (CatBoost) was applied to decode the non-linear driving mechanisms. New Hydrological Insights for the Region PV deployment leads to divergent ecohydrological trade-offs. Retrieval from the coupled SEBS and PV efficiency model showed that PV-induced ET suppression strengthens significantly with aridity (slope=0.81, p < 0.01 ). In arid zones, strong ET suppression (mean relative change in ET, ∆ETr ≈ − 0.5 ) conserves moisture, driving positive vegetation responses relative change in vegetation growth (∆kNDVI) that increase with PV area. Conversely, humid zones exhibit weak ET reductions (mean ∆ETr ≈ − 0.08 ) and negative scale effects on vegetation. Furthermore, CatBoost modeling explained 46% (∆kNDVI) and 76% (∆ETr net ) of the variance. Elevation serves as the primary driver, while secondary drivers diverge: vegetation relies heavily on precipitation, whereas ET is highly sensitive to solar radiation, exhibiting non-linear thresholds that reveal regional ecohydrological response mechanisms.

title: Comparative assessment of monthly evaporation reliability in desert regions using Monte Carlo simulation, Curve method, Point Estimate Method and machine learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jamshid Piri
abstract: Study region Two climatically contrasting desert stations in southeast Iran were examined: Zabol (31°02′N, 61°30′E; 489 m a.s.l.) is an inland continental desert site (Köppen BWk) at the centre of the endorheic Sistan Basin, where the “120-day wind” phenomenon and > 300 clear-sky days per year drive among the highest pan-evaporation rates in the world. Chabahar (25°17′N, 60°37′E; 8 m a.s.l.) is a maritime-modified arid site (BWh) on the Makran coast of the Gulf of Oman, where oceanic thermal inertia and the southwest monsoon compress the annual evaporation cycle. Together these two stations span the full aridity gradient of southeastern Iran and provide an ideal natural laboratory for probabilistic evaporation analysis under contrasting desert hydroclimates. Study focus The study benchmarks four reliability frameworks for the bi-directional (minimum and maximum) historical-constraint problem in monthly pan evaporation: Monte Carlo simulation (MCS), the First-Order Reliability Method (FORM, also referred to as the Curve method), the Point Estimate Method (PEM), and an ensemble machine-learning (ML) framework. A consistent 31-year monthly record (1993–2024; n = 31 for January–July, n = 30 for August–December) is used throughout. Shapiro–Wilk tests reject normality at every month at both stations (p 0.5, establishing a clean empirical skewness threshold beyond which two-point reliability approximations should not be used in arid hydroclimates. These findings translate directly into operational guidance for the Sistan and Makran-coast water-supply systems and, more broadly, for probabilistic evaporation modelling under accelerating climatic variability.

title: Thermal regimes in a monsoon-influenced mountainous river basin: The Nagara River, Japan
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Morihiro Harada, Shigeya Nagayama, Masanao Sueyoshi, Ryouji Fujii, Takeo Onishi
abstract: Study region River water temperature (T w ) variability was investigated in the Nagara River basin, central Japan, a monsoon-influenced mountainous watershed with a near-natural mainstem flow regime and intensive lowland paddy agriculture. Study focus From 2020–2021, T w was measured at 54 mainstem and tributary sites. These observations were integrated with daily air temperature (T a ) and river discharge (Q) estimated using high-resolution climate data and a distributed hydrological model. We analysed air–water temperature coupling, tributary thermal effects, and discharge-dependent summer thermal responses. New Hydrological Insights for the Region T a –T w regression revealed increasing thermal coupling downstream along the mainstem, indicating reduced hydrological and groundwater buffering. Tributaries showed diverse thermal behaviours associated with groundwater contribution and land use. Groundwater-fed tributaries cooled and stabilised mainstem T w , whereas paddy irrigation return flows were associated with localised warming under summer low-flow conditions. Rainfall-driven high flows reduced T w and promoted spatial homogenisation across the river network, while summer low-flow and drought conditions amplified warming and increased spatial thermal heterogeneity, especially in downstream and agriculturally influenced reaches. These responses highlight the combined roles of climate, hydrology, groundwater, and agricultural water use in shaping river thermal regimes. The results support climate adaptation and river ecosystem management in monsoon-region basins by identifying contrasting thermal roles of groundwater-fed tributaries and agriculturally influenced lowland reaches.

title: Research on drought prediction models by multiple machine learning methods in a semi-arid region
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuefen Zhang, Yimin Hao, Jiyang Tian, Kaining Du, Menghan Tian
abstract: Study region The Ziya River Basin (ZRB) is located in northern China, characterized by increasing drought frequency due to climate change. Study focus This study aims to develop and compare three machine learning-based drought prediction models - Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) - for the ZRB. Unlike traditional single-factor drought indices, the proposed models comprehensively integrate multiple meteorological and hydrological variables, including precipitation, temperature, potential evapotranspiration, vegetation characteristics, and soil moisture. The Moisture Index (MI) was identified as the optimal target variable through correlation analysis. Model performances were evaluated using multiple metrics (R², MAE, RMSE, NSE, KGE, and PBIAS) and validated against in-situ soil moisture measurements at various depths. The optimal model was then applied to simulate the spatiotemporal distribution of drought and to statistically analyze drought-affected areas under different land use types, soil textures, elevations, and slopes. New hydrological insights for the region The ELM-based drought prediction model (ELM-DI) significantly outperformed RF and SVM, achieving the highest fitting accuracy (R²: 0.948–0.989; MAE: 0.062–0.158; RMSE: 0.086–0.309; NSE > 0.90; KGE > 0.90; PBIAS < 5%). Validation against measured soil moisture data showed that ELM-DI exhibited the strongest correlation with deep-layer soil moisture. Spatiotemporal analysis revealed that cropland, loam soils, elevations of 1000–2000 m, and slopes of 2°–6° experienced the largest drought-affected areas across all seasonal scales.

title: Rainfall intensity differentiates hydrological functions in alpine permafrost landscapes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jia Qin, Bingfeng Yang, Yongjian Ding, Junhao Cui, Jianfeng Yang, Guangxi Ding, Feiteng Wang
abstract: Study region The source region of the Shule River, northeastern Tibetan Plateau. Focus of study Identifying how rainfall intensity triggering differentiation of hydrological functions in the representative alpine permafrost landscapes (cold desert, alpine meadow, and alpine shrubland), through field-based monitoring and water balance calculation. New hydrological insights for the region This study demonstrates that rainfall intensity differentiates the hydrological functions of the three alpine landscapes. The cold desert consistently functions as an infiltration‑dominated system, with negligible runoff (runoff coefficient 10 mm/d) (0.063)—a pattern explained by rainfall duration and activation of preferential flow pathways. The shrubland shows evapotranspiration exceeding precipitation under light rain (ET/P = 1.30). Under moderate, the meadow shifts to substantial soil water storage (ΔSWS = 6.95 mm), the shrubland reaches high ET (6.22 mm), and the cold desert maintains deep percolation. Soil water storage dynamics further support this functional differentiation. These three landscapes exhibit complementary functions: percolation (cold desert), runoff/storage (meadow), and evapotranspiration (shrubland). This study provides a site‑specific analysis of how rainfall intensity differentiates hydrological functions in alpine permafrost landscapes, enhancing understanding of water cycle processes in cold regions.

title: Rolling recursive prediction model for water level prediction in gate-controlled water delivery canal systems
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Kejie Wang, Lingzhong Kong, Xue Xiao, Guhan Li, Zhongkai Feng, Taotao Zhang, Qian Yang
abstract: Study region This study focuses on a cascade canal section of the Middle Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project (SNWDMRP), China, characterized by large flows and frequent dynamic gate regulations and pronounced hydraulic lag effects over long distances. Study focus Accurate multi-step water-level prediction is vital for large water diversion systems. Existing data-driven models often use static strategies unsuited for artificial gate operations. We propose a novel rolling recursive prediction method for gate-controlled canals that explicitly integrates planned gate operation data to enable scenario-based water-level prediction. Additionally, to overcome imbalanced historical datasets lacking extreme events, we employ a hydrodynamic model for model-based data augmentation to simulate high-fluctuation scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region This study proposes a rolling recursive prediction model for multi-step water-level prediction in gate-controlled canal systems. At each prediction step, the model updates hydraulic state variables with the most recent observations and gate operation inputs, capturing the spatiotemporal coupling among water levels, gate controls, and boundary conditions over extended horizons. The LSTM-Rolling model maintained NSE above 0.8 across all gate sites over a 72 h horizon, while static models dropped below 0.5. Hydrodynamic model-based data augmentation supplemented the training data with physically plausible scenarios that are under-represented in the historical record, reducing the 24 h RMSE from 0.024 m to 0.013 m. Together, the rolling recursive model and targeted data augmentation provide a practical approach for scenario-conditioned water-level prediction in engineered water diversion canals.

title: Uncertainties in water balance and low flow assessment along the network of navigable rivers and canals in Flanders
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Laurens Breugelmans, Patrick Willems
abstract: Study region The network of navigable waterways in Flanders, the northern part of Belgium. These multi-user waterways are characterized by high water demand and low water availability. Study focus This paper proposes a variance-decomposition based framework for the uncertainty assessment of a conceptual water balance model of the network of navigable rivers and canals in Flanders. This model has been developed in support of the water allocation for industry, drinking water production, agriculture and shipping. The model accounts for the water management regulations, evaporation and inflow from nearby regions and catchments. The proposed uncertainty assessment framework includes determination of the total model uncertainty on water availability assessment, by comparison with available discharge measurements, initial assessment of the stochastic uncertainty per model uncertainty source and uncertainty propagation by means of Monte-Carlo simulations. New hydrological insights for the region Results show that the main uncertainty contributors differ from region to region. Along the highly managed Albert canal and Ghent-Terneuzen canal, the model inputs related to the canal management and water abstractions are the dominant sources of uncertainty. For the rainfall-driven rivers, the rainfall-runoff inflow assessment is the most important, whereas for the Yser river in the Belgian polder region it is the river - polder interaction. The framework results in clear recommendations for model improvement and provides detailed insights into the evaluation of model results.

title: Comparison of physics-based and machine learning groundwater models for sustainable aquifer management: A regional study in Emilia-Romagna (Italy)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Ilaria Delfini, Daniel Zamrsky, Alberto Montanari
abstract: Study region 7000 km2 portion of Emilia-Romagna region, north-eastern Italy. Groundwater resources are stored in a complex multi-layered aquifer system. Study focus A MODFLOW 6 numerical groundwater flow model and a random forest algorithm are implemented to compare the performance of a physics-based and a machine learning approach in simulating and predicting historical and future groundwater head values in the same study area. A scenario analysis is carried out to assess the response of the regional multi-layered aquifer system to variations in climatic and anthropogenic stresses. New hydrological insights for the region The MODFLOW 6 model and the random forest algorithm produce consistent results, although the random forest is generally more optimistic and predicts a lower impact of precipitation and pumping changes on the regional aquifer system. Both models indicate that future reduced precipitation combined with increased groundwater withdrawal would negatively affect shallow and deep aquifers. Conversely, decreasing pumping can partially counterbalance lower precipitation, allowing groundwater heads to recover in some areas. The analysis also identifies areas most sensitive to perturbations, where precipitation and abstraction variations lead to the largest groundwater head declines. Results emphasize the advantages of integrating physics-based and machine learning methods to better interpret outcomes and improve model performance. This approach strengthens both the calibration process and scenario analyses, offering a valuable contribution given the growing relevance of groundwater modeling for water management and policy decisions.

title: Multi-scale climate teleconnections amplify extreme precipitation hazards in central-southern Chile
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Roberto Serrano-Notivoli, Oliver Meseguer-Ruiz, Adrian Huerta, Santiago Beguería, Pablo Sarricolea
abstract: Study region: Central-southern Chile (30°S–40°S) is highly vulnerable to hydroclimatic disasters, where extreme precipitation is the primary driver of severe flooding, making the accurate assessment of localized, intense rainfall hazards critical for water security and infrastructure. Study Focus: Traditionally, hydroclimatic hazard assessment has relied on stationary paradigms, neglecting multiscale climate dynamics. We introduce a comprehensive multivariate framework using Non-Stationary Extreme Value Theory (NSEVT) to evaluate daily precipitation extremes from 1981 to 2025. Applying a Peaks Over Threshold approach across a newly reconstructed, high-resolution observational dataset, we isolate the concurrent impacts of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Antarctic Oscillation (AAO), the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), and long-term background trends. New hydrological insights: Our findings reveal that teleconnections act as highly heterogeneous spatial amplifiers or mitigators of hazard. Specifically, warm ENSO phases and active sub-seasonal MJO states can triple the magnitude of 100-year extreme return levels. Conversely, the positive AAO phase generates a spatial dipole, statistically mitigating hazard in central Chile while exacerbating hazards in northern Patagonia. We demonstrate that catastrophic, localized runoff potential is significantly amplified when these atmospheric modes synchronize. These findings highlight that a multivariate extremes analysis provides a better framework for characterizing the temporal variability modes of extreme events, including a more robust assessment of long-term temporal trends.

title: A new daily high-resolution gridded precipitation dataset for the Italian Greater Alpine Region (1951–2023): spatio-temporal analysis and hydrological applications
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Veronica Manara, Michele Brunetti, Bruno Arcuri, Daniele Bocchiola, Jacopo Melada, Davide Nicoli, Leonardo Stucchi, Maurizio Maugeri
abstract: Study region Italian Hydrological part of the Greater Alpine Region. Study focus Setting up a daily high-resolution gridded precipitation dataset over the 1951–2023 period using 7417 quality-checked meteorological stations. It is mainly based on the Italian networks of mechanical and automatic stations, and it has been used to obtain 7.5 arc-second resolution (about 230 m) daily fields by means of the anomaly method. The gridded fields are available at 30 arc-second-resolution at https://doi.org/10.13130/RD_UNIMI/CSYYAP. New insights for the region The monthly 1991–2020 high-resolution climatologies, obtained interpolating the stations by means of a Local Weighted Linear Regression of precipitation versus elevation, range, at annual level, from 521 mm to 3021 mm. The temporal evolution of the relative anomaly series, with respect to the 1991–2020 period, does not show any significant trend, except for summer (about −3% per decade – p-value ≤ 0.05). The obtained fields can be used to reconstruct any precipitation event in the investigated area and period. Together with corresponding temperature fields, they were fed into the Poly-Hydro hydrological model to estimate the runoff series for the Adda River and the Toce River. The resulting series showed an excellent agreement with the corresponding observational series. The slightly underestimation of the model (about 6.3% for the Adda and 5.8% for the Toce) seems to be due to the underestimation of rain gauges of solid precipitation.

title: Human regulation reshapes nitrogen and phosphorus transport in the highly managed Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yuqing Li, Lingling Liu, Dongping Shi, Junhong Ling, Dongxian Kong, Xubiao Yu, Lingfeng Zhou
abstract: Study region Yellow River Basin (YRB), China. Study focus This study quantified how large-scale human regulation reshaped total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) transport in one of the world’s most engineered river systems. Using a basin-wide dataset (2016–2022) of discharge, sediment load, TN/TP concentrations, water allocation, and Water–Sediment Regulation Scheme (WSRS) records, we quantified TN and TP fluxes along the mainstem and 11 major tributaries and assessed the impacts of allocation and WSRS on annual loads and seasonal regimes. New hydrogeological insights from the region Export to the Bohai Sea (Lijin) was 103,626–117,122 t yr⁻¹ for TN and 567–2365 t yr⁻¹ for TP. Tributary inputs were dominated by the Wei River, Huangshui River, and Fen River. Water diversion removed 73.9% of TN and 89.7% of TP relative to downstream export, indicating that human water consumption largely controls the basin’s nutrient balance. In contrast, WSRS redistributed nutrient transport temporally by generating short-term pulses and preferentially enhancing TP export through sediment mobilization. These pulsed P inputs may temporarily alleviate P limitation but do not offset the persistent N enrichment in the Bohai Sea, potentially increasing eutrophication risks. Overall, human regulation overrides natural controls on nutrient transport in the YRB, underscoring the need to incorporate regulated flow and sediment regimes into integrated river–sea nutrient management.

title: A novel approach for disentangling the contributions of different soil and water conservation measures to streamflow reduction on the Loess Plateau, China
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Pengcheng Sun, Miaoyu Li, Qiang Li, Jingshu Wang, Peng Jiao, Yiping Wu, Peiqing Xiao
abstract: Study region The Yanhe River Basin (YHRB) in the middle reaches of the Yellow River typifies the loess hill and gully region of the Loess Plateau, characterized by severe soil erosion and the extensive implementation of soil and water conservation measures (SWCMs). Study focus Climate change and anthropogenic activities, particularly SWCMs, are major drivers of hydrological variability in the Loess Plateau. However, the individual effects of different measures on streamflow remain poorly disentangled. To address this issue, we developed a new attribution framework that integrates dynamic SWCM data on vegetation restoration, terraces, and check dams into the traditional Budyko framework. Using long-term hydrometeorological and SWCMs implementation data from 1976 to 2015 in the YHRB, we quantitatively assessed the contributions of specific SWCMs to streamflow reduction. New hydrological insights for the region SWCMs (i.e., the non-climate component in our Budyko attribution) dominated streamflow reduction in the YHRB, accounting 12.5% (1976–1985) and 34.6% (2006–2015) of natural streamflow , with a strengthening influence over time. Contribution patterns also shifted: check dams dominated in earlier decades, vegetation restoration prevailed in later years, and terraces showed steadily increasing effect. These results reveal changing roles of different measures under policy and ecological restoration. The proposed method also offers practical guidance for optimizing conservation strategies, such as adaptive vegetation management and upgrading aging check dams, to balance soil conservation with sustainable water resources.

title: A hybrid InSAR–artificial intelligence/machine learning ensemble framework for evaluating the potential impact of a dam on land subsidence susceptibility
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Mehri Tabarmayeh, Abdorreza Vaezihir, Maryam Hasanpour
abstract: Study region Dehloran Plain. Study focus This study presents a scenario-based methodology to investigate the potential impact of the Meimeh storage-recharge dam, which is currently in the planning-to-construction phase, on downstream land subsidence susceptibility. A CHART-FLWD framework was developed and optimized using five well-known machine learning and artificial intelligence algorithms: ANN, XGBoost, RF, SVM, and GA, with model evaluation performed against InSAR-derived deformation observations representing the current pre-dam condition. Based on continuous evaluation metrics, GA (R² = 0.82), XGBoost (R² = 0.75), and ANN (R² = 0.70) showed stronger spatial agreement with the InSAR-derived deformation patterns, whereas RF (R² = 0.30) and SVM (R² = 0.40) showed lower continuous prediction performance. The optimized results indicated that groundwater recharge and drawdown are the primary drivers of subsidence susceptibility in the region. Accordingly, a new optimized ensemble LSS model, named GAX, was developed and applied to the current pre-dam condition and to a simulated post-dam scenario by incorporating dam-related variables, including proximity to rivers and the planned irrigation network. New hydrological insights The findings revealed a significant reduction in subsidence intensity, with index values decreasing from 39 to 110 before dam construction to 18–101 under the hypothetical post-dam scenario, highlighting the potential hydrological influence of the dam scenario. High and very-high risk areas declined from 68% to 31%, extreme-risk zones nearly disappeared, while moderate and low-risk areas expanded. Given the increasing subsidence severity, the proposed methodology provides a useful framework for identifying high-risk zones and supporting sustainable groundwater-management strategies. The proposed framework demonstrates potential applicability to hydrogeologically similar arid and semi-arid alluvial plains, although further multi-regional validation is required.

title: Shifting hydroclimate sensitivity of streamflow under warming climate
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Khandaker Iftekharul Islam
abstract: Study region The study encompasses eight headwater watersheds in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of the Upper Rio Grande Basin, spanning southern Colorado and northern New Mexico, USA, supplying water to millions of people. Study focus Climate-driven hydrologic shifts are reshaping the streamflow regime across snow-dominated mountainous watersheds. Rising temperatures and altered precipitation transformed snowmelt timing and runoff, yet the evolution of streamflow sensitivities remains unclear. Studies often examine linear or nonlinear sensitivities and overlook gradual changes in the factors driving streamflow. New hydrological insights for the region This work bridges this methodological gap by simultaneously employing Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) and Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) within a tailored Generalized Information Criterion (GIC) to contrast linear and nonlinear controls on streamflow over four decades (1980–2019). The study investigates how streamflow sensitivity to hydroclimate factors evolved during the dry and snowmelt seasons. Nonlinear GAMs outperformed MLRs during snowmelt seasons (cross-validated R² up to 0.66), while linear MLRs adequately captured dry-season conditions (R² up to 0.62). Minimum temperature remained influential but attenuated and occasionally reversed over decades, while soil moisture gained relative importance in several watersheds. Other factors exhibited notable but inconsistent effects, modulated by snow fraction, elevation, and latitude. Overall, declining explanatory power over time indicates reorganization in hydroclimate-streamflow relationships under a warming climate, which informs seasonal water supply forecasts and adaptive water management.

title: Unveiling the dynamics of flood characteristics and inundation patterns in the Poyang Lake Basin under a changing climate
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Zijing Feng, Lei Zou, Jun Xia, Feiyu Wang, Jiayuan Xu, Liping Zhang
abstract: Study region The Poyang Lake Basin, China. Study focus The Poyang Lake Basin is frequently affected by floods, posing serious threats to lives and property. Assessing potential changes in flood characteristics and inundation patterns across its five major tributaries under climate change is important for flood risk assessment and adaptation planning. This study developed a hydrological-hydrodynamic model (DTVGM-CaMa-Flood) to simulate the flood processes during 2001–2021, and assessed future changes in flood characteristics and inundation patterns during 2030–2100 under two emission scenarios (SSP1–2.6 and SSP5–8.5). New hydrological insights for the region The model reasonably reproduces monthly discharge and water levels at six stations, with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE) over 0.88, and also captures typical daily flood event hydrographs, with NSE above 0.79. The simulated inundation extent generally agrees with MODIS observations, with approximately 84.3%–88.9% inundation occurrence frequency within the model capability. Future projections show that flood characteristics across the five tributaries exhibit spatial heterogeneity, with peak discharges increasing mainly in the eastern and decreasing in the western tributaries, whereas changes in 7-day flood volumes are weaker. Peak discharges at Waizhou, Lijiadu and Meigang may exceed historical maxima, especially under SSP5–8.5, indicating a greater potential for extreme floods. Projected inundated areas generally decrease across depth classes in the Ganjiang River Basin, whereas deep inundation expands in the Fuhe, Xinjiang and Raohe River Basins. In the Xiushui River Basin, moderate-depth inundated areas increase while deep inundated areas decrease.

title: A spatially explicit simulation of phosphorus loads in the Poyang Lake Sub-basins: An improved export coefficient model with landscape resistance
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jinliang Wang, Qing Wang, Yu Zhu, Bingjuan Zhou
abstract: Study region The Poyang Lake Basin (12.21 × 10⁴ km²) in China, encompassing the five major tributaries—Ganjiang, Fuhe, Xinjiang, Lean, and Liaohe Rivers—was selected as the study area. This region experiences a subtropical humid monsoon climate with annual precipitation ranging from 1387 to 1795 mm. Despite its hydrological abundance, the basin faces increasing eutrophication pressure primarily from non-point source (NPS) phosphorus loads delivered by its tributaries. Study focus To overcome the limitation of the classical Johnes export coefficient model (ECM) in reflecting environmental heterogeneity, this study developed an improved ECM incorporating landscape resistance (LR-ECM). Landscape resistance—a concept characterizing spatial heterogeneity in pollutant transport—offers a novel framework to enhance lumped models for simulating NPS phosphorus loads in large watersheds. We systematically quantified nine key environmental factors (relative elevation, slope, surface roughness, vegetation coverage, rainfall, topographic wetness index, soil erodibility, soil leaching index, and flow length) and integrated them via spatial principal component analysis and the minimum cumulative resistance model to construct a comprehensive landscape resistance surface. This surface was then normalized and coupled with the traditional ECM to simulate the 2020 spatial distribution of phosphorus loads, with results validated using monitoring data at the tributaries' outlets. New hydrological insights for the region The study revealed that hydrological and topographic factors dominated the landscape resistance structure. The LR-ECM achieved markedly superior accuracy, reducing the maximum relative error across the five tributaries from 126.26% to below 9%. Simulations identified livestock farming as the primary phosphorus source, with high-load areas concentrated near watershed outlets and in zones of agricultural intensification. The LR-ECM successfully delineated critical source areas at a hydrologically meaningful (sub-basin) scale, providing a scientific basis for targeted NPS pollution control. This work validates that landscape resistance effectively characterizes the constraints of environmental heterogeneity on pollutant transport, offering a robust tool for precise NPS modeling and management in data-scarce large watersheds.

title: High salinity dominates the seasonal thermal stratification and its dynamics in Longmu Co: A hypersaline lake in western Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Hua Wang, Junbo Wang, Jinlei Kai, Weiqiang Ma, Jianting Ju, Liping Zhu
abstract: Study region Longmu Co, a deep hypersaline lake in the western Tibetan Plateau, located in a cold, arid region dominated by the westerlies. Study focus The annual mixing regime, under-ice thermal evolution, and relative roles of salinity, thermal forcing, and meteorological variability in deep hypersaline Tibetan Plateau lakes remain poorly understood. We investigated the thermodynamic regime of Longmu Co using 451 days of high-frequency water-temperature observations, a vertical salinity profile, concurrent meteorological measurements, bathymetric data, and satellite-derived ice phenology. TEOS-10-based density calculations and decomposition of squared buoyancy frequency showed that salinity provided the dominant background stability, separating a seasonally active mixolimnion from a persistently isolated monimolimnion. The mixolimnion exhibited cold monomictic circulation, mixing once annually from mid-November to early February, whereas the deep water column remained density-stratified. During complete ice cover, upper-water temperatures increased after early February, indicating a distinct under-ice thermal transition before ice breakup. Thermal forcing governed seasonal upper-layer stratification, while wind produced rapid but shallow perturbations. New hydrological insights for the region In deep hypersaline lakes of the high-altitude western Tibetan Plateau, persistent haline stratification can prevent full-depth overturn despite strong westerly winds and severe winter cooling. Meteorological forcing acts mainly within the mixolimnion. This buffering effect explains why such lakes may remain meromictic and should be represented explicitly in regional lake models and assessments of climate-driven hydrological change.

title: Numerical simulation of coupled chemical dissolution and nonlinear seepage in a single carbonate-rock fracture
Socio-hydrogeology: The past, present, and future of a people-centred and place-based approach to groundwater science
abstract: Groundwater systems are shaped by deeply interwoven physical processes and social dynamics, yet traditional hydrogeological approaches have often treated these domains separately. Over the past decade, socio-hydrogeology has emerged in response, offering an approach that systematically incorporates social dimensions into hydrogeological investigations. In its initial formulation, socio-hydrogeology was meant to raise awareness among hydrogeologists of the social implications of their work, fostering engagement with water users and interdisciplinary collaboration from the onset of research. Since then, the approach has gained academic traction and institutional recognition, yet it still lacks a clear conceptual definition, posing risks to its coherence and impact. This paper marks 10 years since the term’s inception and critically reflects on the development and future direction of socio-hydrogeology. By critically analysing the evolution of the concept and situating it among broader inter- and transdisciplinary frameworks, this paper proposes an updated conceptualisation to clarify its disciplinary scope, practical relevance, and further encourage its application. Attention is also given to the implications for hydrogeological education, arguing for a shift in pedagogy that better equips researchers to engage with the ethical and cultural dimensions of groundwater science. Socio-hydrogeology offers an opportunity to reframe hydrogeology not only as a natural science but as one deeply shaped by (and accountable to) society.

title: General or specialized programmes in hydrogeology? Insights from long-term experience in Serbia
An adaptive multifidelity surrogates-based data assimilation approach for groundwater contamination sources identification
Isotopic investigations on identification of atmospheric moisture origins and evaluation of runoff source contributions to the Upper Beas River Basin in the western Himalayas
Groundwater–surface water interactions and resilience to hydrological extremes in a data-sparse arid transboundary river basin: Insights from collaborative groundwater modelling
abstract: Abstract Sustainable groundwater management is key to building resilience to hydrological extremes but remains challenging in data-scarce transboundary river basins. In this study, a transboundary, collaborative, physically based groundwater modelling approach has been developed for the Limpopo River Basin (LRB), which is highly vulnerable to floods and droughts. Monitoring data and model results consistently suggest that prolonged wet periods and floods significantly raised groundwater levels, whereas prolonged droughts decreased them, particularly in the upstream and central regions of the basin characterized by low-storage fractured bedrock aquifers. Groundwater–surface water interactions are greater downstream, where water tables are shallower in unconsolidated superficial materials, and intensify during floods, especially in the central region. Modelling results also suggest that baseflow is less responsive to extremes than groundwater recharge across the LRB, highlighting the groundwater system’s attenuation capacity. The model was subsequently used to assess and discuss a series of co-created management scenarios focused specifically on improving groundwater storage during wet periods for use during dry periods. They included: (1) managed aquifer recharge (MAR), using (1a) injection well(s) next to large dams, (1b) rainwater and runoff harvesting (RRH) and infiltration through local wells, (1c) RRH through local ponds and (1d) small reservoirs (e.g. sand dams); (2) deforestation; (3) afforestation; and (4) increased groundwater abstraction. Scenarios suggest that strategy (1b), when widely applied across the basin, may be the most effective to reduce the risk and impact of floods, droughts, and groundwater depletion by supporting the maintenance of groundwater levels and baseflow, while reducing storm runoff.

title: Exploring the benefits of industry and community engagement in hydrogeology teaching
abstract: Abstract The role of industry engagement in hydrogeology education remains undervalued, despite its potential to enhance student learning and career readiness. Integrating both industry and community partnerships can increase student engagement, deepen students understanding of hydrogeological concepts and raise awareness of career opportunities, potentially improving graduate outcomes. This study evaluates the integration of such partnerships in the “Groundwater Systems” unit at the Queensland University of Technology (QUT), Brisbane, Australia. The approach involved collaborating with industry partners, revising assessment and progressively expanding opportunities for student–industry engagement. Surveys were conducted to evaluate the success of this engagement and to identify barriers limiting student participation. The groundwater unit now features semester-long industry interactions, including immersion in community-linked groundwater research projects as part of major assessments. The observed benefits of this include increased interest in the subject material and enhanced understanding of hydrogeology concepts and methods. Alumni participation as industry guest speakers further demonstrates the potential for sustained partnerships to enhance graduate outcomes.

title: A climate change perspective on groundwater vulnerability assessment using a static and non-static variable approach: A regional multi-aquifer case study
Geological and hydrogeological functioning of aquifers in the Gareb Plain, northeastern Morocco: Insights from exploratory drilling and seismic reflection imaging
Correction: Hydrogeological modeling and global climate change impacts on the last permanent sand-dune pond in the Doñana World Heritage Site: Santa Olalla Pond, Spain
Mechanistic insights into heterogeneous saturated–unsaturated seepage dynamics: A paradigm-shifting 3D framework for dam stability analysis
Lithological schematization of the Karnali fluvial fan (Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape) using electrical resistivity tomography as a basis for hydrogeological investigations
abstract: Abstract In the Nepalese and Indian Terai Arc Landscape (TAL), protected nature areas are supported by groundwater systems that have remained largely understudied. This study schematizes the lithology of the Karnali fluvial fan located in the Bardia district (Nepal) as a basis for future hydrogeological investigations. Inversion results of 2D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) profiles at 21 locations were interpreted by comparing with the local borehole lithology and regional geophysical studies. Multiple lithological cross-sections were prepared to develop a 3D lithological model spanning the fan, and the adjacent Bardia National Park up to the Babai River in the east. Sediment resistivities found were in the range of 8–6000 Ω m. Resistivity less than 40 Ω m was identified as clay, 40–80 Ω m represented silt and fine sand, 80–400 Ω m identified as fine to coarse sand and resistivities higher than 400 Ω m were interpreted as coarse sand, gravel and boulders. A coarse sand-gravelly layer is present at the fan apex and along the foot of the Himalayas in the north that functions as a recharge area and aquifer. The central part of the fan has sandy layers which transition to fine sand and silt layers in the distal south and southeast. Clay layers locally create confining conditions, within the sand and silt dominated areas. These findings on subsurface lithology provide valuable insights for the groundwater systems which sustain ecohydrological processes relevant to the protected ecosystem and fills a critical knowledge gap on regional hydrogeology of the TAL.

title: Response mechanisms of surrounding rock and tunnel structures of a karst tunnel under high operational water pressure
Correction: A geological and geophysical database for the assessment of offshore freshened groundwater resources
Determining hydraulic conductivity and porosity sensitivity of grain-size analysis methods using laboratory and small-scale model measurements
abstract: Abstract Hydraulic conductivity (K) is essential for determining seepage flow in porous media. In this study, a small-scale model (SSM) was tested using coarse sand (CS) and medium sand (MS) samples, designed according to the similarity model law. In the SSM, pumping tests were carried out in laboratory conditions to estimate K . This technique combines the advantages of field and laboratory measurements. The results of SSM measurements were validated by a constant head permeameter. Employing the validated SSM-based K values, 31 grain-size analysis methods (GSAMs) were compared and evaluated. For both soil samples, the US Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) method provided the best results. Sensitivity analysis for porosity was performed on 17 GSAMs using four theoretical and two laboratory methods. It was concluded that laboratory-based porosity measurements are recommended to obtain more accurate K values. Of the theoretical methods, Wooster gave the smallest relative difference for CS, whereas the Wu and Wang method performed best for MS. Considering the GSAMs, the Arshad, Carrier, Chapuis, Chapuis and Aubertin, Fair and Hatch, Kozeny-Carman, Mbonimpa, Pavchich, Sauerbrei, and Shahabi methods were found to be very sensitive to porosity, while the Kasenow and Koenders, and Williams methods are the least sensitive. For five GSAMs, the possibility arises that an added constant can be used to improve the calculated K values which was demonstrated in this study through a recommendation for the Kasenow constant.

title: A GIS-based multi-criteria and evolutionary optimization framework for groundwater monitoring network design and well selection
Using pumping tests to understand how sea proximity and karstification influence the hydraulics of a coastal karstic aquifer in the Yucatan Peninsula
Technical design and hydrogeochemical evaluation of a stormwater-based managed aquifer recharge pilot site in an intensively cultivated region (Hallertau, Germany)
abstract: Abstract Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) with stormwater remains underexplored in rural settings due to uncertainties related to source-water variability, treatment performance, and groundwater-quality impacts. This study presents the design and hydrogeochemical evaluation of a stormwater-based MAR pilot site implemented in 2024 in Hüll (Bavaria, Germany), a flood-prone agricultural region underlain by a heterogeneous Tertiary aquifer. The system integrates a stormwater retention basin, treatment units, an infiltration well, and a comprehensive monitoring framework combining multi-parameter online sensors, detailed laboratory analyses, and contextual information on catchment activities. Hydraulic testing confirmed strong aquifer heterogeneity but also demonstrated high injectivity of the target formation. Hydrochemical monitoring evaluated raw water characteristics, treatment efficiency, and groundwater responses. The treatment unit effectively removed pesticides and substantially reduced suspended solids, while stormwater nitrate concentrations were consistently lower than those in groundwater, indicating dilution potential during recharge. The pilot demonstrates that rural stormwater can serve as a reliable MAR source under variable hydrological conditions. The integrated design and monitoring concept provides a transferable framework for similar agricultural regions and supports future calibration of site-scale hydrogeological and reactive transport models.

title: Mechanisms of groundwater circulation driven by coal mining in arid western China: Hydrogeochemical and stable isotope evidence

Kreamer
A lumped model with vadose filtering and quadratic drainage for daily groundwater recharge estimation
abstract: Abstract Quantifying groundwater recharge at a daily temporal resolution is difficult when inputs are sparse. This research presents a simple lumped model that links precipitation to groundwater levels by (1) routing rainfall through a first-order exponential vadose filter followed by an explicit discrete delay, and (2) representing lateral drainage with a nonlinear (quadratic) outflow law. The saturated storage is tracked with specific yield ( S y ), and the model advances at a daily time step, producing time series of recharge, head, and lateral flow. The approach was tested with daily precipitation data from nearby rainfall stations and groundwater levels from four wells in the Bauru Aquifer System (BAS, Brazil). The model reproduces the timing and amplitude of observed hydraulic heads across seasonal cycles, capturing delayed and attenuated recharge pulses and curvilinear recessions, with a normalized root mean square error (RMSE) < 14% against observations. Relative to the water-table fluctuation (WTF) method, the mass balance explicitly accounts for concurrent lateral drainage during recharge events and for vadose delay/attenuation, explaining systematically higher, but process-consistent, recharge fractions than the WTF method. Parameter estimates are hydrologically interpretable, although equifinality requires validating fitted values against independent aquifer information. The method provides fast recharge diagnostics from long daily records without requiring daily evapotranspiration, making it suitable for basin-scale screening and trend attribution, and extensible to multistress forcing where data permit.

title: Impact of changing rainfall patterns on groundwater recharge in semi-arid dune landscapes
abstract: Abstract Climate-induced changes in rainfall patterns, particularly increases in event intensity and altered seasonal distribution, pose significant challenges for groundwater recharge and water resource management, especially in semi-arid Mediterranean environments. This study was motivated by the pronounced scarcity of long-term field data quantifying how rainfall intensity and vegetation cover interact to shape the soil water budget and diffuse recharge under natural conditions. To address this gap, a 3-year lysimeter experiment was conducted in the aeolian dune system of Doñana National Park (SW Spain), utilizing four precision weighable lysimeters of different sizes and vegetation covers (bare soil, pine canopy, and shrubland). Meteorological and hydrological variables were continuously monitored, allowing detailed partitioning of precipitation, evaporation, and drainage at high temporal resolution. The results show that a small number of high-intensity storms (> 20 mm/day) dominated annual rainfall input and were responsible for most groundwater recharge, whereas low-intensity rainfall contributed negligibly to recharge. Bare-soil lysimeters exhibited consistently high and stable recharge rates (50–55% of rainfall), while vegetated lysimeters showed much lower and more variable recharge (11–60%), with intense storms effectively bypassing interception and transpiration limits. These findings illustrate that vegetation cover critically modulates the effect of rainfall intensity on recharge, with groundwater input under vegetation potentially matching bare soil recharge when intense events are frequent. This insight has important implications for understanding and managing groundwater resources in sandy, semi-arid regions undergoing climate-driven changes in rainfall regime.

title: Assessing groundwater potential and recharge zones in the headwaters of the Blue Nile River, Ethiopia
Revisiting the hydrogeological water balance of Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain): Implications for sustainable groundwater exploitation
abstract: Abstract Balancing groundwater exploitation with ecological preservation requires robust conceptual models, particularly in karst systems where aquifer–lake interactions are complex and highly sensitive to human and climatic pressures. Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain) is a groundwater-fed karstic-tectonic system of exceptional ecological value, yet its hydrogeological functioning remains insufficiently understood. This study revisits its water balance by integrating meteorological, limnological, hydrochemical, and isotopic data into an updated hydrogeological analysis. Results indicate that regional groundwater inflow from the Banyoles–Alta Garrotxa system contributes ~11.4 × 10 6 m 3 /year, equivalent to ~54% of total inputs to the lake, while local recharge through runoff and shallow aquifers represents only ~23%. Outflows are dominated by drains (~16.2 × 10 6 m 3 /year, 77% of total) and evaporation (~2.3 × 10 6 m 3 /year 11%). The refined conceptual model highlights the predominance of upward vertical flows from confined limestone aquifers through a karstified gypsum formation, which govern lake recharge and explain the observed sulphate enrichment of lake water. This framework challenges conventional interpretations that treat the lake surface as a constant-head boundary, instead recognizing it as a dynamic hydrogeological unit controlled by potentiometric head of the aquifer beneath, which has seldom been addressed in the hydrogeological literature. By clarifying the processes sustaining Banyoles Lake hydrogeology, this report provides a novel conceptual framework essential for sustainable groundwater governance under increasing climatic stress.

title: Water–rock interaction controls on hydrogeochemical evolution of alluvial groundwater in high-altitude alpine regions of China

Evaluating the interaction between karst and evaporite formations to identify the origin and mechanism of groundwater salinization
Educating for groundwater sustainability in a changing world: A joint, applied, interdisciplinary and inclusive postgraduate approach
abstract: Abstract Safeguarding groundwater, a vital resource in adaptation to global change, yet increasingly under pressure, requires robust knowledge and capacity. While strong foundations in hydrogeology remain indispensable, there is a clear need for joint, interdisciplinary and applied groundwater education at the postgraduate level to address the complex and multifaceted nature of groundwater science. Building on these arguments, the Joint Master’s Programme Groundwater and Global Change was successfully launched a decade ago. This essay presents the rationale behind this approach.

title: Participatory groundwater management in peri-urban areas with informal water markets: Insights from a socio-hydrogeological case study in Jaipur, India
abstract: Abstract In many peri-urban areas of the Global South, formal water supply systems are insufficient. This gap is largely filled by a diverse informal water market and widespread informal water use, both of which depend heavily on groundwater. Peri-urban low-income communities are particularly affected. Research in such contexts requires participatory and interdisciplinary approaches. This paper aims to equip hydrogeologists with the knowledge needed to implement participatory management, thereby fostering deeper engagement with participatory methodologies and strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration. The findings are also intended to support NGOs in planning more comprehensive water projects by integrating hydrogeological considerations. Two low-income communities in peri-urban Jaipur, India, representing different hydrogeological, infrastructural, and socio-cultural conditions, were selected as study areas in cooperation with a local NGO. The study comprised four components: initial socio-hydrogeological assessments to gain baseline information; water workshops to raise awareness and exchange knowledge on groundwater; the recruitment and training of women assistants to teach a small group more advanced groundwater-related skills; and finally, the production of films to disseminate the results. The research demonstrated that the applied methods generated relevant insights and enabled the implementation of a participatory approach. However, future studies should engage more thoroughly with the literature on participatory methodologies, ideally in collaboration with social scientists experienced in such approaches. Despite these limitations, the study contributes to the growing field of participatory and socio-hydrogeological research and shows that these approaches can enhance groundwater awareness among local communities and NGOs while sensitizing hydrogeologists to the importance of inter- and transdisciplinary work.

title: 25 years of PEST courses: A few reflections
Hydrogeology education in Germany: Did things develop since 2001?
abstract: Abstract The essay describes the development of hydrogeology education in German universities over the past 25 years, based on the author’s own experience and an informal poll among German-speaking hydrogeology lecturers. Hydrogeology is an integral part of geoscience degree programmes in Germany, where it is increasingly recognized as an indispensable player in interdisciplinary efforts to solve societal, environmental and health-related problems. This is reflected by faculty positions in Germany shifting towards a focus on (bio) geochemistry and away from groundwater quantity-focused research.

title: Reflections on hydrogeology education and lifelong learning
abstract: Abstract There is a strong global demand for hydrogeological expertise, yet educational opportunities for hydrogeologists are not so widely available. Taught masters programmes can provide hydrogeologists with the fundamentals of groundwater science and many of its wider applications. Groundwater engineering (including well design, construction and pumping systems) should feature more strongly in such hydrogeology courses. Scientific associations such as the International Association of Hydrogeologists (IAH) can make a significant contribution to lifelong learning through training courses, mentoring and educational materials.

title: A simulation-surrogate-optimization model for inversion of groundwater contamination source characteristics in fractured aquifers
The use of pumping for hydraulic characterisation of dykes
abstract: Abstract Faults and dykes can control groundwater flow, acting as barriers, conduits, or composite conduit–barrier systems. This study investigates dyke hydraulic behaviour using numerical modelling of field-scale pumping tests at two sites in Western Australia, supported by a uniquely detailed hydrogeological dataset. At each site, pumping tests were conducted across dykes that impeded groundwater flow, as evidenced by asymmetric drawdown cones and delayed responses in observation wells situated across the dyke from the pumping well. High-resolution three-dimensional geological frameworks were developed, and transient groundwater flow models were calibrated using automated inversion with and without spatially variable parameterisation (pilot points) to represent heterogeneity. In all calibrated models, the horizontal hydraulic conductivity ( K h ) of dykes was estimated to be one to eight orders of magnitude lower than that of the surrounding formations. Representation of dykes in the model produced the largest improvement in model fit at both sites, reducing the parameterisation objective function by one to two orders of magnitude relative to model parameterisations without dykes. Further improvements in model fit were achieved by introducing heterogeneity into formations, dykes or both. Although including formation heterogeneity reduced posterior uncertainty in dyke K h estimates, posterior variance patterns revealed that, in some locations, calibration preferentially adjusted K h in formations adjacent to dykes rather than within the dykes. Dyke K h was tightly constrained in areas with available field data and observable drawdown. These findings demonstrate the importance of representing structural features when interpreting pumping-test responses in structurally complex groundwater systems.

title: Divergent transport behaviors of fluorescent nanoparticles versus sodium fluorescein in fractured media
Integrated conceptual–numerical modeling of high-flux groundwater seepage during deep excavation on coastal reclaimed land
abstract: Abstract High-flux groundwater seepage occurred during deep excavation at a landfill construction site on coastal reclaimed land in South Korea. In this study, the cause of the groundwater seepage was analyzed using integrated conceptual and numerical modeling techniques. Ten candidate hydrogeological conceptual models (HCMs) were developed by combining various configurations of subsurface hydrogeological units (HGUs) and different magnitudes of the seepage phenomenon. Numerical groundwater models, based on these HCMs, were built using a three-dimensional stratigraphic model derived from borehole data to simulate the distribution of HGUs and groundwater seepage. Among the numerical models, the one that best reproduced the observed water levels, seepage, and drawdown was selected and further refined through model calibration. The final HCM provided insights into the site’s hydrogeological system and enabled a forensic interpretation of the groundwater seepage mechanism. The high-flux groundwater discharge was attributed to a groundwater upwelling phenomenon that hydraulically connects deep permeable media to the excavation surface. Weathered bedrock located approximately 22 m below the ground surface were found to be sufficiently permeable to serve as a source layer for the seepage. Through case studies of additional excavation and drainage strategies, the integrated conceptual–numerical modeling approach demonstrated its potential as a reliable predictive tool for designing response strategies to groundwater seepage. This approach also facilitates interdisciplinary communication and supports adaptive site management throughout the project lifecycle, highlighting its practical engineering relevance.

title: Hydrochemical and sedimentary effects on hydrogeological properties following mine-water reinjection into low-permeability sandstone aquifers
Radon (222Rn) activation processes in shallow aquifers in fractured crystalline rocks: A model constrained by long-term monitoring and tracer tests
abstract: Abstract Sixteen years of monitoring at St. Vojtěch Springs (Giant Mountains, Czech Republic) form the basis for a calibrated model explaining variations in 222 Rn activity in crystalline aquifers. The model enables estimation of activation zone length (fractures rich in parent radioisotopes) and saturated 222 Rn activity. Eleven springs with an activation zone of primary uranium mineralization in orthogneiss at the contact with dolomite have 222 Rn activities in the range of 185–5469 Bq L −1 , which varies with flow rate. The objective of this study was to quantify the relationship between flow velocity and 222 Rn activity using tracer data and long-term observations. An exponential mathematical model was calibrated at one of the springs with an average flow velocity of 0.44 m h −1 , the saturated 222 Rn activity was 5160 Bq L −1 , and the length of the activation zone was 44 m; these parameters determine 222 Rn activity at each flow rate point. Subsequently, the model was expanded to include various lengths of activation zones and decay zones in which 222 Rn activity decreases due to missing parent isotopes. In fractured, crystalline bedrock aquifers where 222 Rn activity and flow rate relationships are established across various flow conditions, this model provides robust analytical capabilities. With sufficient monitoring data, the lengths of both the activation and the decay zone can be estimated. Without tracer tests, the model can still be applied, estimating the effective pore volumes of both zones instead of their lengths. This research advances the fundamental understanding of radon transport mechanisms in fractured crystalline bedrock aquifer systems.

title: Groundwater-based water services as complex socio-hydrogeological systems: insights from Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
abstract: Abstract Groundwater systems are critical to global water security, yet the complex interactions between household coping strategies, resource sustainability, and climate change remain difficult to govern. This study applies qualitative systems mapping to characterise socio-hydrogeological dynamics in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta, a region currently facing intensifying saline intrusion and rapid land-use change. Drawing on a household survey ( n = 404) and in-depth interviews ( n = 25) in Sóc Trăng and Trà Vinh provinces, three critical system interactions were identified: (1) climate variability and household adaptation intensify groundwater system pressures, (2) policy-practice gaps undermine effective management of a multisource water system, and (3) social vulnerability and water stress constrain resilience. Together, these interactions illustrate how household behaviours, institutional arrangements, and resource conditions are interconnected in ways that shape system behaviour. These findings advance socio-hydrogeological frameworks by using systems mapping to make visible the relationships and interactions that influence groundwater-based water services. The research offers evidence for policymakers, suggesting that inclusive, climate-resilient service delivery depends on integrating actual household water behaviours into planning and groundwater governance, moving beyond a singular focus on piped supply.

title: Comparative analysis of lineament mapping using Sentinel-1A, Landsat 8 OLI, and ALOS PALSAR for hydrogeological applications in the Moroccan Central Massif
Risk assessment of tunnelling-induced hydrogeological interference on springs using a machine learning approach
abstract: Abstract Tunnel excavation through mountain ranges can alter groundwater regimes, affecting spring discharge and dependent ecosystems. Anticipating these interferences is essential for environmental risk management, cost–benefit analysis, and effective mitigation planning. Conventional assessment methods are largely parametric, not physically based, and heavily dependent on expert judgment, introducing subjectivity and uncertainty. This study proposes a data-driven approach based on machine learning (ML), specifically a Random Forest (RF) model, to evaluate hydrogeological risk and spring vulnerability during the preliminary design phase of tunnels. The method exploits geological information typically available in early stages and is validated using two well-documented Italian case studies: The Bologna–Florence high-speed railway line, excavated in fractured sedimentary formations of the Northern Apennines, and the Gran Sasso highway tunnels, driven in karstified carbonate rocks of the Central Apennines. Both datasets are published, hydrogeologically validated, and supported by detailed pre- and post-excavation monitoring, ensuring robustness and consistency. The ML framework demonstrates strong predictive performance across standard classification metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the curve (AUC). While it employs input parameters comparable to those of parametric methods such as the drawdown hazard index (DHI), it differs by deriving parameter weights directly from data. Moreover, the use of Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values enhances interpretability, mitigates black-box behaviour, and allows expert knowledge to be effectively integrated. The innovation, therefore, lies in offering a transferable and reproducible tool to support early-stage tunnelling decisions, representing a clear improvement over traditional qualitative or semi-quantitative approaches.

title: Quantitative evaluation on non-Darcian flow and non-Fickian transport: Visualization experiments on fracture networks
Effect of flow velocity and contact area on solute transport in rock fractures
Karst hydraulic scale effect in confined and unconfined zones of the Neoproterozoic Sete Lagoas Karst Aquifer System (Brazil)
abstract: Résumé L'effet d'échelle de la perméabilité karstique décrit la variation des paramètres hydrauliques mesurés à différentes échelles spatiales, en réponse à l'hétérogénéité et à la structure de porosité complexe des aquifères karstiques. À Sete Lagoas (État du Minas Gerais, Brésil), le système aquifère karstique néoprotérozoïque de Sete Lagoas (SLKAS) comprend des zones captives et libres. La compréhension de cet effet d'échelle sous différentes conditions hydrostatiques est essentielle pour affiner les modèles conceptuels d'écoulement, l'estimation des paramètres et la gestion des eaux souterraines dans de tels systèmes hétérogènes. Cet article intègre des investigations en laboratoire et sur le terrain, combinant des essais de perméamétrie, des essais à charge variable avec injection instantanée, des essais de pompage de longue durée et des analyses régionales avec délimitation de la zone d’alimentation, afin d'estimer la perméabilité, la conductivité hydraulique et la transmissivité à quatre échelles spatiales : matrice (< 10⁻² m), petite échelle (10⁻²– 10 0 m), puits (10 0 –10³ m) et régionale (> 10³ m). Les résultats montrent une augmentation de la perméabilité de quatre à six ordres de grandeur entre la matrice et la petite échelle, suivie d'une diminution à l'échelle du puits et d'une nouvelle augmentation à l'échelle régionale. Ce modèle non linéaire à plusieurs échelles diffère des systèmes karstiques récents classiques, où la perméabilité augmente généralement de façon progressive avec l'échelle. La partie captive du SLKAS présente des valeurs de perméabilité inférieures d'un à deux ordres de grandeur à celles de la zone libre, reflétant une karstification et une connectivité réduites sous l'influence de facteurs tectono-structuraux et stratigraphiques. Ces résultats offrent une nouvelle approche multi-échelle intégrant les méthodes de laboratoire et de terrain pour quantifier les effets d'échelle hydraulique sous différentes conditions de pression hydrostatique, et les comparent à ceux observés dans des systèmes karstiques plus récents.

title: Community views on hydrogeology education: A global perspective from 2024
abstract: Abstract Groundwater is the Earth’s largest reservoir of available freshwater. As climate change and increasing anthropogenic pressures continue to affect its availability and quality, the discipline of hydrogeology is evolving rapidly. Training enough professionals capable of understanding and managing groundwater resources effectively is therefore more critical than ever. However, there is a perceived global shortage of adequately trained hydrogeologists—raising concerns about society’s capacity to address future groundwater-related challenges. To obtain quantitative data regarding this perception and to evaluate the current state of hydrogeology education and workforce dynamics more generally, a global survey was conducted of hydrogeology professionals, recent graduates, and current students. Five hundred seventy-three individuals from 82 countries responded, providing contemporary insights into the discipline’s demographics, education pathways, and perceived training gaps. Here, a synthesis of the key findings is presented—offering a snapshot of current trends and challenges in hydrogeology education from various perspectives. Notable findings include the observations that: (i) female hydrogeologists remain underrepresented; (ii) some countries act as major “exporters” or “importers” of hydrogeologists; (iii) many practitioners consider new graduates to be insufficiently prepared; (iv) most hydrogeological work is conducted by those without formal education in the field; and (v) hydrogeology is expected to contribute to a growing range of challenges, calling for both disciplinary depth and interdisciplinary breadth in curricula. These findings highlight a need for better alignment between academic training and professional demands. The full dataset is openly shared, offering a resource for educators, researchers, and policymakers to support training and engagement with global water issues.
